title: 中美双IND获批！现货型细胞疗法破解眼科治疗困局
summary: 2026年9月7日，睿健毅联医药自研眼科细胞治疗产品NouvSight001正式获得中美双临床许可（IND），标志着其在平台型Biotech全球化进程中取得重大突破。该进展不仅体现了企业从单一产品到技术体系出海的实力跃升，更关键的是为视网膜色素变性（RP）治疗带来新希望。RP作为常见遗传性眼底退行性疾病，全球患者达150万，但因现有唯一获批基因疗法Luxturna仅适用于极少数特定基因突变人群，导...
full_content:
细胞治疗赛道的惊喜，从来都层出不穷。

 

就在昨天（2026年9月7日），国内细胞治疗企业睿健毅联医药科技有限公司（以下简称“睿健”），甩出了一个含金量极高的行业里程碑：自研眼科细胞治疗产品NouvSight001，正式拿下中美双临床许可（双IND）。

 

可能很多人看惯了各类新药获批、临床获批的资讯，觉得这只是又一次常规管线进展。

 

但深耕医疗创新赛道多年，我想说，这次的突破完全不一样。

 

它不是一次简单的产品出海，而是彻底打破了传统眼科基因疗法的局限，给上百万视网膜色素变性（RP）患者，打开了一条全新的治疗路径。

 

过去几年，睿健从帕金森管线NouvNeu001，到多系统萎缩NouvNeu004，再到眼科NouvSight001，接连多个管线拿下中美临床批件，走出了一条平台型Biotech的成长路径，实现了从单一产品出海到整套技术体系全球化的硬核实力跃升。

 

1、百万患者无药可医，眼科治疗长期陷入“小众困局”


 

先和大家聊一个残酷的现实。

 

视网膜色素变性（Retinitis Pigmentosa, RP），是常见的遗传性眼底退行性疾病之一，全球患者有150万人。

 

这个病的折磨，是循序渐进、慢慢摧毁光明的。

 

早期只是夜里看不清、夜盲频发；随着病情发展，周边视野不断缺损，眼底的感光细胞会持续凋亡、萎缩；到了中晚期，绝大多数患者会视力骤降，最终彻底失明。

 

更让人无力的是，面对这场缓慢的“失明进程”，临床上几乎没有有效的根治手段。

 

很多人以为基因疗法普及后，这类眼病就有救了。但真实的临床现状，远比大众认知的残酷。

 

目前全球唯一获批的RP基因疗法只有Luxturna，但它的适用人群极其狭窄，仅针对携带双等位RPE65基因突变的患者。

 

这个群体，在所有视网膜色素变性患者中，占比微乎其微。

 

换句话说，90%以上的患者，都没有匹配的基因突变靶点，彻底被基因疗法“拒之门外”。

 

长久以来，这部分患者只能靠维生素A制剂、营养调理、低视力康复这些保守手段勉强维持。这些方式算不上治疗，更像是“延缓拖延”，根本挡不住感光细胞凋亡的进程，更逆转不了视力衰退的结局。

 


 

为什么基因疗法救不了大部分患者？核心逻辑的局限性，从根源上就注定了。

 

基因疗法的本质，是“补缺陷”：患者哪个基因坏了，就外源补充正常基因，修复病灶。这就意味着，它必须精准匹配基因突变类型，容错率极低。

 

而睿健这次的核心突破，就是彻底跳出了这套受限逻辑。

 

NouvSight001作为一款通用现货型光感受器细胞治疗产品，走的是完全不同的“替换重生”路线。

 

它不需要筛查患者的基因突变，不挑基因型，核心原理简单直白：直接移植健康、有功能的光感受器前体细胞，替换掉眼底已经凋亡、坏死的感光神经元。

 

这和传统眼科治疗形成了本质区别。

 

以往的视网膜色素上皮（Retinal Pigment Epithelium，RPE）细胞产品、药物干预，都是“保护残存细胞”，尽量延缓损伤；而NouvSight001是“重建细胞功能”，直接补齐眼底丢失的感光能力。

 

除此之外，这款产品还有两个非常亮眼的临床优势：

 

第一，超低免疫原性，通用型现货。临床无需搭配口服免疫抑制剂，大幅降低治疗风险和患者负担；

 

第二，广谱适配性。不依赖致病基因突变，理论上可以覆盖绝大多数视网膜色素变性患者。

 

值得一提的是，它还是国内CDE受理的首个化学诱导来源的光感受器前体细胞产品。放眼全球，同赛道竞品仅有拜耳旗下的OpCT‑001。而依托睿健独创的“AI+化学诱导”平台，这款产品拥有极强的差异化技术优势。

 

此次中美同步开启临床，核心目的就是验证安全性、耐受性，同时捕捉初步疗效信号。

 

如果临床顺利推进，困扰行业多年的“基因分型受限、多数患者无药可医”的困局，将被彻底打破。

 

另外值得关注的是，NouvSight001国内Ⅰ/Ⅲ期临床研究，由北京协和医院睢瑞芳教授牵头。作为国内遗传性视网膜疾病领域的领军团队，睢瑞芳教授课题组深耕该领域三十余年，沉淀近万例遗传性视网膜变性家系样本，完成五千余例患者的基因解析，掌握了中国人群视网膜色素变性真实突变谱。

 

睢瑞芳教授团队搭建了完整的眼遗传病临床评估体系，拥有多项眼科基因治疗first‑in‑human临床研究实操经验，擅长视网膜结构与视功能的精细化终点评估。

 

对于光感受器细胞移植疗法而言，如何客观判断移植细胞是否存活、视网膜功能能否实现重建，是临床试验的核心难点，而这套评估能力恰恰是试验能否读出有效信号的关键保障。依托扎实的国际学术积淀，团队也能够更好地配合中美两地研究设计，为中美联合临床方案的协同提供有力支撑。

 

更值得期待的是，RP只是它的首个适应症。

 

放眼全球市场，糖尿病视网膜病变、年龄相关性黄斑变性，都是过亿级的庞大患者群体。目前临床主流的抗VEGF药物、激光治疗，只能抑制新生血管、延缓病情，无法修复已经坏死的神经元，挽回丢失的视力。

 

而NouvSight001的细胞重建机制，理论上可以覆盖所有视网膜变性、视网膜损伤导致的视力损伤，未来的临床和商业想象空间，更加广阔。

 

3、真正的核心壁垒：不是单品突破，是平台体系的全球化胜利


 

很多人只看到了NouvSight001的双IND成果，但在我看来，产品获批临床只是结果，真正的核心底气，是睿健成型的平台化能力。

 

当下细胞治疗行业，很多企业的模式是“一个技术、一款产品、一次出海”，属于单品突围。

 

而睿健已经完成了迭代，从“单品全球化”，跃迁为“一套平台、多线产出、全球同步开发”的体系化全球化模式。

 

支撑这一切的，正是其自主研发的AI+化学诱导底层技术平台。

 

这套体系最厉害的地方，就是避开了基因编辑、病毒载体的安全隐患，全程依靠小分子化合物调控细胞基因表达，完成iPSC细胞的定向分化。

 

简单拆解它的核心逻辑：AI高通量筛选核心靶点与化合物组合，纯化学诱导精准重塑细胞功能，最终把复杂、不稳定的细胞分化过程，变成了可标准化、可规模化、可复刻的工业化生产流程。

 

这恰好击中了细胞治疗行业的最大痛点：批次不稳定、生产成本高、难以规模化、跨适应症复用难。

 

成熟的平台能力，从来都不是单一赋能。

 

这套技术底座，已经在多条重磅管线中得到验证：

 

帕金森管线NouvNeu001，拿下FDA快速通道+再生医学先进疗法双认定，中美Ⅱ期临床稳步推进；

 

多系统萎缩管线NouvNeu004，实现中美双报双批，是全球首个进入临床的iPSC来源MSA治疗产品；

 

如今NouvSight001中美临床落地，正式把这套成熟技术，延伸到了眼科退行性疾病赛道。

 

从神经退行性疾病，到眼科眼底疾病，同一套底层技术，持续输出全球合规的创新管线，这就是平台型企业的核心壁垒。

 

 

拿到中美双IND只是纸面结果，现货型细胞治疗想要真正落地全球临床，要跨过监管合规、CMC生产、跨境供应链、多中心临床运营等一连串现实门槛，考验企业完整的综合执行力。

 

细胞药物不同于普通小分子药物，现货型iPSC细胞产品对生产质控要求极高。

 

而睿健最难得的一点，就是面向NMPA与FDA两套监管标准，搭建了统一的CMC与质量体系。

 

依托这套体系，公司建立了标准化的现货型细胞产品生产平台，破解细胞药物规模化生产的行业痛点。这也是多条管线能够实现中美双报的重要基础。

 

在此之上，睿健搭建起覆盖中美两地的供应链体系，打造跨境冷链物流能力，保障现货细胞制剂可以同时供给中国、美国不同临床中心，解决细胞药物运输、投递的现实难题。

 

在临床端，睿健已经搭建中美两地临床中心执行网络。前期NouvNeu001、NouvNeu004的中美申报、临床推进，已经积累了和两国监管机构沟通、设计全球临床方案的成熟经验。这些经验可以复用到NouvSight001项目之上。

 

睿健CFO阮添士曾表示，全球化并不是睿健在单一产品上的尝试，而是从公司创立之初就嵌入研发体系的长期战略。“同一底层技术平台能够持续产出符合全球开发标准的候选产品，意味着单位管线的开发路径与监管路径具备可复制性。”未来睿健还将继续推进核心管线的中美临床开发，积极探索全球多中心研究和国际商业合作机会。

 

在细胞治疗领域，前沿创新药的全球竞争，本质是技术、监管、产业化与团队执行力的全方位较量。不少企业有创新技术，却很难把产品同步推到中美两地临床阶段。

 

从帕金森到多系统萎缩，再到眼科的视网膜色素变性，我们看到睿健接连多个管线完成中美双报双批，正是这套全球化执行体系的直接体现。

 

在视网膜色素变性治疗领域，基因疗法打开了一扇窗口，但只能惠及小部分携带特定突变的患者。NouvSight001代表的现货型细胞替代疗法，和基因疗法并非替代关系，二者互为补充，一起扩充遗传性视网膜疾病的治疗工具箱。

 

对于产业而言，NouvSight001更大的意义，在于完成对这套平台模式的验证：依托同一套 “AI+化学诱导” 底层技术能力，企业可以面向神经、眼科等多个衰老相关退行性疾病，持续输出可全球同步开发的候选产品，推动更多具备临床转化价值与规模化商业潜力的细胞治疗产品走向全球开发。

title: 442款创新医疗器械产品，有多少销售额能过亿？
summary: 截至2026年8月，累计442款创新医疗器械通过“绿色通道”获批，近三年占比近半，年均复合增长率达48%。尽管审批加速，但高门槛与高昂临床成本使得商业化成功并非必然。动脉网分析指出，获批仅是起点，赛道选择、持续迭代及全球化与集采能力才是实现销售额破亿的关键。从赛道分布看，心血管\u002F介入以105款居首，放疗\u002F肿瘤与影像设备紧随其后，手术机器人正迎来产品井喷拐点。地域上，北京、上海、...
full_content:
2014年，当首款产品通过创新医疗器械特别审查程序（“绿色通道”）获批时，这条通道还是一条窄路。十余年后的今天，它已演变为一条奔涌的河流。

 

截至2026年8月，累计已有442款产品、306家企业拿到这张“创新通行证”。从首批1款到2025年的76款，年均复合增长率高达48%；尤其近三年（2023–2025），合计202款产品获批，几乎占据了总量的半壁江山。2026年仅前八个月，又有51款产品闯关成功，全年有望再度刷新纪录。

 

通过创新医疗器械审批的产品越来越多，迈过商业化大关实现销售额破亿的产品有多少？

 

创新医疗器械特别审查程序的准入门槛高，递交申请需要满足国内同品种首个、显著的临床价值、拥有发明专利等基本条件，后续还需要更大的临床成本投入，产品风险高、临床复杂的三类创新医疗器械产品临床成本就高达千万，人工心脏就是典型。

 

历经严苛审批获批的创新医疗器械，是否等同于商业化的成功？

 

动脉网整理了2014年以来获批的创新医疗器械以及近五年有公开销售数据的创新医疗器械，透过审批数字看本质：在审批大潮中哪些创新医疗器械真正实现转换为商业化的成功？

 

获批是创新的起点，而非商业化的终点。赛道选择决定天花板，持续迭代决定生命力，全球化与集采能力决定规模化速度。对于创新医疗器械企业而言，注册证只是第一张门票，将临床价值转化为可持续的商业价值，才是真正的终局考验。


数据截止2026年8月



从创新医疗器械获批赛道分布来看，心血管/介入以105款获批创新医疗器械位列首位，血管介入是国内医疗器械创新的成熟赛道，多个细分领域的拓展、已获批产品的持续迭代是血管介入赛道创新勃发的原因。

 

放疗/肿瘤（71款）与影像/成像设备（64款）两大赛道分列二、三位。这两大领域创新由国产替代浪潮、大型医疗设备配置计划扩容，以及质子治疗系统、光子计数CT、7T高场磁共振成像系统等新一代产品推出拉动。

 

手术机器人/导航以19款、占比4.3%的数据位列第五，这一赛道正经历从概念验证到产品井喷的拐点，临床渗透率加速提升。近三年的获批数量呈加速态势，腔镜、骨科、血管介入等多条产品线同步开花。

 


国内已获批创新医疗器械细分领域分布

 

从获批创新医疗器械产品分布地域来看，北京87款、上海85款、江苏65款、广东60款、浙江35款，五省市合计约占获批创新医疗器械产品的75.1%。北京偏神经调控、血管介入赛道（品驰医疗一家就有19款）、上海偏微创系与影像、江苏偏苏州工业园区器械集群、广东偏深圳植介入与IVD。


 

从获批企业分布来看，国内获批的创新医疗器械中，北京品驰医疗设备以19张证登顶，神经调控（脑深部电刺激/脊髓/骶神经）领域品驰医疗占据主导地位。平台型头部企业在持创新医疗器械证方面更具优势，联影医疗、微创电生理、先健科技、美敦力等头部企业在多个领域带来创新医疗器械产品。

 

 

如果说创新药的死亡谷是在研发阶段，那么创新医疗器械的死亡谷则是在商业化阶段。

 

获批只是入场券。把注册证换成真金白银的营收，中间隔着一条并不平坦的商业化之路。

 

动脉网（微信号：vcbeat）复盘整理了近五年已公开销售额的创新医疗器械商业化情况，试图从已获批数据中解答创新医疗器械从获批到破亿要多久？

 

在近五年获批的343个创新医疗器械产品中，有19个产品公布了获批上市后的销售额或装机量，其中10个产品销售额过亿。受限于企业信息披露，已公开销售数据的样本量较小（19/343），以下分析更适用于已跨过商业化门槛的产品。

 

部分赛道在商业化方面具备先天优势，耗材领域TAVRTAVR（经导管主动脉瓣置换术）、CGM（动态血糖监测）、密网支架、IVUS（血管内超声）、颅内药物洗脱支架系统等创新医疗器械在获批两年后销售额破亿元。

 

大型医用设备领域也有产品表现出色，根据已披露销售额数据的产品信息，质子治疗系统、腔镜手术机器人两类产品凭借高价值、高装机量的特点实现获批两年内销售额超过亿元。


  

复盘近1–2年内销售额突破亿元的高值耗材产品——TAVR、密网支架、CGM、IVUS等——可以发现，其商业化成功并非单点突破，而是满足多维度条件。我们将其归纳为以下五个核心维度：

 

1.选择处于渗透率快速提升期的赛道。

成功的创新器械往往切入一个临床旧方案存在明显瓶颈、新技术刚获批上市的赛道。TAVR之于外科开胸换瓣、CGM之于指尖采血、PFA之于传统射频消融，均符合这一特征。

从市场容量角度看，天花板由赛道决定，而非由排名决定。大市场赛道中，即便排名第三的产品也有望实现亿元销售；而小众赛道即便占据绝对统治地位，商业化天花板依然受限。因此，赛道本身的可及患者群体规模与渗透率提升斜率，是决定商业化速度的首要变量。

 

2.持续迭代实现性能领先

获批仅是拿到入场券。复盘可见，商业化表现优异的产品在上市后普遍进入了快速迭代周期，从早期国产替代逐步演进至性能超越进口。缺乏持续迭代能力的产品，通常在2–3年内即被后来者追平，丧失先发红利。

 

以赛诺医疗颅内药物洗脱支架为例：首款NOVA系列获批后，公司持续推出自膨式颅内药物洗脱支架等迭代产品，通过产品矩阵化而非单品依赖，构建了竞争壁垒并稳固市场份额。

 

3．先发优势：将时间窗口转化为战略资产

“首个获批”或“独家适应症”在商业化早期具有显著的杠杆效应。全球首款颅内狭窄专用药物洗脱支架（NOVA）、国内首款TAVR产品等案例表明，首发产品可以快速抢占临床教育的话语权，抢先铺设渠道，掌握定价主动权。先发者在此期间建立的品牌认知和临床数据积累，构成后来者难以逾越的护城河。

 

4.全球化布局：构建第二增长曲线与品牌背书

海外市场已成为国产企业的必选项和增量来源，敢于出海不仅带来收入，更重要的是，海外商业化不仅贡献收入，还能通过国际市场的品牌背书反哺国内准入与临床信任。


一个反直觉的事实是，国内高精尖的医疗设备正在快速打通出海通道，例如手术机器人，精锋医疗2025年全球累计订单119台中海外装机54台、占比过半；微创机器人图迈全球商业化订单突破220台。


另一款全球只有少数企业能研发的产品人工心脏，国产也实现了出海，同心医疗2025年营收2.13亿元，其中，面向全球市场的升级版本BrioVAD产品及配件，在2025年贡献了1.07亿元营收，较2024年增长10倍，占公司总收入的50.51%。



5.集采驾驭：以价换量的规模化博弈能力

集采也可以大幅提升产品渗透率。密网支架、IVUS等国产产品在获批后迅速借助集采实现国产份额跃升。集采可以帮助新进入者快速扩大市场份额，但这背后也是需要企业拥有过硬的质量控制、成本管控能力、丰富的产品矩阵，以及对集采规则的深度理解。才能真正以价换量。

 

上述五个维度并非孤立存在，而是相互强化的有机整体：赛道决定天花板，迭代决定生命力，先发决定窗口期，出海决定安全边际，集采决定规模化速度。满足的条件越多，产品从获批到过亿的转化概率越高。对于创新医疗器械企业而言，单一维度的领先不足以保证商业化成功，唯有在多维度上形成系统能力，才能在激烈的行业竞争中脱颖而出。

 

 

与TAVR、CGM等1–2年内即突破亿元销售额的产品形成鲜明对照，部分创新器械赛道的商业化周期被显著拉长，平均需要4年以上才能实现亿元级销售突破。这类赛道通常具备三个共性特征：单价高企、医生学习曲线陡峭、医保覆盖滞后。其商业化受阻的根源，可归结为以下三重瓶颈：

 

1.支付端缺位：临床价值无法完成商业闭环

缺乏独立的医疗服务价格条目和医保支付编码，是创新器械商业化的首要堵点。医院即便认可技术的临床价值，也因无收费依据和报销通道而采购动力不足。此时，再充分的临床证据也难以转化为可持续的商业回报。这一点在智能辅助影像软件类产品中表现突出。

 

2.缺乏资源投入，获批即退市

商业化是一场资源持续追加的长跑，而非获批即终点。西门子医疗旗下CorPath GRX血管介入机器人的案例颇具警示意义：该产品于2023年6月刚在中国获批冠脉适应症，旋即被集团战略性放弃，退出中国冠脉市场。全球巨头的资源腾挪深刻提醒行业：产品获批仅是商业化的必要条件，绝非充分条件。当企业战略重心转移或资源重新配置时，即便已获批的创新产品也可能面临上市即边缘化的困境。

 

3.市场培育与渠道能力的双重考验

部分新兴品类面临单品天花板低与渠道能力不足的叠加约束。临床认知尚在培育期，市场容量有限，市场参与者不多，反而导致先发者往往需独自承担高昂的市场教育成本。在缺乏成熟渠道网络和规模化推广能力的情况下，即便是技术领先的产品，也难以快速打开市场。

 

获批是创新的起点，而非商业化的终点。赛道选择决定天花板，持续迭代决定生命力，全球化与集采能力决定规模化速度。对于创新医疗器械企业而言，注册证只是第一张门票，将临床价值转化为可持续的商业价值，才是真正的终局考验。

title: OpenAI发布GPT-6 Astra模型，增强医疗行业特性与网络安全功能
full_content:
来源：HIT专家网       编译：小虫

OpenAI已向特定的机构用户发布了GPT-6 Astra——并表示它将很快通过OpenAI API、Microsoft Azure和AWS Bedrock提供给相关用户。

该公司表示，这版最新的模型在护理咨询、医疗文档和医学研究等领域，超越了以前的模型和竞争对手的模型测试基准，而且它还可以通过安全代码审查和补丁来帮助网络安全防御。

Astra或GPT 6.0旨在处理自主任务，并提供卓越的编码和安全功能。

该公司表示，GPT 5.6（称为Sol）曾在对医疗用途的响应基准评估——护理咨询、医疗文档和研究等方面取得了最高分，这是来自Anthropic和谷歌的Gemini 3.8 Flash的三个最新Claude模型。而在最低开销环境下，Astra已经超过了Sol的最佳得分，同时API成本降低了约53%。

虽然Astra正在启动代码审查和修补能力，但OpenAI表示，它暂时阻止了高级任务，例如编写测试安全缺陷的代码。Astra将拒绝执行更先进的网络安全任务，例如为漏洞创建概念验证漏洞。

不过，通过该公司网络防御堆栈OpenAI Daybreak提供的更新，将帮助网络安全团队获得恶意软件分析、检测工程等功能。

2025年12月，OpenAI表示，医疗行业是最快的人工智能采用者之一，不仅在孤立的试点中部署，而且在自定义模型和工作流程自动化中部署。

2026年初，OpenAI推出了ChatGPT for Healthcare，AdventHealth、Baylor Scott & White、Boston Children’s、Cedars-Sinai和HCA Healthcare等多家医疗机构是其早期用户。

紧接着是ChatGPT for Clinicians，它借助OpenAI的GPT-5.4模型来引用源自医疗领域的答案，并帮助医疗机构制作文档，助力其科研。

本周，该公司宣布，通过Epic Systems的电子健康记录数据插件和OpenAI的医疗保健公共数据插件，医疗机构可以将其数据接入ChatGPT。这些系统集成工作，使得临床医生能够在组合工作区评估患者背景、医疗证据和人口健康数据。

虽然OpenAI表示，医生和模型的对话不会用于训练公司的人工智能模型，但生命科学行业咨询专家们建议，医疗机构在应用该公司临床人工智能工具时，要认识到这些新工具相关的风险，并采取相应的措施保护医疗机构和医护人员。

上个月，OpenAI短暂暂停了新模型的培训，因为网络安全问题，该公司的700个自主代理在Hugging Face上攻击了Hugging Face——这是一个用于构建、测试和部署人工智能模型的平台。

当Hugging Face发现OpenAI代理意外访问互联网、相互通信并在无人监督的情况下协作完成任务时，一些人将其比作“潘多拉盒子”时刻。

OpenAI声称，Astra建立了一个被称为“思想链监控”的流程，通过更深入的监督，加强对潜在网络滥用和越狱的保护。新的多阶段监控设置在相关活动浮出水面后30分钟内发出警报。如果安全、安保和研究团队无法“在30分钟内最终确定标志是假阳性”，相关活动将暂停。

OpenAI表示，在Astra有限发布之前，其内部和外部测试包括红色团队攻击。

title: OpenAI expands initiatives to support journalism from classrooms to newsrooms
summary: OpenAI is expanding support for journalism with tools, training, and partnerships for students, educators, journalists, and news organizations....
full_content:
OpenAI is launching a major, multi-faceted initiative to support the journalism ecosystem with tools, training, partnerships, shared learning, and practical enablement for students, educators, journalists, and news organizations.

It begins with the next generation of reporters at CUNY’S Newmark J-School and Northwestern University’s Medill School.

For the new 2026–2027 academic year, OpenAI is collaborating closely with the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at the Newmark J-School and the Medill's Knight Lab, two of the leaders in journalism and technology in the country, and providing more than 400 ChatGPT Edu1 subscriptions to interested graduate students and faculty at those schools.

Journalism students entering classrooms this year are preparing to enter one of the most dynamic and difficult moments in the history of the news industry. AI is helping reporters, editors, and business teams analyze public records faster, translate stories for broader audiences, uncover patterns in large datasets, search archives, improve reader experiences, assist in marketing, build new products, and spend more time on the work that matters most: reporting, verification, storytelling, strengthening business, and serving communities.

For journalism schools, this creates an important opportunity. Students should graduate not only understanding how AI is changing the profession, but also knowing how to use it thoughtfully, creatively, ethically and responsibly to make their journalism, as well as the business of journalism, stronger. Through these collaborations, OpenAI and the Newmark and Medill communities will seek to further this outcome.

“Generative AI is a transformative technology that will remake the information landscape, and one that the journalism industry will need to adapt to and shape in order to fulfill our mission of informing the public. We intend for the Newmark community to be at the forefront of this transformation, and it’s critical that they learn about and be immersed in this technology. We’re very grateful to OpenAI for making the tools available to our students and faculty so they can better prepare themselves for this future.”

—Gina Chua, Executive Director of the Tow-Knight Center.

“The media industry is rapidly evolving, and AI is a major driver of this change. The Knight Lab is committed to ensuring that any Medill graduate students who want to use the latest AI tools and techniques can do so without cost being a barrier. Offering equity of access is crucial when incorporating new technologies. The Knight Lab has been working at the intersection of media and AI for more than a decade. This support from OpenAI helps us to continue to explore the future of media and technology, allowing faculty to teach and practice journalism in countless new ways.”

—Jeremy Gilbert, Medill Professor and Knight Chair in Digital Media Strategy.

“Over the past three years, OpenAI has partnered closely with leaders across the news industry to help both established and aspiring journalists make the most of AI, while keeping their human expertise front and center. We’re excited to see what the next generation of reporters and editors will accomplish with AI as they carry forward journalism’s proud tradition of serving communities through their vital work. OpenAI is expanding on our longstanding commitment to journalism and furthering our mission by providing students and faculty at the Newmark J-School at CUNY and Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern access to the technology, sharing successes and challenges, and engaging in deep dialogues about strengthening journalism’s future.”

—Tom Rubin, Chief of Intellectual Property and Content at OpenAI

The Tow-Knight Center at the Newmark J-School and the Knight Labs at Medill are the first partners in this latest phase of OpenAI’s commitment to journalism, and additional efforts are already underway to expand support across the journalism education ecosystem.

Giving journalism students practical experience with AI

AI can help journalism students work more ambitiously. It can support deeper investigations, faster analysis, stronger brainstorming, new storytelling formats, and more pointed questioning.

But access to the technology alone is not enough. Students need opportunities to experiment, develop responsible workflows, understand its limitations, and learn where human judgment matters most.

Through this program, the Tow-Knight Center and the Knight Lab will help students at the Newmark J-School and Medill explore how AI can support their work while preserving the essential roles of reporters, editors, producers, and newsroom leaders.

Building on years of investment in journalism

This new initiative builds on OpenAI’s yearslong and ongoing support of the journalism ecosystem, which includes:

  • Through our renewed partnership with the American Journalism Project, all 50+ of the news organizations in their portfolio will have the opportunity to access ChatGPT enterprise and API credits. AJP’s Product & AI Studio will turn the strongest uses cases into reusable tools and infrastructure, and share playbooks and lessons across the portfolio and with the broader nonprofit and local news community.
  • OpenAI’s continued support for the Lenfest Institute for Journalism’s AI Collaborative and Fellowship program, providing major local news organizations with funds to hire AI engineering fellows dedicated to building, scaling, and sharing projects that strengthen journalism and the business of news. Projects have focused on reporting on public data, making news archives more accessible to staff, developing new products that expand audience reach, and growing advertising, subscription, and membership revenue.
  • An ongoing partnership with WAN-IFRA, launched in 2024, through which OpenAI has supported multiple stages of its Newsroom AI Catalyst accelerator program, which has served over 165 newsrooms across Europe, Asia Pacific, South Asia, Latin America, and Australia and New Zealand. The program offers practical training, technical assistance, strategy development, and OpenAI API credits.
  • OpenAI’s ongoing work with INMA to support international news organizations to understand and shape the role AI can play across journalism and the business of news. The partnership has supported dedicated regional discussions with industry leaders from Europe, Latin America, and Asia Pacific, alongside webinars, and OpenAI API credits for hands-on building.

The new Tow-Knight Center and Knight Lab program at the Newmark J-School and Medill program builds on these efforts and expands this work further upstream: helping future journalists build the skills, fluency, and confidence they will need before they enter the newsroom

Supporting the full journalism ecosystem

Enabling Newmark J-School and Medill students and faculty is the latest step as OpenAI extends its broad, multi-faceted collaborations with news industry leaders. Additional phases are actively being developed to expand tools, training, partnerships, shared learning, and practical enablement across the journalism industry. This work builds on OpenAI’s early support of journalism and education. In 2023, OpenAI provided a grant to help launch the Ethics and Journalism Initiative at NYU’s Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute that studies, among other things, AI and journalism.

It continues the dialogues and collaborations across the industry. Just this year, for instance, OpenAI has hosted meetings with journalists and given trainings at the National Association of Black Journalists conference, National Association of Hispanic Journalists conference, Asian American Journalists Association conference, and NLGJA: The Association of LGBTQ+ Journalists conference. These convenings brought together reporters, editors, producers, students, educators, newsroom leaders, and media entrepreneurs from communities that have long shaped how journalism serves different audiences.

At these conferences, OpenAI has listened to journalists’ needs, shared hands-on examples, and helped reporters explore practical ways to use AI in their daily work. That engagement has also informed the continued expansion of OpenAI Academy for News Organizations⁠(opens in a new window), a learning hub with practical training, newsroom-relevant use cases, playbooks, and real-world examples for journalists and publishers using AI.

Together, these educational collaborations, professional partnerships, and industry conferences are helping shape the next phases of OpenAI’s journalism work—ensuring the deployment and use of AI is grounded in the real needs and experiences of the people building the future of news.

title: 平安跨境康：AI多语言服务化解外籍在华就医难题
summary: 在深圳科创展上，平安好医生推出“平安跨境康”，旨在利用AI多语言服务解决外籍人士在华就医难题。针对语言不通、流程陌生及服务断层三大痛点，该产品提供“线上音视频问诊+境内线下全程陪诊”的一站式闭环服务。其核心优势在于搭载支持19种语言实时互译的AI引擎，精准覆盖医学术语，并联合北大医疗认证家医团队，实现从在线评估、专车接送到院内陪诊的高效衔接。用户无需下载App，通过轻量化入口即可便捷接入。案例显示...
full_content:
9月5日，以“中国方案·科创互联”为主题的深圳科创展，在深圳平安金融中心云际观光层开幕，展期将持续至11月。科创展旨在呼应APEC“开放的区域主义”精神，推动产业交流对接，集中呈现中国科创的开放姿态与深圳的创新实践。大疆、腾讯、华为、平安产险、平安好医生等代表企业悉数亮相，多维度展示中国科创的技术实力与创新活力。


其中，平安好医生旗下新品“平安跨境康”尤为瞩目，该产品依托AI多语言翻译与线上线下闭环服务，为外籍来华人士提供一站式医疗健康服务。


 


随着中国对外开放持续深化，来华工作、学习、生活的外籍人士数量稳步增长。然而，“看病难”始终是困扰这一群体的突出问题。语言不通是第一道坎。三甲医院门诊量大、节奏快，外籍患者往往词不达意，难以充分沟通病情，就医效率随之大打折扣。流程不熟是第二道坎。挂号、分诊、缴费、检查、取药，国内医院的就医流程与海外差异显著，外籍人士常常一头雾水、来回奔波。服务断层是第三道坎。线上咨询与线下就诊衔接不畅，翻译、陪诊、随访等缺乏统一衔接，一次就医往往要折腾大半天。正是瞄准这些痛点，平安跨境康以“线上音视频问诊 + 境内线下全程陪诊”一体化服务，从根本上破解来华用户就医堵点。

 

不久前，来自美国的Michael突发腹痛，却因语言障碍无法顺利就医。他通过平安跨境康发起线上视频问诊，AI翻译引擎实时转译医患对话。通过北大医疗集团旗下成员认证的平安家医在线快速评估后，立即安排专员全程陪诊。从线上问诊、专车接送到院内陪诊，一气呵成，原本可能折腾一整天的流程，仅用三小时便全部完成。事后Michael感叹：“AI翻译非常精准，陪诊师全程的协助也让我很安心，没想到在中国看病这么便捷高效，平安跨境康真的帮了我大忙。”

 


平安跨境康拥有坚实的技术底座与扎实的专业服务团队。AI技术方面，平安跨境康搭载先进AI智能翻译引擎，可支持19种语言语音、文字双向实时互译，精准覆盖医学专业术语，进一步消除医患沟通壁垒。产品特别考虑外籍用户使用习惯，采取轻量化设计，无需下载App，依托H5、小程序扫码即可接入，兼容198个国家和地区手机号登录，全球用户触达便捷高效。


医生团队方面，平安跨境康的家医服务团队通过了北大医疗旗下成员资质认证，服务体系获得世界家庭医生组织（WONCA）、中华医学会全科医学分会、澳大利亚皇家全科医学会（RACGP）三大权威认证，诊疗标准全面接轨国际。团队成员大多为拥有三甲医院背景、副高及以上职称、平均20年行医经验的资深医师，为每一次问诊提供专业又有温度的支撑。


整体服务覆盖线上问诊评估、线下就医专业陪诊的全流程闭环，实现“线上评估→专员接送→全程陪诊”的一站式就医陪伴，让跨境医疗有品质、更有温度。



在本次深圳科创展现场，熙来攘往的参展嘉宾近距离体验了平安跨境康的多语言视频问诊功能，直观感受跨境医疗数字化服务的便捷与高效。来自马来西亚、俄罗斯等多个国家的参展观众纷纷扫码体验，并对AI翻译的准确率和响应速度给予高度评价。



平安好医生相关负责人表示，平安跨境康是公司为解决来华外籍人群医疗服务需求的一次创新尝试，目前仅在深圳地区开放，欢迎各国友人给予体验意见和建议反馈。未来，公司将持续完善跨境医疗服务能力，进一步丰富平安“四到”（到线、到院、到家、到企）服务网络，助力多层次健康服务体系建设，为国内外用户提供更加省心、省时、又省钱的全流程健康管理服务。


在APEC倡导的开放区域主义精神下，平安跨境康以“科技+医疗”的中国方案，正在让跨境就医从“难题”变为“易事”，为亚太医疗健康协同发展贡献平安力量。

title: 补体破局、支付破冰、产业破圈，罕见病能否成为撬动中国生物医药未来的“支点”？
summary: 随着补体科学从机制研究迈向临床精准干预，中国罕见病产业正经历从“缺药难诊”到“诊疗体系完善、创新疗法涌现”的关键阶段切换。全国罕见病诊疗协作网已覆盖419家医院，诊断周期大幅缩短至数周，阿斯利康等企业助力超160家医院建立诊疗中心，推动资源下沉。当前，补体靶点开发延伸至整个网络，AI等新技术赋能全病程管理，“异病同治”理念重塑治疗逻辑。然而，技术突破并非终点，如何提升创新治疗可及性、构建匹配的保障...
full_content:
“现在罕见病的本土创新，我觉得技术、人才都不是问题，未来还需更多政策支持，为本土创新提供持续的‘东风’。”在近日召开的第三届中国补体日学术大会上，阿斯利康中国副总裁、罕见病事业部负责人胡轶清把话题直接引向了一个比药物研发更现实的问题。

 

过去几年，补体科学正从机制研究走向精准干预。从PNH、aHUS到gMG，越来越多曾经缺乏有效治疗手段的罕见病开始拥有新的选择。与此同时，全国罕见病诊疗协作网已覆盖419家医院，罕见病诊断周期从过去的平均数年缩短至数周左右。这一变化背后，是一个清晰的产业信号：补体科学已从“机制发现”进入“临床兑现”阶段。

 

这也意味着，罕见病产业正在经历重要的阶段切换。过去行业最担心的是“没有药”“诊断难”，如今诊疗体系快速完善、创新疗法不断增加，越来越多患者被发现、被确诊。如何进一步提升创新治疗的可及性，并建立与之匹配的保障环境，正在成为罕见病发展的下一阶段核心议题。

 

 

补体正在成为理解罕见病的一条新“主线”。

 

人体补体系统承担着重要的免疫防御功能，但当通路异常激活或失衡时，便可能造成不同器官和组织损伤。过去，这些疾病分属血液、肾脏、神经免疫等不同专科；如今，随着机制研究深入，医学界开始发现，多种疾病背后可能存在相似的补体异常机制，“异病同源、异病同治”由此从理念走向临床。

 

本届大会上，专家们的关注点已不再局限于C5、C3等相对成熟的靶点，而是延伸至整个补体网络。超过50种蛋白参与其中，意味着这条通路仍存在大量尚未被充分开发的治疗机会。

 

在肾脏领域，从aHUS、C3G等典型补体介导疾病，到IgA肾病、狼疮性肾炎及ANCA相关性血管炎，补体研究正推动疾病从传统病理分类走向机制驱动的精准治疗。神经免疫领域同样如此。以gMG为代表的疾病正获得更多补体靶向治疗选择，AI、VR等新技术也开始进入疾病认知、辅助诊疗和全病程管理。技术的价值不再只是帮助医生提高诊断效率，更延伸到患者长期治疗和生活质量的改善。

 

与此同时，中国的罕见病诊疗体系也在快速成熟。截至2024年10月，全国罕见病诊疗协作网已覆盖419家医院，诊疗体系从少数头部医院逐步向区域协作、MDT及基层下沉延伸。胡轶清介绍，阿斯利康目前已支持全国超过160家医院建立罕见病诊疗中心，帮助更多患者尽早确诊。

 

然而，这也揭示了罕见病产业正在发生的一个结构性变化：诊疗能力越强，支付问题就越无法回避。

 

过去，患者未被发现，意味着“无药可治”；如今，患者被发现、药物已出现，如果因支付能力无法接受治疗，产业依然未能完成闭环。因此，罕见病生态的真正闭环，不仅在于诊疗能力和创新药物的持续突破，还在于支付保障能否同步跟上。

 

一些地方已率先探索。浙江、江苏建立罕见病用药保障专项基金，珠海“大爱无疆”提高罕见病自费药保障比例，深圳惠民保则将部分高值罕见病特效药纳入专项保障。同时，建立国家层面的罕见病专项保障机制，正在成为越来越多代表委员和专家共同关注的方向。2026年全国两会期间，孙洁、蔡威等多位代表委员围绕罕见病多层次保障、专项基金及产业支持提出建议，推动在基本医保之外探索更适配罕见病特点的保障路径。

02 支付打通之后，中国罕见病创新或迎“弯道超车”

 

支付问题之所以重要，是因为它最终决定的不仅是患者能否买药，还关系到能否形成支持持续创新的市场环境。没有商业回报，企业无法通过产品销售反哺研发；没有持续研发，就很难继续投入新靶点、新适应症及更前沿的技术。最终，支付问题会从患者端传导至企业端，再传导至整个产业的创新能力。

 

相比之下，肿瘤等患者基数较大的领域已形成相对成熟的循环。部分企业通过Me-better产品实现商业盈利，再将收入投入下一轮研发，逐步从Me-too、Me-better走向Best-in-Class乃至First-in-Class。

 

胡轶清表示：“中国罕见病创新已经具备了不错的‘天时、地利、人和’：政策环境持续改善，罕见病诊疗协作网络逐步建立，临床和研发队伍不断成熟。”真正需要补上的，是让这些人才、技术和创新成果能够持续转化的产业环境——这或许正是中国罕见病创新进一步突破所需的“东风”。

 

而从研发端看，中国恰恰具备“弯道超车”的条件。

 

一方面，中国人口基数大，大型医学中心能接触到更多罕见病患者。某些海外中心一年只能看到几个患者，而中国大型中心可能形成几十甚至数百人的患者队列，这意味着中国在临床研究和真实世界数据积累方面具备独特优势。另一方面，中国专家过去20年的临床能力提升明显。胡轶清认为，中国专家已从“追随”逐步走向与国际水平接轨，部分领域甚至开始参与国际诊疗理念和标准的制定。

 

这种优势正在进一步融入全球研发体系。目前，阿斯利康在中国已实现新药研发与全球三期临床100%同步，中国患者能够更早参与全球临床开发；同时，公司也在探索更早期的IIT研究，让中国专家发现的新适应症、新靶点和临床信号有机会进入更大规模的全球开发。这意味着中国在全球罕见病创新中的角色正在变化：从“海外研发、中国引进”，走向“中国临床参与、全球同步开发”，甚至未来可能实现“中国发现、全球验证”。

 

胡轶清将阿斯利康在其中的角色概括为“桥梁”：一方面支持中国证据和本土创新，另一方面推动国际交流，让中国专家和患者更深度地进入全球研发网络。公司也正通过投资基金等方式，加强与本土创新企业的合作。

 

如果支付保障能够进一步破局，这条产业链的想象空间将被真正打开：患者获得治疗，企业获得回报，资本重新进入研发，科研成果得到转化，新的产品再反哺下一轮创新。这也是为什么，罕见病不能只被看作一个患者数量有限的“小市场”。许多新机制、新靶点和前沿疗法都率先在罕见病领域得到探索，并进一步拓展至更广泛的疾病领域。推动罕见病创新，不仅是满足少数患者的临床需求，也是在为下一代生物医药创新积累科学突破、临床证据和产业化经验。

 

因此，补体破局之后，真正值得关注的已经不是又出现了多少个新靶点，而是能否把“防、诊、治、付、管”真正串起来。当创新药已经证明“可以治”，支付体系需要解决的是“治得起”；当患者已经能够被发现，诊疗体系还要进一步解决“治得准”；而当中国已经拥有越来越丰富的临床资源和创新能力，产业最终需要回答的，则是如何让这些能力形成一个可持续循环的生态。

 

这，或许才是补体破局之后，罕见病真正的“下半场”。

title: Dialysis access and heart failure need one care plan
summary: For decades, vascular care has focused on solving problems within the circulatory system. When an artery narrows, we restore blood flow. When a patient requires dialysis, we create reliable vascular a...
full_content:
For decades, vascular care has focused on solving problems within the circulatory system. When an artery narrows, we restore blood flow. When a patient requires dialysis, we create reliable vascular access. These interventions are critical, but they represent only part of the picture.

Today’s vascular patients rarely have disease confined to a single organ system. Many are living with chronic kidney disease, heart disease, and diabetes simultaneously. As these conditions become increasingly intertwined, one lesson is becoming clear: Decisions made to treat one condition can have a positive or negative impact on another. The future of vascular care will depend not only on better procedures, but on better understanding how the vascular, cardiac, and renal systems interact.

One procedure can affect multiple organ systems

One example is the creation of dialysis access for patients with kidney failure. An arteriovenous fistula or graft provides the lifeline many patients need to receive dialysis, but creating that access also changes how blood flows through the body. By creating a low-resistance pathway between an artery and vein, these procedures increase the amount of blood the heart must pump. For patients who already face a substantial cardiovascular burden because of kidney disease, that additional workload can have meaningful consequences.

Historically, vascular access planning has been viewed primarily through the lens of dialysis readiness and long-term access durability. Increasingly, however, evidence suggests it should also be viewed as a cardiovascular decision.

Real-world data is changing what we know

Large-scale clinical data is helping reshape our understanding of these risks. Our research, which was presented at the Society for Vascular Surgery’s Vascular Annual Meeting, found that within Medicare data from more than 210,000 vascular access procedures, approximately 40 percent of patients were hospitalized for a cardiac event within one year of access creation, with heart failure accounting for many of those hospitalizations. Most events occurred during the first year following surgery.

We also observed that patients receiving arteriovenous grafts experienced higher rates of cardiac complications and mortality than those receiving fistulas, even among individuals without pre-existing heart disease. While additional research is needed to better understand the mechanisms involved, one possible explanation is that grafts often generate higher blood flow than fistulas, particularly during the first year after surgery, placing greater demands on the heart.

Studies of this size allow us to identify risks that smaller investigations often cannot detect. More importantly, they help quantify the broader impact of treatment decisions across large patient populations.

Building the next generation of vascular care

Emerging technologies designed to create lower-flow fistulas may help reduce cardiovascular complications while preserving effective dialysis access. At the same time, advances in predictive analytics could help physicians identify which patients are most likely to experience high-flow complications before they occur.

Equally exciting is the opportunity to combine large real-world datasets with clinical information such as echocardiograms, vascular ultrasound findings, biomarkers, and patient-reported outcomes. Together, these data can provide a more complete understanding of how individual patients respond to treatment and help clinicians make more informed decisions throughout their care.

Perhaps the most important innovation, however, is not technological. It is the growing recognition that caring for patients with vascular disease requires collaboration across specialties. As vascular surgeons, nephrologists, and cardiologists work more closely together before and after intervention, we have an opportunity to move beyond treating isolated conditions and instead care for the whole patient.

That shift toward integrated, patient-centered care has the potential to improve outcomes not only for patients requiring dialysis access, but for vascular medicine as a whole.

Mohamad A. Hussain is a vascular surgeon.

title: Patient trust in AI starts with human accountability
summary: Patients are hearing more about artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine. Some are excited. Some are worried. Many are unsure what it means when a clinician, hospital, insurer, or digital health compa...
full_content:
Patients are hearing more about artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine. Some are excited. Some are worried. Many are unsure what it means when a clinician, hospital, insurer, or digital health company says AI is being used in their care. That uncertainty matters.

Trust is not created by telling patients that a tool is advanced. Trust is created when patients understand what is happening, why it is happening, who is responsible, and how their safety is protected. Health care AI will not earn trust through technical performance alone. It will earn trust through human accountability.

As an emergency physician, I have learned that patients rarely ask only for an answer. They want to know whether someone understands their fear. They want to know whether the plan makes sense. They want to know what could go wrong. They want to know who will help them if their symptoms change.

AI can support that work. It can summarize records. It can help translate medical language. It can identify patterns. It can draft instructions. It can help clinicians prepare for a visit. It can help patients ask better questions.

But AI cannot be the person responsible for care. That responsibility must remain clear.

One of the biggest mistakes health systems can make is treating AI as invisible. If patients discover later that AI shaped a message, summary, recommendation, or workflow without any explanation, the result may not be efficiency. It may be suspicion.

Patients do not need a technical lecture about models. They need plain language. They need to know when AI is being used to support care. They need to know that a clinician reviewed the output when clinical decisions are involved. They need to know how errors can be corrected. They need to know that privacy is protected. They need to know that they can ask for a human explanation.

This does not mean every AI-assisted task requires a long consent process. A spelling tool, transcription assistant, or scheduling system is different from a diagnostic recommendation or risk prediction model. The level of transparency should match the level of clinical influence. The more AI affects a patient’s care, the more accountability must be visible.

Physicians and other clinicians also need a practical framework for trust. First, use AI for the right task. AI is often safest and most useful when it reduces low-value work. It can help organize information, draft routine documentation, prepare patient education, and make complex instructions clearer. These are real gains if the clinician remains in control.

Second, review before relying. AI output can sound confident even when it is incomplete. Clinicians should treat it as a tool, not a conclusion. The final decision still requires history, exam, context, risk tolerance, and judgment.

Third, explain simply. Patients should not be left wondering whether a machine made the decision. A simple statement can help: I used a tool to help organize your information, but I reviewed it and I am responsible for the plan.

Fourth, preserve the relationship. Technology should never make a patient feel less seen. If AI saves time, that time should be returned to listening, examining, explaining, and answering questions.

Fifth, make accountability operational. Hospitals should define who monitors AI tools, who reviews errors, how patients report concerns, how clinicians override outputs, and how performance is measured over time.

Patient trust will also depend on what we measure. If health care leaders measure only speed, they may miss harm. A faster message that confuses a patient is not better care. A faster note that misses a key concern is not progress. A faster workflow that shifts burden to nurses, physicians, or patients has not solved the problem. We should measure whether AI improves understanding, safety, access, follow-up, clinician time, and patient experience.

The future of medicine should not ask patients to choose between human care and technological progress. The goal should be better human care supported by better tools. That is the promise of AI in health care. Not replacing responsibility. Strengthening it.

Patients will trust AI when they know a human is still accountable. They will trust it when it helps clinicians listen better, see earlier signals, prevent avoidable harm, and explain care more clearly. They will trust it when technology makes medicine feel more human, not less.

Harvey Castro is an emergency physician, author, keynote speaker, chief AI officer, and physician futurist known as DR GPT™. He writes and speaks about artificial intelligence in health care, digital health, space medicine, and the future of human-centered care. Learn more at his website.

Castro has held a range of roles across his career, including CEO, physician, and medical correspondent for major media outlets. He has developed multiple health care apps and consulted for health care companies, with the goal of increasing awareness of digital health and driving practical change in how technology reaches patients and clinicians.

He is the author of Bing Copilot and Other LLM: Revolutionizing Healthcare With AI, Solving Infamous Cases with Artificial Intelligence, The AI-Driven Entrepreneur: Unlocking Entrepreneurial Success with Artificial Intelligence Strategies and Insights, ChatGPT and Healthcare: The Key To The New Future of Medicine, ChatGPT and Healthcare: Unlocking The Potential Of Patient Empowerment, Revolutionize Your Health and Fitness with ChatGPT’s Modern Weight Loss Hacks, Success Reinvention, and Apple Vision Healthcare Pioneers: A Community for Professionals & Patients.

He shares updates on LinkedIn, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and X. #DRGPT

title: 全球首款1针1次给药保护9个月抗RSV单抗——新多妥获批上市
summary: 2026年9月3日，珠海泰诺麦博自主研发的全球首款长效抗RSV单抗“新多妥”（芮特韦拜单抗注射液）获国家药监局批准上市。该药适用于预防新生儿及婴儿RSV所致下呼吸道感染，填补了现有预防方案保护期短、无法全覆盖流行季的空白。基于Hitmab平台研发的全人源抗体精准靶向病毒F蛋白，具备低免疫原性优势。其核心突破在于单次给药即可提供长达9个月的保护，显著优于传统5个月周期，能完整覆盖南北方RSV流行季。...
full_content:
2026年9月3日，珠海泰诺麦博制药股份有限公司（股票代码：688806）自主研发的全球首款1针1次给药保护9个月的重组抗呼吸道合胞病毒（RSV）全人源单克隆抗体新药——新多妥（通用名：芮特韦拜单抗注射液，曾用名：TNM001注射液，）正式获国家药品监督管理局（NMPA）批准上市，适用于即将进入或出生在第一个呼吸道合胞病毒（RSV）流行季的新生儿和婴儿预防 RSV 所致的下呼吸道感染。




呼吸道合胞病毒（RSV）是5岁以下儿童下呼吸道感染（LRTI）最常见的病毒病原体。根据2024年《柳叶刀》发表的数据，全球每年有3,300万例RSV相关下呼吸道疾病发生在5岁以下儿童中，导致360万人住院、11.8万人死亡。其中1岁以内婴儿感染占比超60%，胎龄<35周的早产儿以及患有CHD（先天性心脏病）和/或CLD（早产儿慢性肺疾病,又称BPD）的婴儿,甚至免疫抑制的婴儿等高危人群感染后毛细支气管炎、肺炎发生率及住院率显著偏高。


RSV南北流行特征存在差异：北方流行季主要集中在10月至次年4月，南方则无明显季节性，呈现全年持续流行的特征。这意味着已上市RSV预防药物5个月的保护周期在部分地区已无法完整覆盖流行季。而目前全球尚无RSV特异性抗病毒治疗药物获批，预防是疾病防控的关键抓手。




芮特韦拜单抗基于泰诺麦博自主知识产权的高通量全人源单克隆抗体研发综合技术平台Hitmab研发，其抗体分子完全筛选自人体天然免疫细胞，精准靶向RSV病毒表面F蛋白（融合蛋白）的保守表位，在病毒准备入侵人体细胞时"锁住"它，从而阻止感染发生。作为重组全人源IgG1型单克隆抗体，其免疫原性风险低，天然适配婴儿群体，具备以下四大核心优势，保护1岁以内所有新生儿和婴儿人群（足月宝宝、早产儿以及各类高危婴儿均可适用）：


优势一： 1针1次给药保护覆盖9个月


根据临床和药代动力学/药效学（PK/PD）数据，本品单次注射提供的保护时效可达 9 个月，远超典型的150天RSV流行季。


Ⅲ期临床试验数据显示，注射后9个月（270天），对需要就医RSV下呼吸道感染的保护效力仍保持在69.9%，对需要就医严重RSV下呼吸道感染的保护效力为90.2%，一针足以覆盖整个RSV流行季，甚至可能更长。


优势二：覆盖高危与非高危婴儿


Ⅲ期临床结果显示，单剂肌肉注射后（建议在大腿前外侧注射），能够显著降低健康足月儿、晚期早产儿发生RSV相关下呼吸道感染风险，对重症RSV下呼吸道感染具备突出的预防保护作用。给药后150天内对需就医和导致住院的RSV下呼吸道感染保护效力达71.3%和71.7%，对严重RSVLRTI保护效力达93.9%和90.1%。


此外，值得一提的是，即使某些RSV病毒株发生了变异，对帕利珠单抗或尼塞韦单抗产生了耐药性，芮特韦拜单抗对这些变异病毒仍然有可能保持高效的中和活性，为临床用药提供了更多保障。


优势三：安全性良好，不良反应发生率低


在两项随机、双盲、安慰剂对照试验中，共1204名新生儿及婴儿接受了芮特韦拜单抗120 mg单次肌内注射。安全性数据显示，整体不良反应发生率极低，且所有不良反应均为轻度至中度，无需特殊处理即可自行缓解。在RSV重症风险更高的婴儿中，安全性特征与健康足月儿一致。


免疫原性方面，仅极少数婴儿在注射后检测到抗药抗体，这些抗体均未产生中和活性，对药物的有效性、安全性和体内代谢没有产生临床意义上的影响。


优势四：给药简便，适配临床场景


芮特韦拜单抗采用120mg单一固定规格，无需根据婴儿体重调整剂量，适用于1岁以内所有新生儿和婴儿人群，单支通用操作便捷。在RSV流行季出生的新生儿，在出院前即可注射；在RSV流行季前出生的婴儿，应在流行季开始前注射。



保护周期对比：9个月 vs 5个月，临床意义何在？


这是目前RSV预防领域最受关注的话题之一。临床研究数据显示，芮特韦拜单抗单次注射保护期可达9个月（270天），而进口尼塞韦单抗（Nirsevimab）保护周期约为5-6个月。


这一差异的临床意义需结合流行病学规律来看：RSV的传播和流行并非严格限定在5个月内。在北方地区，RSV流行季通常从10-11月延续至次年4-5月，且流行高峰、起始和结束时间在不同年份、不同地区之间存在显著差异。而进口同类药品约5-6个月的保护周期在部分地区已无法完整覆盖流行季，而在南方地区全年流行的特征下，5-6个月的保护期更显不足。目前全球尚无RSV特异性抗病毒治疗药物获批，预防仍是疾病防控的关键抓手。




泰诺麦博为源头创新生物药企，2026年7月登陆上交所科创板（股票代码：688806）。芮特韦拜单抗是泰诺麦博继2025年获批的全球首款"破伤风针"新替妥（斯泰度塔单抗注射液）后的第二款自主原研新药，实现靶点挖掘、工艺开发到商业化的全链条自主可控。

该药研发获国家高度支持：2026年2月新药上市申请（NDA）受理，3月纳入优先审评，5月入选国家科技重大专项，承担"婴幼儿呼吸道合胞病毒长效单抗Retavibart大规模生产工艺优化及上市临床研究"子课题。多重加持，充分彰显国家对源头真创新的肯定，以高质高效审评助力守护“健康中国”。

title: 最赚钱的5家上市械企，一家靠投资，一家卖手套
summary: 2026年上半年，175家A+H械企财报揭示行业并非简单复苏，而是呈现深刻的结构性大分化。尽管超六成企业营收正增长，但净利润榜单暴露出严峻的“含金量”拷问：迈瑞医疗虽以50.47亿元净利断层领先，占据行业近四分之一利润，却出现“增收不增利”现象，折射出利润率下行压力。更引人深思的是，九安医疗凭借投资月之暗面、DeepSeek等AI硬科技获得的巨额公允价值变动收益，净利暴增至30.74亿元跃居第二，...
full_content:
2026年半年报披露季落幕，175家A+H医疗器械上市公司交出了成绩单。

 

如果只看一个数字，你会觉得行业已经复苏：140家A股器械公司上半年合计营收1314.11亿元，64.3%的企业实现营收正增长，营收增速中位数4.18%。

 

但如果列出净利润排行榜，你会发现完全是另一番景象：最赚钱的10家公司里，一家靠投资，一家卖手套，还有6家利润在下滑。

 

医疗器械行业的“含金量”，正在经历一场前所未有的拷问。

 

这就是2026年上半年医疗器械行业的真相：不是简单的“复苏”或“承压”，而是一场深刻的结构性大分化。175家企业正在被重新分类：有的在筑坝，有的在裸泳，有的已经扬帆远航。

 

让我们用2张榜单，把这个行业的底牌翻出来。

 

最赚钱的10家公司：第一名断层领先，第二名“不务正业”

 

先看最直观的一张榜单：谁最赚钱。

 

（数据来源：各公司2026年半年报；取净利润口径）

 

这张榜单的信息量很大，有几个数据值得细品：

 

首先，第一名断层领先，但利润在缩水。迈瑞医疗以50.47亿元的净利润一骑绝尘，是第二名九安医疗的1.6倍、第三名英科的5.6倍。在140家A股器械公司总净利润209.28亿元中，迈瑞一家就占了24%：接近四分之一的行业利润，被一家公司赚走了。

 

但迈瑞的归母净利润同比下滑5.37%，扣非下滑3.32%。行业龙头都开始“增收不增利”（营收+6.00%，利润-5.37%），这本身就是一个强烈的信号：医疗器械行业的利润率下行压力，比想象中更大。

 

其次，第二名“不务正业”，靠投资赚了30亿。九安医疗上半年净利润30.74亿元，同比暴增234%，在所有A股器械公司中排名第二。但它的营收只有5.31亿元，同比还下滑了30.58%。

 

30亿净利润，是投资收益的功劳：上半年，九安医疗此前投资的月之暗面（Kimi）、DeepSeek、国产GPU企业沐曦股份、智元机器人等AI与硬科技企业，估值持续暴涨，共同推高了九安医疗的整体公允价值变动收益。

 

一家医疗器械公司，通过投资赚取的收益，远远超过了主业利润，并靠“投资”排进了盈利榜第二名，这本身就是行业的一个黑色幽默。


更幽默的是，2026年8月，Kimi和DeepSeek又启动了新一轮融资，估值再一次上涨，如Kimi 7月F轮投后估值350亿美元，8月投前估值‌500亿美元‌。不出意外，九安医疗又要赚翻了。

 

再次，卖手套的比卖影像设备、高值耗材的还赚钱。英科医疗的主营业务为一次性PVC手套与丁腈手套，其上半年净利润为9.04亿元，排名第四，超过了联影医疗（8.89亿）、新产业（8.68亿）、鱼跃医疗（8.48亿）等一众企业。

 

从净利率看，以高端医学影像设备为主的联影医疗，上半年营收70.52亿元，净利润8.89亿元，净利率12.6%；低值耗材龙头英科医疗营收69.09亿元，净利润9.04亿元，净利率13.1%。

 

这背后的逻辑是：高端医疗设备虽然技术壁垒高，但研发投入大、销售费用高、价格战加剧，净利率并不一定比“低端”耗材高。尤其是在集采和国产替代的双重压力下，高端医疗设备的利润率正在被持续压缩。

 

不过，切换至归母净利润口径，格局将发生反转：英科医疗受合资子公司少数股东损益分流利润影响，归母净利润为8.37亿元，低于联影（8.97亿）、新产业（8.68亿）、鱼跃（8.43亿）等企业。

 

（数据来源：各公司2026年半年报；取归母净利润口径）

 

这意味着：联影、新产业、鱼跃等上市公司股东，实际享有的利润水平，反而高于英科。

 

最后，10强里6家利润下滑，行业赚钱越来越难。如鱼跃医疗归母净利润同比下降29.92%，乐普医疗同比下降27.71%，威高股份下降23.23%，安图生物下降12.94%。

 

不止如此，140家A股器械公司中，净利润负增长的有71家，占比50.7%。一半的公司，今年上半年赚的钱比去年少。扣非增速中位数更是低至-3.32%，超过一半的上市公司核心主业盈利能力在下降。

 

行业里最能赚钱的头部公司都在利润下滑，中小公司的处境可想而知。

 

 

看完了“谁最赚钱”，再看“谁增长得最快”。营收增速是观察企业活力最直观的指标。

 

本次统计整合A+H股医疗器械上市企业数据，按照营收同比增速进行排序，行业增速TOP10企业具体如下：


（数据来源：各公司2026年半年报）

 

乍一看，这份榜单相当震撼。真健康增长31倍，健世科技接近4倍，美因基因、精锋医疗也都翻倍以上。3000%、300%、100%的增速，放在任何行业都是“炸裂”级别的表现。

 

但往下多看一眼营收数字，就会发现一个有点尴尬的事实：增速最猛的几家，营收体量其实很小。真健康医疗半年营收只有567万，堃博医疗只有329万，健世科技也才6413万。百万、千万级别的营收，增长几倍甚至几十倍，更多是“从0到1”的起步，而非“从1到10”的扩张。

 

不过，这也说明它们的商业模式已经跑通、产品已经被市场验证。增速高，意味着产品正在加速放量，市场需求正在快速打开。

 

若跳出单一榜单、放眼全部175家A+H股医疗器械企业，可以发现：不同企业的增长背后是不同细分赛道、经营模式催生的多元化增长路径，可归为四大类。

 

第一类是周期复苏型，如英科医疗、蓝帆医疗、中红医疗等。

 

（数据来源：各公司2026年半年报）

 

这三家企业的增长逻辑高度一致：手套业务订单增长，销量和单价双双回升。

 

先说销量。一次性手套行业经历了产能大扩张、市场收缩后，供过于求、价格暴跌，很多中小企业被淘汰出局。经过2024-2025年两年的产能出清，全球手套市场需求终于稳步复苏，头部企业的订单量明显增长。这是典型的周期复苏型增长。

 

再说单价。原油价格波动带动丁腈胶乳、PVC等核心原材料成本上涨，成本压力向下游传导，叠加供需格局改善，手套产品价格实现修复。

 

最能说明问题的是利润增速。英科医疗扣非净利润增长165%，蓝帆医疗增长141%，中红医疗更是增长975%，利润增速远高于营收增速，说明英科、蓝帆、中红的这轮增长是量价齐升，盈利能力在快速修复。

 

第二类是国产替代型，如心玮医疗、北芯生命、归创通桥、奕瑞科技等。

 

（数据来源：各公司2026年半年报）

 

这一类企业的增长，核心是政策、产品、供应链三重驱动下的国产替代红利，具体不再赘述。

 

值得一提的是，上述企业中，不同细分赛道的替代节奏有所分化：

 

影像零部件赛道奕瑞科技，已经完成国内市场的进口替代，进一步切入GE、西门子、飞利浦全球供应链，实现国内+海外双向替代；

 

高值介入耗材赛道，惠泰、北芯、心玮、归创通桥，在电生理、IVUS、神经介入等赛道，持续抢夺强生、波科、美敦力的存量市场份额，既往被进口垄断的手术耗材，逐步实现院端放量；

 

健信超导的超导磁共振，面向基层及中端医院，打破海外厂商在核磁设备的长期垄断。

 

当然，国产替代并非一帆风顺。部分赛道仍然面临进口品牌的客户粘性、院端学术壁垒，且国产玩家涌入之后，内部价格竞争加剧，出现“收入高增、利润承压”现象。华大智造就是典型案例，营收保持双位数增长，但扣非层面仍处于亏损状态，替代进程仍需要持续投入。

 

第三类是出海驱动型，如奕瑞科技、爱伦医疗、采纳股份、力诺药包等。

 

（数据来源：各公司2026年半年报）

 

出海已经成为医疗器械企业公认的第二增长曲线，但不同企业出海模式、成长逻辑差异巨大。

 

上述企业中，一部分是ODM/OEM模式的低值耗材企业，如爱伦医疗、采纳股份。这些企业依托国内制造业成本优势，为海外品牌代工，产品直接销往欧美、全球市场，海外收入占比极高。

 

这类企业的增长，一方面受益全球下游需求回暖，另一方面来自海外大客户订单扩容，优势在于起量快，但短板是自主品牌弱，利润受下游客户议价影响较大。

 

另一部分是具备自主品牌的硬件、零部件企业，以奕瑞科技、联影医疗为代表。这类企业不是简单代工输出，而是依靠产品技术实力，直接参与全球市场竞争。

 

奕瑞科技海外收入增速超过100%，切入全球头部影像设备厂商供应链；联影医疗海外收入17.65亿元，同比增长54.45%，亚太市场实现爆发式增长。代表国内高端医疗器械产品已经具备全球竞争力。

 

需要说明的是，出海也会面对现实挑战：海外地缘政策壁垒、海外渠道建设投入、汇率波动都会侵蚀企业利润，出海放量不等于利润同步释放。

 

第四类是赛道红利型，如微泰医疗、精锋医疗、可孚医疗、瑞迈特、时代天使。


（数据来源：各公司2026年半年报）

 

该类企业的增长，是赛道红利+企业产品力共振的结果。细分赛道本身迎来需求爆发，叠加企业产品落地、商业化推进，共同推高营收增速。

 

以手术机器人为例，2026上半年，院端采购数量及采购金额增长，加之国产手术机器人加速出海，促使相关企业实现翻倍增长。如精锋医疗营收3.19亿、增速113.76%；微创机器人预告收入同比增长约200%至230%。

 

CGM（持续血糖监测）也是如此。经过多年市场培育与市场教育，糖尿病患者对CGM的需求持续增长，市场规模快速扩容。受此影响，CGM相关企业营收均实现高速增长：微泰医疗CGM产品上半年收入3.13亿元，同比增长118.7%；三诺生物CGM业务上半年收入同比增长超60%；鱼跃医疗上半年CGM业务营收规模实现翻倍以上增长。

 

此外，家用医疗器械、隐形正畸等赛道市场需求均持续增长，推动可孚医疗、瑞迈特、时代天使等领域内企业实现38%-43%的营收增长。

 

血液净化赛道中，山外山、天益医疗均保持高增速。不过，两者的增长原因并不相同。


山外山29.8%的营收增长显著受益于基层医疗市场的需求释放：县域医院、基层医疗机构的设备更新与血透服务能力建设，带来大量设备新增采购需求，同时自产耗材放量形成“设备-耗材”联动。

 

天益医疗48.8%的高增长，核心来自收购意大利子公司带来的报表合并+CRRT产品放量（CRRT主要面向ICU），传统透析耗材业务同比增长21.75%。

 

还有最后一类企业，营收和扣非净利润双双下滑。140家A股器械公司中，营收负增长且扣非负增长的有34家，占比24.3%：接近四分之一的企业，收入和利润都在下滑。内卷之下，营收降低，利润降低，这类企业的成长性或许将受到质疑。

 

 

翻看2026年医疗器械半年报，上市企业的冷暖百态，正是整个行业深度洗牌的真实缩影。

 

要知道，当前A股、港股百余家上市械企，早已是国内三万余家医疗器械生产企业中的绝对翘楚，是历经技术筛选、市场竞争、资本洗礼后脱颖而出的头部力量。

 

但即便是行业优等生，也普遍陷入增收不增利、利润收缩、增速分化的困境：24.3%的医疗器械上市企业营收与扣非净利润双降，50.7%的A股器械公司净利润负增长，超过一半的上市公司核心主业盈利能力在下降。

 

头部上市企业尚且步履维艰，行业内数量庞大、体量微小、资源薄弱的中小器械企业，生存处境只会更加严峻。

 

那么，行业该如何实现健康良性发展？这需要政策、企业、市场多方协同、双向奔赴。

 

政策层面持续纠治行业低价内卷，优化集采规则、完善公平竞争机制，为企业创新留存合理利润空间，引导行业从“价格竞争”转向“价值竞争”；

 

行业层面，头部企业需依托技术、资本、渠道优势，持续深耕高端创新、加速国产替代与全球化布局，发挥产业引领作用，带动上下游产业链协同升级。

 

而数量众多的中小企业，需摒弃盲目扩张、同质化跟风的发展思路，走出低价内卷误区，深耕差异化市场，实现错位竞争。

 

我们相信，随着行业持续出清、产业结构不断优化，劣质产能退出，优质企业突围，中国医疗器械行业终将摆脱“小散乱弱”的旧格局，完成从规模扩张到技术突围、从低价内卷到价值增长的蜕变，开启高质量发展的全新征程。

 

数据说明：

本文数据基于140家A股医疗器械上市公司+35家港股医疗器械上市公司2026年半年报数据整理

财务数据均来自公司公开披露的2026年半年报

title: Supporting independent journalism in Ukraine
summary: OpenAI, AIRPPU and WAN-IFRA launch an AI program to help Ukrainian news organizations strengthen innovation, resilience, and independent journalism....
full_content:
The following was issued as a joint press release on Monday 7th September 2026 from WAN-IFRA, AIRPPU and OpenAI.

The Newsroom AI Masterclass Series and Newsroom AI Catalyst support Ukraine’s independent news sector with a focus on AI adoption, innovation and resilience.

OpenAI, WAN-IFRA and the Association of Independent Regional Press Publishers of Ukraine (AIRPPU) have announced a new initiative to support and strengthen Ukrainian news publishers by building practical artificial intelligence capabilities and accelerating innovation across their organisations. During a time of continued conflict and unrest, the new initiative—developed by AIRPPU in partnership with WAN-IFRA and OpenAI—aims to help news organisations harness the opportunities of artificial intelligence to strengthen the sustainability, efficiency and resilience of independent journalism.

The programme combines two complementary components:

  • Newsroom AI, supporting news organisations selected by AIRPPU in developing and implementing AI-driven newsroom projects, and;
  • Business Transformation, supporting AI-driven commercial and operational transformation projects.

The Newsroom AI Masterclass Series will build on prior successful initiatives of WAN-IFRA and OpenAI and bring together international experts and practitioners to share practical knowledge, case studies and implementation strategies. The topics span a broad range of critical news organisation priorities, including editorial workflows, audience engagement, product development, revenue generation, organisational change and responsible AI adoption.

Building on this foundation, the Newsroom AI Catalyst will provide deeper, hands-on support to ten participating Ukrainian news organisations as they identify high-impact use cases, develop implementation roadmaps and pilot AI-enabled solutions tailored to their specific needs.

All organisations participating in the programme will also receive credits to OpenAI’s API to facilitate the development of bespoke newsroom solutions.

  • Oksana Brovko

  • Stig Ørskov

  • Tom Rubin

The programme builds on WAN-IFRA’s extensive global work supporting AI adoption in news organisations—including leadership programmes, industry research, peer-learning communities and practical implementation initiatives—and OpenAI’s continued partnership with news organisations around the world to help support their vital missions.

The Newsroom AI Masterclass Series began on August 5, 2026, with the Newsroom AI Catalyst set to launch on September 17, 2026. Further details regarding participation and full programme dates can be found here⁠(opens in a new window).

WAN-IFRA, the World Association of News Publishers, unites media globally to strengthen the business of trusted journalism and defend press freedom.

The Association of Independent Regional Press Publishers of Ukraine (AIRPPU) is the largest network of independent regional and local news publishers in Ukraine. The association supports media sustainability, professional journalism and press freedom through capacity-building programmes, emergency support, innovation initiatives and international partnerships, working with independent news organisations across the country.

title: Is personalized antithrombotic therapy ready for practice?
summary: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) affects millions of Americans and remains a leading cause of disability, repeat hospitalizations, and limb loss. Advances in endovascular devices, surgical techniques, ...
full_content:
Peripheral artery disease (PAD) affects millions of Americans and remains a leading cause of disability, repeat hospitalizations, and limb loss. Advances in endovascular devices, surgical techniques, and medical therapies have dramatically improved our ability to restore blood flow to the legs. Yet despite this progress, one challenge continues to limit long-term success: what happens after the procedure.

Following lower extremity revascularization, most patients are prescribed blood thinners to help prevent clot formation and keep arteries or bypass grafts open. These medications are a cornerstone of vascular care, but the way we prescribe has changed remarkably little over time. As medicine becomes increasingly personalized, it is time to rethink whether a one-size-fits-all approach is still the best path forward.

Where current treatments fall short

Current treatment guidelines are based on large clinical trials and have helped establish effective standards of care. However, these recommendations are designed around population-level data rather than the biology of individual patients.

We know that patients respond differently to antithrombotic medications. Some remain at high risk of developing thrombosis despite receiving guideline-directed therapy, leading to restenosis, repeat interventions, or even major amputation. Others may receive more aggressive therapy than necessary, increasing their risk of bleeding complications.

The challenge is that we often have no objective way of knowing which patients fall into either category. In many respects, we are still prescribing blood thinners based on what works for the average patient rather than understanding how each individual patient’s platelets respond to treatment.

Using this approach made sense when more personalized tools weren’t available. Today, it’s time to reconsider our approach.

Bringing precision medicine into vascular surgery

Across medicine, precision medicine is transforming how clinicians approach treatment decisions. Oncology has demonstrated the power of tailoring therapy to a patient’s unique biology, while cardiology and other specialties are increasingly adopting more individualized approaches.

Vascular surgery is poised to follow a similar path.

Emerging technologies, including thromboelastography with platelet mapping, allow physicians to evaluate how a patient’s platelets respond to antithrombotic medications. Rather than assuming every patient will respond similarly, these tools provide objective information about clotting function that can help guide personalized treatment decisions.

Instead of relying solely on population averages, clinicians can now better understand the patient sitting in front of them. That shift represents an important step toward more personalized, data-driven vascular care.

What personalized therapy could mean for patients

Our research, recently presented at the Society for Vascular Surgery’s Vascular Annual Meeting, demonstrated just how much platelet function can vary between patients receiving the same medications after lower extremity revascularization. By identifying patients with inadequate platelet inhibition and personalizing their antithrombotic therapy, we observed significantly lower rates of thrombosis and clinically significant restenosis, along with improvements in amputation-free survival, without an increase in major bleeding.

A more personalized approach allows clinicians to identify patients who remain at elevated thrombotic risk before complications occur. Rather than reacting after a bypass or stent has already failed, clinicians may be able to intervene earlier and optimize therapy based on an individual’s unique biology.

Moving from innovation to standard practice

While the research is promising, personalized coagulation profiling is not yet ready to become routine practice everywhere. The next step is validation through larger, multicenter randomized clinical trials to confirm that individualized treatment strategies consistently improve outcomes across diverse patient populations. Broader adoption will also require greater familiarity with platelet function testing, thoughtful integration into clinical workflows, and continued evidence demonstrating cost-effectiveness.

While these are important areas to address, these represent practical challenges rather than scientific barriers. Technology already exists, and the growing body of evidence suggests that individualized antithrombotic therapy deserves serious consideration as the next evolution in vascular care.

Looking ahead

The future of vascular patient care is not centered around prescribing more medication or performing more procedures. It is about delivering the right therapy to the right patient at the right time. As precision medicine continues to gain momentum, individualized antithrombotic therapy offers the potential to improve limb salvage, reduce complications, and fundamentally reshape how we care for patients living with peripheral artery disease.

About the author

Dr. Dua is an associate professor of surgery at the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH)/Harvard Medical School. She is the director of the peripheral artery disease center, associate director of the wound center, clinical director of research, and director of the sub-internship in vascular surgery. She is the past director of the vascular lab at the MGH. She developed and currently leads the Limb Evaluation and Amputation Program (LEAP) at the MGH. She also founded and runs the only comprehensive vascular surgery homeless clinic in the country at the MGH.

Anahita Dua is a vascular surgeon.

title: Incomplete medical records are the real AI blind spot
summary: A patient comes to you with a story you’ve heard in countless variations. She’s seen a nurse practitioner at an urgent care, a rheumatologist two states away when she was between jobs, and...
full_content:
A patient comes to you with a story you’ve heard in countless variations. She’s seen a nurse practitioner at an urgent care, a rheumatologist two states away when she was between jobs, and, more recently, an AI symptom checker that told her it was probably stress. By the time she’s in the exam room, you have maybe fifteen minutes, and a chart that reflects exactly one of those encounters.

During several decades in practice, I’ve watched the conversation around AI in health care shift from “Will this replace me?” to something more grounded: Patients are increasingly consulting an AI model before they call the doctor’s office. A physician podcast recently captured it well: Doctors are becoming the second opinion, with AI serving as the first. That framing is accurate, but it misses the part that actually matters.

During those same decades, documentation of clinical records has evolved significantly, from barely legible handwritten scribbles on paper charts, kept by individual providers and rarely shared, rife with opportunities for errors, to a current state where information is digitally collected and maintained within walled, proprietary ecosystems. Through all those years, until this very moment, one thing has not changed; it doesn’t matter whether the first opinion comes from a chatbot or the second opinion comes from a board-certified physician. Both are only as good as the record they’re reasoning over. And in 2026, that record is still, overwhelmingly, incomplete.

The chart you have is not the chart that exists

Every clinician knows this intuitively. The “complete” record in front of you is simply whatever happened to make it into your EHR. It’s not the walk-in clinic across town. It’s not the specialist visit from the insurance plan the patient had two jobs ago. It’s not the medication list from the pharmacy they switched away from.

Most systems that claim to unify records still rely on the patient logging into a separate portal for every prior provider, remembering a password they set once, and manually authorizing each release. Most patients don’t do that, and frankly, we shouldn’t expect them to.

The result is a chart that looks complete because it’s formatted like one, but functions like a fraction of the story. Modern EHR interfaces reinforce the illusion: tidy medication lists, clean problem summaries, and neatly organized timelines that imply completeness even when half the patient’s medical life is missing.

AI systems are now being asked to reason over that same partial picture.

A composite case we’ve all seen

Here’s a generalized example, not one patient, but a pattern many clinicians have encountered. A patient on a stable anticoagulant regimen arrives in an ED with new confusion. The ED has no record of the anticoagulant. It was prescribed by a physician outside their system, at a visit that predates the patient’s current insurance. A well-meaning resident, working from what’s visible in the chart, orders a workup that doesn’t account for the medication at all.

Nothing catastrophic happens this time. But the near-miss is real, and it wasn’t caused by poor clinical judgment. It was caused by an incomplete record that looked, on screen, indistinguishable from a complete one.

That’s the critical point: An incomplete chart doesn’t announce itself. There’s no banner that says, “Forty percent of this patient’s history is missing.” It just looks like a chart. And a physician (or increasingly, an AI system doing first-pass triage) has no way to distinguish “This problem doesn’t exist” from “This problem exists but isn’t visible to me.”

AI adds another layer of risk: When it fills gaps with statistical guesses, those guesses can appear authoritative. A human clinician can sense when something is missing. An AI model cannot.

This is becoming a liability question, not just a quality one

We don’t discuss this enough, perhaps because it’s uncomfortable. But a decision made on an incomplete record, where a fuller record was reasonably obtainable, is a different kind of exposure than a decision made on genuinely unavailable information.

As more of the “first pass” shifts to AI (symptom checkers, triage bots, documentation assistants), the standard for what counts as a reasonably complete record before a clinical judgment gets made will be scrutinized. Quality committees will examine it first. Plaintiffs’ attorneys will examine it next.

There’s also an equity dimension: Patients who move frequently, change insurance often, or rely on urgent care instead of primary care are disproportionately likely to have fragmented records. Incomplete data doesn’t just create risk; it creates unequal risk.

This is not alarmism. It’s a systems problem we should address deliberately now, rather than relearn case by case.

What actually needs to change

The solution is not asking patients to be better record-keepers, nor asking physicians to spend more of their fifteen minutes chasing down old charts by fax. Patients have never been good at being their own medical records custodians, and it’s not a fair expectation to place on someone who is sick. The fix must happen at the infrastructure level.

We need retrieval systems that:

  • Do not depend on a patient logging into every portal they’ve ever touched
  • Work through the provider relationship rather than around it
  • Surface gaps instead of quietly presenting a partial record as a whole one

We already have the technical building blocks to do this. What’s missing is the institutional will to treat “Does this AI or physician have the full picture?” as a patient-safety question worth solving, not a background inconvenience we’ve learned to tolerate. Until record completeness is treated as a core requirement, AI will continue to reason over partial stories, and clinicians will continue to inherit the consequences.

The question that actually matters

The next time an AI tool hands a patient a first opinion, or a physician forms a second one, the question worth asking isn’t simply, “Was the reasoning sound?” It’s “What fraction of this person’s actual medical life was that reasoning based on?”

Until we can answer that with confidence, every opinion in the chain, human or otherwise, is doing its best with less than the full story.

Miguel Venereo is a board-certified obstetrician-gynecologist and senior health care executive serving as chief medical officer at Medikarma, where he leads clinical strategy and data-integrity initiatives aimed at improving the reliability, completeness, and clinical usability of medical records across diverse care settings. His career spans hospital systems, Medicaid plans, and Medicare Advantage organizations.

Venereo has held leadership roles within Community Care Plan, Centene, and UnitedHealthcare, where he directed programs in utilization management, care coordination, predictive modeling, and quality-measure performance. His work in both Medicaid and Medicare Advantage environments has centered on strengthening documentation accuracy, reducing avoidable variation, and improving outcomes through better information flow and record completeness.

Across his career, including major administrative roles at Memorial Healthcare System, Venereo has led multidisciplinary initiatives that modernized peer review, enhanced patient-safety practices, and advanced system-level performance improvement. His ongoing work focuses on leveraging reliable clinical data and interoperable records to support equitable care delivery, reduce readmissions, and improve decision-making for clinicians, health plans, and patients. Medikarma’s About and For Organizations pages describe this work in more detail.

title: The structural causes of burnout no dashboard captures
summary: Modern health care has never measured more. Patient satisfaction scores. Throughput. Productivity. Readmission rates. Quality metrics. Efficiency benchmarks. Engagement surveys. Dashboards filled with...
full_content:
Modern health care has never measured more. Patient satisfaction scores. Throughput. Productivity. Readmission rates. Quality metrics. Efficiency benchmarks. Engagement surveys. Dashboards filled with indicators intended to quantify nearly every aspect of care.

The impulse is understandable. Measurement drives accountability, identifies variation, and helps organizations improve. But after years of navigating health care as a patient, a parent, a caregiver, and someone paying close attention to the people working inside these systems, I have begun to wonder whether we are measuring many of the right outcomes while overlooking the conditions required to produce them.

One of the most persistent assumptions in health care is that burnout is primarily an individual problem: a matter of resilience, stress management, or self-care. What I have observed suggests something different. Burnout is often a system outcome.

You cannot continuously increase documentation requirements, inbox volume, insurance friction, patient complexity, and productivity expectations while expecting unchanged levels of attention, empathy, and cognitive availability. At some point, the issue is no longer endurance. It is design.

Modern health care increasingly runs on invisible labor. It depends on unpaid caregiving by family members. It depends on nurses absorbing emotional distress that no metric captures. It depends on physicians completing hours of documentation after clinic ends. It depends on care coordinators, medical assistants, social workers, receptionists, and countless others quietly compensating for gaps that emerge elsewhere in the system.

Patients contribute invisible labor as well. They gather records, reconcile medication lists, coordinate appointments across disconnected specialties, navigate insurance requirements, follow up on referrals, monitor portal messages, and repeatedly retell the same story to different clinicians.

This is often described as patient engagement. Sometimes it is. But when patients become the primary coordinators of fragmented systems simply to receive appropriate care, that is not empowerment. It is system displacement.

Fragmentation magnifies these burdens. Care is increasingly distributed across siloed specialties, automated phone systems, delayed communication pathways, and disconnected digital portals. In many cases, patients and families become the only consistent thread holding the story together.

Health care organizations continue measuring outcomes with increasing sophistication. Yet far less visible are the conditions that make those outcomes possible: adequate staffing, cognitive bandwidth, continuity of relationships, psychological safety, thoughtful communication, and the time required for clinical judgment. We are becoming exceptionally skilled at measuring outputs while slowly eroding inputs. Over time, that imbalance becomes self-defeating.

Corporate medicine increasingly emphasizes measurable efficiency while relational medicine (the trust, continuity, and human connection that allow health care to function) becomes more difficult to sustain. The consequences are not merely emotional. They are clinical.

Fragmented care leads to missed context. Cognitive overload increases the likelihood of error. Administrative burden narrows attention. Time compression reduces opportunities to recognize nuance. None of this means clinicians care less. In my experience, the opposite is true. Many continue to provide extraordinary care despite systems that demand more while giving them less control over how that care is delivered.

Perhaps the most striking reality is that exhaustion is no longer confined to one group. Patients are exhausted by navigating health care. Clinicians are exhausted by working within it. Families are exhausted by coordinating between its parts.

Yet many institutional responses continue to focus on additional layers of optimization: more dashboards, more surveys, more training modules, more wellness initiatives. These efforts may be well intentioned, but they often address the consequences of structural overload rather than the overload itself.

Not everything that matters can be measured. Trust cannot be fully captured by a survey. Cognitive overload rarely appears on a dashboard. Continuity, attention, thoughtful listening, and the quiet work of helping another human being through illness resist easy quantification.

Yet these are not peripheral to health care. They are among its essential conditions.

Health care has become extraordinarily good at measuring performance. The next challenge may be learning to protect the human capacities that make high performance possible in the first place.

Sarah Whaley is a patient advocate.

title: AI strategy for hospitals: the 5 mistakes boards make
summary: Artificial intelligence is no longer a future issue for hospital boards. It is already affecting clinical documentation, patient communication, revenue cycle operations, imaging, scheduling, research,...
full_content:
Artificial intelligence is no longer a future issue for hospital boards. It is already affecting clinical documentation, patient communication, revenue cycle operations, imaging, scheduling, research, cybersecurity, and physician workflow. In many organizations, AI is entering through the side door before leadership has created a clear strategy. That is risky.

A hospital does not need an AI strategy because AI is fashionable. It needs one because unmanaged AI creates clinical, operational, legal, financial, and reputational risk.

The first mistake is treating AI as an IT project. AI touches technology, but it is not only a technology issue. It changes how work is done, how decisions are supported, how patients experience care, and how clinicians spend their time. That makes it a board-level governance issue.

The second mistake is chasing tools before defining priorities. A hospital can buy an AI product for documentation, another for patient messaging, another for imaging, another for coding, and another for analytics. Each may look useful in isolation. Together, they can create confusion if they do not fit a coherent plan. Boards should start with a simple question: What problem are we trying to solve?

  • If the priority is clinician burnout, measure time in the record, inbox volume, documentation quality, and after-hours work.
  • If the priority is access, measure scheduling delays, referral friction, patient navigation, and no-show patterns.
  • If the priority is safety, measure near misses, communication failures, handoff problems, and delayed follow-up.
  • If the priority is financial performance, measure denial rates, documentation gaps, coding accuracy, and operational bottlenecks.

AI should be attached to real problems and real measures.

The third mistake is failing to create guardrails. Health systems need clear rules for what AI can and cannot do. Which tools are approved? Which data can be entered? Who reviews output? How are errors reported? What happens when the AI recommendation conflicts with clinical judgment? How will bias, privacy, security, and patient transparency be handled? Answer these questions before a crisis.

The fourth mistake is excluding clinicians from the process. No board should approve an AI initiative without meaningful input from the people who will use it. A tool that looks impressive in a boardroom may fail in a clinic, emergency department, operating room, or nursing workflow. Clinicians know where work breaks. They also know when a tool creates risk that a vendor demo will not show.

The fifth mistake is assuming adoption equals success. A tool can be widely used and still be poorly designed. It can save time for one department while creating work for another. It can improve documentation volume while weakening note quality. It can speed up a process without making it safer.

Boards should require outcome reporting. Not only usage. Outcomes.

They should also ask who is accountable when the tool is wrong. Accountability cannot be left vague. If a machine summary misses a key result, if a patient message is routed incorrectly, or if a recommendation creates confusion, the organization needs a clear process for review and correction. That is not a reason to avoid AI. It is a reason to govern it carefully.

A practical AI health care strategy should include several parts:

  • A governance structure with clinical, technical, legal, compliance, security, and operational leadership
  • A prioritized list of use cases tied to measurable problems
  • A review process for vendors and internally built tools
  • Clear rules for data use, privacy, patient communication, and human oversight
  • Training for clinicians and staff
  • A way to report errors, concerns, and unintended consequences
  • Regular board-level review of results

None of this has to slow innovation. Done well, governance speeds the right innovation by reducing confusion and building trust.

Hospitals are entering a period where patients, clinicians, vendors, regulators, and competitors will all move quickly around AI. Organizations that wait for perfect certainty will fall behind. Organizations that deploy without strategy will create avoidable risk. The responsible path is to lead deliberately.

Every hospital board should know where AI is already being used, where it is being considered, what risks it creates, what problems it is meant to solve, and how success will be measured. AI in health care is not just about algorithms. It is about leadership.

Harvey Castro is an emergency physician, author, keynote speaker, chief AI officer, and physician futurist known as DR GPT™. He writes and speaks about artificial intelligence in health care, digital health, space medicine, and the future of human-centered care. Learn more at his website.

Castro has held a range of roles across his career, including CEO, physician, and medical correspondent for major media outlets. He has developed multiple health care apps and consulted for health care companies, with the goal of increasing awareness of digital health and driving practical change in how technology reaches patients and clinicians.

He is the author of Bing Copilot and Other LLM: Revolutionizing Healthcare With AI, Solving Infamous Cases with Artificial Intelligence, The AI-Driven Entrepreneur: Unlocking Entrepreneurial Success with Artificial Intelligence Strategies and Insights, ChatGPT and Healthcare: The Key To The New Future of Medicine, ChatGPT and Healthcare: Unlocking The Potential Of Patient Empowerment, Revolutionize Your Health and Fitness with ChatGPT’s Modern Weight Loss Hacks, Success Reinvention, and Apple Vision Healthcare Pioneers: A Community for Professionals & Patients.

He shares updates on LinkedIn, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and X. #DRGPT

title: Postpartum pelvic floor therapy protects you at 75
summary: 1. The 6-week myth vs. the 30-year reality We all know the current standard of maternal health care operates on a dangerous illusion: the big ole’ 6-week checkup. We tell moms that once they pas...
full_content:
1. The 6-week myth vs. the 30-year reality

We all know the current standard of maternal health care operates on a dangerous illusion: the big ole’ 6-week checkup. We tell moms that once they pass this test, congrats! Recovery is complete and they are cleared to return to normal life and exercise.

It would be convenient if bodies healed by the calendar, wouldn’t it? What really happens during pregnancy, birth, and lactation triggers a profound physical structural shift, one that casts a 30-year echo forward into your life.

How you heal right now can dictate your health decades down the line. This is true for any injury, but I’d like to focus on changes unique to the female body. Actual postpartum recovery isn’t just about bouncing back to chase a toddler today. It is about protecting your independence, mobility, and survival when you are 70, 80, and beyond.

2. The invisible depletion of matrescence (or is it not that invisible?)

Pregnancy and nursing are beautiful, but they are also a literal drain on your physical reserves. To build a new human life, your body willingly bankrupts its own resources if left unmanaged.

  • The mineral tax: If your dietary intake isn’t optimal, a growing baby will pull calcium and vital minerals directly out of your bones and muscle tissue.
  • The biomechanical shift: Carrying a child radically alters your center of gravity, causing severe postural compensations, stretched core muscles, and deep pelvic imbalances.

The good news is most women recover their bone density within 6-12 months following lactation. However, some structural changes do not heal spontaneously. When left uncorrected, a stretched deep core and a weakened pelvic floor don’t just go away. Spines, ribs, and pelvises don’t just realign themselves. Muscle doesn’t just magically rebuild itself. It all silently waits, setting the stage for chronic back pain, urinary urgency and incontinence, and other problems like pelvic organ prolapse, metabolic changes and weight issues, future bone loss and fragility, and a decreased quality of life.

3. The menopause compound effect

In my clinic, I routinely treat women in their 50s and 60s who trace their current physical limitations back decades. They sit across from me and say, “My back pain started right after I had my second child,” or, “I’ve been dealing with this leaking ever since my son was born.”

For years, they tolerated these symptoms, believing they were just the unavoidable “price of motherhood.” But uncorrected postpartum issues do not stay static. We can compensate for a long time; our bodies still have to move; we still have to do our daily tasks, work, and take care of our families. These patterns can break down over time, or wait for a catalyst like menopause.

When menopause hits, the protective blanket of estrogen drops. This sudden hormonal shift can act as an accelerant on an already weakened physical foundation:

  • The bone and muscle melt: Decreased estrogen triggers accelerated bone density loss and muscle wasting.
  • The structural collapse: A pelvic floor and deep core that were already struggling, silently or not, are stripped of their hormonal support. Taking estrogen from a vagina is like taking my chocolate away from me and expecting me to still be happy. What was once occasional bladder urgency or leaking, or mild back pain morphs into debilitating pain, or more severe urinary symptoms, vaginal dryness, or pelvic pain. The pelvis starts having a tantrum.
  • The systemic domino effect: When pain and muscle loss make movement difficult, a woman’s activity level plummets. This physical stagnation increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.
  • The ultimate issue: Our 30-year problem presents itself. Adding faster bone loss to decreasing muscle support and balance creates opportunity for bone fractures. For an aging woman, a hip or spine fracture is not just an injury. The resulting frailty and loss of mobility directly lead to a tragically higher rate of early mortality.

4. Pelvic and women’s health rehabilitation: banking your capital

Pelvic physical therapy should not just be a reactionary treatment for when things break down. Instead, specialized pelvic and women’s health rehabilitation is essential, preventative longevity medicine.

Just as you invest financially for retirement, you have to invest physically in your structural reserves. Treating postpartum muscle weaknesses and imbalances is how you bank structural capital before the chaos of menopause arrives.

  • Rebuilding the foundation: Specialized therapy targets the deep core and pelvic floor. It restores optimal neuromuscular coordination. It stabilizes the entire lumbo-pelvic-hip complex to reduce chronic back pain and manage pressures to control urine.
  • Correcting the imbalances: We can retrain postural shifts and muscular compensation patterns developed during pregnancy. This slows premature joint wear and tear to reduce pain.
  • Future-proofing your body: By building muscle mass, optimal bone loading patterns, and deep core integrity in early adulthood, you create a physical buffer. When menopause eventually reduces your estrogen, your body declines from a position of strength, not baseline vulnerability.

5. Takeaway: Postpartum care is longevity care

The cultural narrative surrounding motherhood needs a wild upgrade. Prioritizing your physical recovery after having a baby is not selfish, it is certainly not cosmetic, and it is completely non-negotiable for your long-term survival.

The leaking, the back pain, and the core weakness you push through today are the vectors for the frailty and loss of independence you could face tomorrow.

Taking care of your postpartum body is a profound act of future-proofing. When you step into a pelvic health clinic today, you are not just healing the mother of a newborn. You are actively protecting the vibrant, independent, and fiercely mobile 75-year-old woman you are destined to become.

Amy Bourne Rozelle earned a Doctor of Physical Therapy and is a double board-certified specialist in pelvic rehab and women’s health, affiliated with the Rehabilitation Institute of Michigan. She works directly with women to bridge the gap between early maternal care and healthy aging, transforming how we view physical recovery. She shares updates on LinkedIn.

title: Physician burnout and the question science cannot answer
summary: I left Nepal to train in a country I barely knew, carrying the kind of ambition that doesn’t leave room for doubt. Internal medicine residency, then a rheumatology fellowship at the National Ins...
full_content:
I left Nepal to train in a country I barely knew, carrying the kind of ambition that doesn’t leave room for doubt. Internal medicine residency, then a rheumatology fellowship at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). I pictured a career built in clinical research, publishing, discovering. That was the plan, and for years I didn’t question it.

The turning point

Then our daughter was born, and everything about that plan stopped making sense. Her medical needs were complex from the start, the kind that reorganize a family overnight. I remember the specific disorientation of that period, not just the exhaustion, but the deeper uncertainty of not knowing which direction was even right anymore. The research path I had built my identity around no longer fit the life in front of me, and I had no map for what came next.

Building something new

What came next was a shift I didn’t plan and couldn’t have designed on purpose. I moved from an employed physician position toward building my own practice, Empowered Arthritis and Rheumatology Center. I didn’t build it because I had a five-year plan. I built it for two reasons. The employed position wasn’t giving me what I needed either, no real growth, no sense that I was creating anything beyond seeing the next patient on the schedule. And it was the only structure flexible enough to hold everything that mattered to me at once, our daughter’s needs, our son growing up watching how his parents handled hard things, my wife’s own work building something to help other mothers through complicated pregnancies and postpartum periods, and a clinical practice I could actually shape instead of just work inside of.

Where faith came from

I did not walk through any of that certain I was making the right call. What carried me through it was faith. Not a tidy, confident faith. A faith that showed up mostly as the willingness to keep going when I could not see the outcome, and to trust that the effort itself had meaning even when the results were nowhere in sight yet.

That’s not where I started. My father was deeply religious, and for a long stretch of my early life I rebelled against that so completely that I called myself an atheist, mostly to prove I could think for myself. Life has a way of correcting overcorrections. Somewhere in the middle of raising a medically complex child, building a practice from nothing, and trying to be present for a marriage and two kids at the same time, I became a genuine believer again, not out of inherited habit this time, but because I needed something bigger than my own control to hold onto, and it held.

There was another piece to it too.
