title: 全球首证！金匙科技mNGS试剂盒获三类证，高通量病原诊断迈入标准化时代
summary: 金匙科技自主研发的mNGS试剂盒获国家药监局三类医疗器械注册证，为国内病原宏基因组检测领域首张三类注册证，也是全球首个国家级药监机构批准的mNGS感染病原诊断试剂盒。目前，美国FDA尚未批准任何mNGS诊断试剂盒上市，欧盟也暂无广谱感染病原mNGS测序试剂盒完成注册审批。中国能够率先突围，源于旺盛的真实临床需求及技术迭代带来的明确临床获益。国内病原微生物检测市场持续增长，mNGS、tNGS处于低渗...
full_content:
金匙科技自主研发的mNGS试剂盒，正式取得国家药品监督管理局（NMPA）三类医疗器械注册证。这既是国内病原宏基因组（mNGS）检测领域首张三类注册证，也是全球首个由国家级药监机构批准上市的mNGS感染病原诊断试剂盒。



放眼全球，mNGS技术的临床转化与产品注册，是各国监管机构共同面对的难题。


美国FDA至今尚未批准任何mNGS诊断试剂盒上市。UCSF团队开发、Delve Bio商业化的脑脊液mNGS检测仅拿到FDA突破性器械认定，依旧以LDT（实验室自建项目）模式在CLIA认证实验室开展，其IMPACT临床研究直到2026年5月才启动入组。Karius针对免疫低下患者肺部感染的血浆cfDNA检测同样取得突破性器械认定，但仍依托CLIA中心实验室做LDT服务，并未获得FDA试剂盒上市批准。


欧盟IVDR法规正式实施后，对IVD产品临床证据、性能验证、公告机构审核提出更严格要求，目前暂无广谱感染病原mNGS测序试剂盒完成注册审批。


中国能够率先突围源于旺盛的真实临床需求，以及技术迭代带来的明确临床获益。根据弗若斯特沙利文数据，国内病原微生物检测市场体量持续走高：2020‑2024年国内医院病原微生物检测量由8800万次增长至1.48亿次，年复合增长率13.9%；预计2035年检测量将达到3.315亿次。mNGS、tNGS处于低渗透高增长阶段，2020‑2024年两类技术检测量从30万次攀升至310万次，复合年增长率79.3%。


临床端的迫切需求，倒逼技术走向标准化，也推动产品审批、收费政策落地。当美国仍停留在LDT探索、欧盟处于法规过渡的时候，中国已经完成严苛的三类医疗器械全流程审评，实现mNGS血流感染病原诊断从LDT服务到标准化IVD产品的法规跨越。伴随着三类试剂盒上市、收费条目建立，行业将迎来百亿级增量空间。



感染性疾病带来的全球疾病负担，与心血管疾病、肿瘤相当。mNGS凭借无需预设靶标、病原覆盖广、可检出未知病原体的优势，是重症感染、疑难感染、免疫抑制人群感染的核心诊断工具。


但在此之前，全球mNGS病原检测大多以中心实验室服务为主。不同医疗机构的试剂配方、实验流程、测序深度、生信分析规则缺少统一标准，检测结果可比性不足，严重限制此技术在临床广泛使用。


本次三类证获批彻底改变这一现状。试剂盒从试剂组分、实验操作、数据质控到生物信息分析，全部通过注册检验、多中心临床试验及临床试验现场核查，可实现不同机构、不同批次检测结果稳定、可比，为mNGS试剂盒进入医院广泛使用扫清了核心障碍。




2021年12月，国家发改委发布《“十四五”生物经济发展规划》，将高通量基因测序列为前沿生物技术创新重点。



临床专家陆续发布mNGS临床应用专家共识，明确其在疑难、重症感染中的临床价值及使用建议。



2025年12月31日，国标GB/T 46943‑2025《临床实验室检测和体外诊断系统 病原宏基因组高通量测序性能确认通用要求》正式发布，将于2027‑01‑01实施，填补国内mNGS实验室性能评价国家标准空白。2026年4月，《宏基因组高通量测序技术临床实验室规范化应用指南（2026版）》刊发于《中华医学杂志》，围绕实验室环境、人员、标本、干湿实验流程、质控、报告解读输出15条推荐意见，指导各级医院规范开展mNGS检测。



2026年8月14日，国家医保局发布《检验类医疗服务价格项目立项指南（试行）》，设立全国统一的mNGS、tNGS病原检测独立收费项目：mNGS按次计费，不限病原数量；tNGS按检测面板计价。



面对mNGS注册全球无先例可循的现状，国家药监局持续与企业沟通，多次组织专家会，逐个解决病原验证范围、阳性判断值、对比方法、实验室管理和报告范围等多个难题。金匙科技历时八年，完成两次临床试验（累计约4000例样本）并通过临床试验现场核查，最终获批首证。


从临床应用场景，到实验室规范化开展，再到收费条目的落地和首张三类证获批，中国临床宏基因组检测的全链路合规路径已经全部打通，从局限的实验室自建项目模式（LDT）跨越进质量标准化的体外诊断模式。



拿到血流感染mNGS试剂盒注册证，只是金匙科技产品布局的开端。下一步公司将拓展呼吸道等更多样本类型适应症，同步推进靶向测序试剂盒、AI辅助诊断软件的注册申报，搭建覆盖多临床场景、多样本类型的病原诊断完整产品矩阵。


纵观产业发展，细分赛道的规模化爆发，总是始于关键技术的标准化、产品化。中国诞生全球首个mNGS感染病原诊断三类证，既验证本土企业的创新实力，也标志我国引领了mNGS病原诊断赛道的规则建设，行业正式迈入标准化新时代。

title: Student loans are not blocking your practice ownership
summary: Clinicians are trained to demand certainty before they act. In the operatory or the exam room, that risk-averse instinct is exactly what keeps patients safe. Applied to career decisions, the same inst...
full_content:
Clinicians are trained to demand certainty before they act. In the operatory or the exam room, that risk-averse instinct is exactly what keeps patients safe. Applied to career decisions, the same instinct becomes one of the most expensive habits in modern health care.

There is a sentence I hear almost every week from young clinicians, and it sounds so responsible that nobody ever questions it: “I’ll think about ownership once my student loans are under control.” I work in dentistry, where I’ve spent years as a buyer-side advisor helping associates purchase practices, and I want to make the case that this sentence, spoken by dentists, physicians, and veterinarians alike, deserves far more scrutiny than it gets.

Call it debt-phobia. Today’s graduates leave training with historic loan balances, often $350,000 or more. The debt feels like a guillotine hanging over the doctor’s neck. And who wants to take on more debt with that over their head? So the new clinician settles into an employed role that feels safe, planning to revisit ownership “in a few years,” and starts writing student loan payments. Three years become five. Five become a career. The cage is comfortable enough, the salary is good enough, and the door was never actually locked.

Here is what the dental data shows, and it is worth every employed clinician’s attention. The share of private-practice dentists who own their practices has held steady at about 89 percent for decades. However, while younger dentists still end up as owners, the data show they’re taking between 5 to 7 years to get there. Young dentists aren’t avoiding ownership. They are delaying it, and paying dearly for the delay. The average dental practice owner out-earns the average employee dentist by $151,700 per year once the practice is stabilized. Stretch a five-to-seven-year delay across a career and the foregone earnings alone, assuming a 6 percent rate of return, is $1.15 million, before counting the equity built in someone else’s business the entire time.

Many doctors’ bias toward certainty and attention to detail get them into analysis paralysis with career choices. However, I’ve noticed that once clinicians understand the data around how willing banks are to lend them money, they start to feel more confident. Without the data, clinicians assume the balance of their student loans disqualifies them for ownership, because that is how mortgages work. Practice acquisition lending doesn’t work that way. Even though it feels scary to layer on a practice loan on top of a high student loan balance, banks don’t deal in feelings. The data show doctor acquisition loans are the second safest small business loans on the planet (funeral homes take first place). In dentistry, banks routinely finance one hundred percent of a practice purchase for buyers plus an additional $50,000 to $100,000 in working capital with no collateral beyond the diploma on the wall. What lenders actually examine is whether the business can cover its overhead, service the note, and pay the owner, and whether the buyer’s payment history suggests a person who doesn’t spend every dollar they make.

In other words: The debt-on-debt fear treats two unrelated questions as one. “Can I afford more monthly payments?” is a household question. “Can this business fund its own purchase?” is the question the bank is asking, and it is the one that decides.

None of this means every employed clinician should run out and buy something. Ownership is not a moral imperative, and some excellent careers are built deliberately as employees. My argument is to make a deliberate choice. Most young clinicians are not choosing employment. They are defaulting to it, on the strength of a fear that doesn’t survive contact with the facts around how the financing actually works, and then narrating the default as prudence.

So here is the reframing I offer the associates I work with, and it travels well beyond dentistry. Stop asking whether you feel ready for ownership; that feeling arrives after the leap, never before it, in business exactly as in parenthood. Ask instead whether you are prepared: a couple of years of clinical speed, a modest cash reserve, a clean payment history, and honest scrutiny of any business you might buy, starting with whether its revenue can genuinely support the overhead, the loan, and your family at the same time. Preparation is a finishable checklist. The feeling is a horizon that recedes as you walk toward it.

The golden cage is real, and it is genuinely comfortable. But the door has been unlocked the entire time, and the clinicians who eventually walk through it almost all say the same thing afterward: The debt was never the barrier. The story they told themselves about the debt was.

Brian Hanks is a dental accountant.

title: The buyer is not the user in electronic health records
summary: I have practiced medicine for more than three decades, thirty years of obstetrics and gynecology, and now addiction medicine. For seventeen of those years, I have worked inside electronic medical reco...
full_content:
I have practiced medicine for more than three decades, thirty years of obstetrics and gynecology, and now addiction medicine. For seventeen of those years, I have worked inside electronic medical records that waste my time, interrupt my thinking, and stand between me and the person in front of me.

Like a lot of clinicians, I kept notebooks, running lists of what a truly helpful record would do, scribbled after long evenings of clicking. When I finally compared my notes against the published literature, I found something both consoling and damning. A national initiative, a database of half a million clinician surveys, and colleagues on every platform have been writing the same list, in remarkably similar words, for years. The problem is not that no one knows what to build. The problem is that the people who know are not the people who buy.

That sentence is the whole disease in miniature. Electronic health records are not designed by physicians, or with meaningful physician input. They are built by software developers with little firsthand experience of everyday clinical work, then marketed and sold to the administrators who run health care organizations. The buyer is not the user. Administrators purchase for billing efficiency and regulatory compliance (legitimate concerns), but those are valued far above the needs of the providers who touch the software hundreds of times a day, and above the needs of the patients the whole enterprise exists to serve. Members of the C-suite never chart in these systems themselves. So the damage stays invisible from where they sit, and the productivity quietly destroyed every day never shows up on their dashboard.

The market compounds it. The pile of federal requirements for certified records, well-meaning but overbuilt, makes entering the market expensive, so it consists of a few large vendors with little reason to court the end user (who is not buying) and little reason to innovate (the package already sells). The result is software that, on user-friendliness, lags a decade or more behind ordinary commercial tools, behind Word, behind Excel, and further still behind the website of any large internet company. Software was invented to eliminate repetitive data entry. The electronic record, uniquely among every category of software I know, multiplies it. It is the biggest time thief in medicine, and, renewed every year through license fees, medicine’s most expensive software failure.

There is really only one way to make a chief executive understand what this feels like. So here is a thought experiment.

Take away the executive assistant. Replace the sleek laptop with a machine running an antique operating system and a version of Word stripped of every modern convenience: no autosave, no autocomplete, no memory of anything typed before, no ability to pull in information that already exists elsewhere in the system. Require a full login every time the program opens. Then have the system log the executive out at random intervals, without warning, mid-sentence, displaying only the words “YOU have logged out,” with everything unsaved erased. When the executive calls IT, have IT explain that this is for security reasons. Make reformatting a paragraph take five or six checkboxes. Route every print job through a network that crashes at random, to a printer three rooms away. Let the executive work like that for one quarter, while being told, weekly, to increase output.

That is the everyday reality of the record for the people documenting in it. Then, and only then, let us talk about volume targets.

And this is not only my complaint. The data agree with the notebooks. The KLAS Arch Collaborative, the largest standing dataset of clinician record experience, with more than 500,000 standardized surveys since 2017, reports that 59 percent of over 25,000 surveyed physicians say their record does not enable efficiency. Among clinicians reporting burnout, the record is named as a contributor by 62 percent of physicians and 43 percent of nurses. In the Collaborative’s 2026 report, spanning 92 organizations and more than 121,000 clinicians, only 22 percent of physicians, and a dismal 12 percent of nurses, rate their experience at the top level.

The AMIA 25×5 initiative, funded by the National Library of Medicine, later echoed by the Surgeon General’s advisory on health worker burnout, was motivated partly by a finding that deserves to be far better known: U.S. clinicians spend 75 percent more time on documentation than clinicians in other wealthy countries, in some cases using software from the very same vendor. The burden is not an inevitable property of digitization. It is a property of American implementation choices, which means it is a property we can change.

And when Black Book Research asked 274 hospital-affiliated physicians in 2025 to name the single most urgent improvement they wanted, the winner, by a wide margin, was AI-powered documentation. The sufferers are unanimous about where the pain is. The only people who seem unable to see it are the ones holding the purchase order.

Matthias Muenzer is an obstetrician-gynecologist.

title: The hidden payment gap crushing independent physicians
summary: The health care system is supposed to put the patient first. Physicians evaluate, diagnose, treat, and manage risk. Hospitals, insurers, administrators, and regulators exist to support that clinical r...
full_content:
The health care system is supposed to put the patient first. Physicians evaluate, diagnose, treat, and manage risk. Hospitals, insurers, administrators, and regulators exist to support that clinical relationship and not to displace it.

Yet the current structure of American medicine produces the opposite outcome. Patients face longer waits and higher barriers. Independent physicians confront declining real reimbursement and mounting administrative demands. Practices are acquired by health systems. Physicians spend more time on documentation and prior authorization than on patients. And the same clinical service can generate dramatically different payments depending solely on who owns the facility where it is delivered.

This is not a failure of individual doctors, hospitals, or insurers. It is a structural problem created by the interaction of payment policy, administrative requirements, and market incentives that increasingly reward institutional ownership over independent clinical care.

Payment does not treat equivalent care equally

One of the clearest distortions is the difference between payment for services in a freestanding physician office versus a hospital outpatient department. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) has repeatedly documented substantial site-of-service differentials. In 2023, an epidural injection in a freestanding office generated roughly one-third of what is being done in the hospital outpatient department. Depending on the service, total payments can differ by 80 percent or more.

MedPAC has stated that when a service can be safely provided in different settings, a prudent purchaser should not pay more simply because it occurs in a more expensive institutional setting. KFF has noted that these payment differences create financial incentives for hospitals to acquire physician practices, because converting an independent office into a hospital outpatient department can generate higher total payments for the same clinical work. If the patient receives the same physician, the same evaluation, and the same treatment, a large payment differential based primarily on ownership functions as an ownership premium rather than payment for additional clinical value.

Independent physicians are being asked to do more with less

While institutional settings enjoy higher total payments, independent practices face a stark arithmetic problem. Adjusted for inflation in practice costs, Medicare physician payments have declined approximately 33 percent since 2001. Between 2001 and 2026, Medicare physician payment rose only about 10 percent, while the cost of running a medical practice rose approximately 63 percent, according to American Medical Association (AMA) analyses. Those costs include staff, technology, liability insurance, supplies, facilities, and regulatory compliance.

When reimbursement fails to keep pace with expenses, practices have limited options: see more patients, shorten visits, reduce staffing, cut clinical hours, stop accepting certain plans, consolidate, or close. None of these options improves patient care. They simply redistribute scarce physician time away from the exam room.

Administrative work is displacing clinical work

Prior authorization illustrates the burden with particular clarity. The AMA’s 2025 physician survey found that physicians and staff spend an average of 13 hours per week per physician on prior authorization. Practices process roughly 40 requests per physician each week. Forty percent of physicians report having staff dedicated exclusively to this task.

The clinical consequences are measurable. Ninety-five percent of physicians reported that prior authorization delays necessary care. Seventy-nine percent said patients abandon treatment because of authorization barriers. Ninety-two percent said it negatively affects clinical outcomes. In a separate AMA survey, 29 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event for a patient, including hospitalization, permanent harm, or death. A system designed to control costs has layered on bureaucracy that consumes hundreds of hours of clinical labor annually, time that could otherwise be spent evaluating patients or coordinating complex care.

The rock and the hard place

Physicians are trapped between two opposing forces. On one side, payers reduce real reimbursement and intensify scrutiny of coding and medical necessity. Independent practices lack the negotiating leverage and administrative infrastructure of large systems, so the pressure falls hardest on them. Survival often requires higher volume and shorter visits.

On the other side, medical boards, regulators, and retrospective reviewers treat documentation as primary evidence of whether the standard of care was met. A clinically appropriate decision that was imperfectly documented because the system demanded greater volume can become the basis for investigation or discipline. A documentation deficiency is not automatically a clinical deficiency. Treating them as identical creates an unfair accountability system that ignores the operational realities physicians face.

Consolidation becomes the rational response

When independent practices receive lower effective reimbursement while hospital-owned settings can generate higher total payments for comparable services, ownership itself becomes financially valuable. Acquisition becomes rational. Once a practice is converted, the physician’s clinical work may remain essentially the same, yet the billing pathway and total payment change. The patient still needs the same clinical judgment; the organizational structure surrounding that judgment has simply become more expensive. This produces a self-reinforcing cycle: higher institutional payments → greater financial advantage for consolidation → fewer independent practices → greater institutional market power → continued consolidation.

A simple analogy

Imagine a family-owned restaurant and a large franchise. Both employ equally skilled chefs who prepare essentially the same meal. If the franchise is reimbursed substantially more solely because of its institutional structure, the higher payment does not prove the customer received a better meal. It may simply support the layers of administration surrounding the chef. Health care now operates under a similar incentive structure.

Patients ultimately pay the price

The consequences extend far beyond physician dissatisfaction. When independent practices close or merge, patients lose choices. When physicians reduce hours or retire early, wait times lengthen. When prior authorization delays care, patients wait for medications, procedures, and specialist visits. When payment policy encourages consolidation, costs rise and independent options shrink. MedPAC has warned that financial pressures on physician practices can threaten access and that higher payments in institutional settings increase costs for beneficiaries and taxpayers. The result is a vicious cycle: lower real physician payment → financial pressure → higher volume and administrative burden → less time per patient → burnout and consolidation → fewer independent physicians → reduced access → greater institutional dependence.

What reform should prioritize

A sustainable system must restore a clear hierarchy: patient first, clinical team second, supporting organizations third. Practical steps include:

  • Moving toward site-neutral payment for services that can safely be provided in lower-cost settings, as MedPAC has repeatedly recommended.
  • Restoring physician payment that reflects the actual cost of running a modern practice.
  • Subjecting prior authorization and documentation requirements to rigorous cost-benefit analysis. A process that consumes 13 hours per physician each week must demonstrably improve outcomes or reduce total costs.
  • Ensuring independent practices are not artificially disadvantaged by ownership-based payment differentials.
  • Distinguishing, in regulatory review, between clinically inappropriate care, reasonable judgment under uncertainty, and documentation or administrative shortcomings.
  • Measuring success by patient access, time with clinicians, timely delivery of needed care, and whether health care dollars reach clinical care.

Conclusion

The patient is the reason the health care system exists. Physicians translate medical knowledge into individualized care. Every other component of the system should support that relationship rather than compete with it for resources.

The evidence shows a clear pattern: Physician payment has failed to keep pace with practice costs; administrative burdens consume substantial clinical time; prior authorization produces measurable delays and harm; and site-of-service payment differences create incentives for consolidation. Intentional design to eliminate independent practice is not required for these incentives to produce consolidation. A system does not need deliberate hostility to generate harmful outcomes.

If current incentives make it rational for physicians to spend less time with patients, for independent practices to sell, and for additional layers to insert themselves between doctor and patient, the system is sending the wrong signals. Reform should realign payment, regulation, and organizational incentives with the system’s stated purpose: accessible, high-quality care for patients. Anything less will continue to drive capable physicians out of independent practice, reduce patient choice, and worsen access for those the system is supposed to serve.

Kayvan Haddadan is a physiatrist and pain management physician, and president and medical director of Advanced Pain Diagnostic & Solutions, a multidisciplinary pain management practice in California that he founded in 2012. A physician and surgeon licensed by the Medical Board of California, he is double board-certified in pain medicine and physical medicine and rehabilitation. He is also certified in controlled substance registration through the DEA and serves as a qualified medical examiner through California’s Department of Industrial Relations Division of Workers’ Compensation.

Dr. Haddadan earned his Bachelor of Science degree from the College of Alborz in Tehran, Iran, and his medical degree from Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences. He later received his Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates certification in Philadelphia, completed an internship in medical surgery at Loyola University Medical Center’s Stritch School of Medicine in Illinois, and finished his residency in physical medicine and rehabilitation at the same institution. He completed his fellowship in pain medicine at California Pacific Medical Center’s Pacific Pain Treatment Center and also trained in medical acupuncture for physicians at the University of California, Los Angeles David Geffen School of Medicine.

Dr. Haddadan has contributed to 29 research publications across multiple specialties, including pain management, cardiology, pulmonology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, and infectious disease. His work has examined topics such as hyperlipidemia in high cardiovascular risk patients, hyperuricemia and gout management, type 2 diabetes and hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma therapies, influenza treatment, irritable bowel syndrome, and opioid related complications in chronic pain care. His research has also included clinical outcome studies in spinal cord stimulation and award-winning presentations on neuropathic pain management and neuromuscular disorders.

title: 重磅解读！首部《医疗保障法》通过，它将如何改变医疗创新？
summary: 8月28日《医疗保障法》三易其稿后正式通过，2027年1月1日起施行。作为我国医疗保障领域首部专门法律，共7章56条，覆盖关键环节，将多项权益纳入统一法律框架，解决报销等待等痛点，为高价创新疗法拓宽支付通道。该法出台改变了医疗创新运行逻辑，医保规定将固化为完整制度框架，对创新药企等产生深远影响。其带来三个核心转变：医保角色从“付款人”转向“价值购买者”，驱动产业竞争规则重组；创新竞争从“获批即商业...
full_content:
8月28日下午，经过十四届全国人大常委会第二十四次会议表决，《医疗保障法》在三易其稿后正式通过，将于2027年1月1日起施行。《医疗保障法》共7章56条，覆盖医疗保障体系、基金、服务、监督管理与法律责任等关键环节。

 

《医疗保障法》是我国医疗保障领域首部专门法律。这是一项与人们生活息息相关的法律，将参保、待遇、异地结算、医疗救助、长护险等权益纳入统一法律框架，重点解决垫资跑腿、报销等待等痛点，同时通过多层次保障体系为高价创新疗法拓宽支付通道。

 

更重要的是，《医疗保障法》的出台，改变了时下方兴未艾的医疗创新的运行逻辑。以后，医保的各项规定将从分散的支付政策、采购规则和监管要求，固化为从筹资、准入、支付到结算、监管的完整制度框架。对于创新药企、医疗器械企业而言，医保不再只是产品上市后的一个准入关口，而将对产品定义、临床证据、定价策略、渠道供应与数据合规的完整链路，产生深远影响。



《医疗保障法》立法带来的底层逻辑转变，是医保的角色从单纯的"付款人"转向"价值购买者"。这一定位变化，驱动了整个产业竞争规则的重组。

 

第一，创新竞争从"获批即商业化"转向"连续闯关"。过去，创新药获批上市就等于拿到商业化入场券。医保谈判更多被视为价格博弈，企业公关能力往往比临床价值更能决定结果。

 

如今，这个逻辑正在失效。药监注册回答"安全、有效、质量可控"。医保支付则追问，相较现有方案，产品多创造了多少临床价值？新增成本是否合理？能否被真实世界的医疗服务体系承接？获批只是第一关，后面还有证据关、定价关、可及关。 企业需要在立项阶段即考虑：临床试验终点是否对标医保评审标准？真实世界数据从哪里来？药物经济学模型怎么做？供应保障能力能否支撑放量？

 

第二，企业获得制度化参与接口，但证据责任同步加重。全国人大常委会法工委发言人黄海华表示，国务院医疗保障行政部门在组织制定基本医疗保险基金支付范围、组织开展循证医学和经济性评价时，除了征求有关部门意见外，还应当采取适当方式听取医疗机构、药品经营单位、相关企业、专家和参保人员的意见，增强相关工作的科学性、民主性。

 

这给了企业一个制度化的发言渠道，但不是让企业主导目录或定价。权利对应义务。企业递交的注册研究、真实世界数据、药物经济学模型、供应保障承诺，将正式进入制度化讨论场域。材料质量决定能否进入讨论，能进入讨论才有机会争取合理定价。

 

第三，确定性背后是更高的合规底线。从药品追溯码、耗材编码到基金结算、医院端规范使用，这些过去被视为运营部门的流程问题，只会产生局部影响。未来，它们将直接决定产品能否顺利结算、是否会触发智能监管风控、企业商业化的现金流是否安全等系统性问题。

 

比如，三审稿明确，医药企业中标后无正当理由放弃资格、不履行供货承诺，处中标项目金额5‰-10‰罚款，并限制参与集采资格，法定代表人也面临5年限制从业的处罚。由此，合规不再是成本项，而是决定企业能不能继续参赛的资格项。



具体来看，《医疗保障法》三审稿带来的五条核心制度增量，从循证定价、集采结算到多元支付、智能监管与长护险入法。它们共同把医保改革从政策探索推向法律保障，也倒逼药械企业的商业化逻辑，从上市后找支付前移到研发期嵌支付。

 

增量一：循证与经济性评价权重提升

三审稿将循证医学和经济性评价明确为医保支付调整的基础，并新增听取相关企业意见的环节。这使得企业对支付标准的博弈从谈判桌前移到规则制定阶段，证据准备得越充分，后续准入的主动权越大。这意味着医保准入不再只是上市后的价格谈判，而是从临床开发后期就要开始的价值证明，药企的竞争由此前移到临床开发阶段。往后，企业在研发立项阶段，就得把医保可支付性写进产品策略，提前准备药物经济学与预算影响分析，具体包括真实世界证据、头对头研究，以及面向中国人群与诊疗路径的成本效果模型。

 

对于罕见病新药、CAR-T、ADC等高值产品而言，还要注意要预设基本医保+商保的组合路径，而非等到商业化才被动应对。比如此前的医保和商保双目录，就提供了现实样本，新版国家医保目录纳入114种药品，商保创新药目录承接新靶点单抗、细胞治疗等高值产品，直指基本医保覆盖适宜人群+商保承接增量价值的分层路径。换言之，高值创新药不应再押注单一报销通道，而要在立项时即规划不同支付方各自的覆盖边界与证据要求。基本医保保"适宜人群"通常按适应证与线数设限，商保承接的则是超出基保范围的增量价值。

 

增量二：集采制度化叠加直接结算，重塑企业现金流

在《医疗保障法》三审稿中，集采被写入长期制度安排，同时医保经办机构可直接与定点机构结算基金支付部分。前者确认集采不可逆，后者直指医院回款慢顽疾，企业须把中选后的产能、配送、库存等履约能力，与回款确定性当作商业化生存变量来经营，医疗器械报价还应纳入全生命周期成本，并将直接结算状态纳入滚动现金流预测。现金流改善不只是财务数字，更直接关系到企业能否持续投入研发与维持临床供应。对器械企业，报价模型还要把培训、维修、耗材与版本升级等售后成本前置算清，否则中标即亏损。

 

在此前的集采实践中，海南等9省直接结算后企业回款从6个月压缩至30天内，江西2020年以来累计结算296亿元。在冠脉支架接续采购中，27个产品拟中选、主流普遍入选，则表明集采把竞争拉回临床质量与持续迭代。自2021年首轮集采以来，已使用超1000万个中选支架、约700万人次受益，新获批产品仍可增补中选。对器械企业而言，这意味着迭代速度和维护响应能力，正取代渠道关系成为集采续约的核心筹码。

 

增量三：DRG/DIP下，创新器械必须算清医院的经济账

三审稿提出，针对不同医疗服务特点实行多元复合式支付方式，促进药械合理使用与服务提升。药械产品不仅要闯目录、过集采，还要经得起按病种付费下医院经济账的检验，仅技术先进不够，必须被翻译为能缩短住院日、减少并发症的临床路径，否则会被粗放打包付费一刀切挤出，市场团队还须与医院医保办、病案室协同，让产品在收费与编码层面看得见。否则即便临床价值成立，也会因无法计入病组成本而被医院拒用。DRG分组依赖病案首页的主诊断与手术操作编码，编码一旦错配，技术再好也拿不到对应支付。

 

此前，更新后的DRG/DIP 3.0版已为机器人辅助手术设出9个DRG组，并以特例单议为复杂病例留出口。在这个过程中，企业需建立含住院日、并发症率、资源消耗的支付证据包，确保收费项目、病案首页与产品编码在医院端一一对应。特例单议机制虽为复杂病例留了口子，但企业必须主动把病例数据喂给医院的医保办，才能争取到合理分组。

 

增量四：追溯与智能监管穿透全链条

根据规定，定点医药机构须遵守药品、医疗器械信息化追溯制度，三审稿进一步完善监管与法律责任。这意味着，货已发出不再等于合规，流向真实、数据一致、异常可追责成为渠道管理刚性要求，追溯码现已深入医保支付与基金监管场景，数据回传与异常预警须写入经销商合同与CSO考核。这等于把合规责任从药企自身，沿供应链延伸到了每一级经销商与终端。追溯码已与医保结算直接挂钩，未扫码或断链，对应费用可能被拒付或暂缓拨付。

 

此前，深圳"入库必扫码、卖药必扫码"累计上传8.72亿条，对未上传费用暂缓拨付163万元，医保与药监已联合核查。此外，企业须完成追溯码、医保编码与ERP批次的全链路映射，对中小包装、拆零、退货、冷链转运设定可审计规则，方可随时拿出从发票流向、签收到扫码、终端的完整证据链。在医保飞检与基金监管常态化的背景下，追溯断链已不只是管理瑕疵，而可能直接触发费用拒付与行政处罚。

 

增量五：长护险入法，康复辅具迎支付窗口

审稿新增建立健全长期护理保险制度，具体办法参照基本医保执行。其中，辅具商业模式正从一次性卖设备，转向"租赁+上门适配+持续维护+数据管理"的长期服务合同，本地服务网络、洗消标准与可计量结算体系成为真正门槛，企业还须积累对照护强度、压疮、跌倒改善的临床证据。长护险尚处制度起步期，各地评估标准与支付水平差异明显，企业须以省为单位逐地摸排。长护险按失能等级评定支付，辅具能否入目录，取决于其改善失能结局的证据强度。

 

据报道，山东滨州长护险辅具租赁目录已扩至36类70种，电动护理床月租470元、长护险付70%后个人月负担仅14元。企业应尽早研究各地评估标准与服务目录，在产品上强化可清洁、可维修、可回收、可远程监测，把硬件翻译成"可计量、可质控、可循环"的服务。谁能先把硬件变成可持续结算、可量化质控的服务，谁就能在院外与居家场景抢到支付红利。一省一策仍是基本打法，企业需针对各地目录与评估标准分别适配。



过去，药械商业化常被拆分为注册、准入、市场、销售和合规等多个职能。医疗保障法通过后，这些环节将被支付端重新串联：注册阶段决定证据底座，目录和价格决定支付空间，DRG/DIP决定医院使用动力，集采和直接结算决定规模与现金流，追溯和智能监管决定合规边界，长护险等新制度则打开院外与居家场景。

 

创新企业现在最需要的不是等待最终细则，而是提前建立跨部门的医保战略机制：研发、医学、市场准入、供应链、财务、数字化和合规共同参与。以产品、临床路径、省份为颗粒度，提前回答四个问题，产品给患者带来什么不可替代的获益？基金为什么应该为此付费？医院为什么愿意使用？企业如何保证每一次使用都合规、可追溯、能结算？

 

首部医疗保障法的落地，意味着医疗创新正式进入价值治理的深水区。对真正具备临床价值与系统交付能力的企业来说，这未必是更窄的门，反而可能是一条更可预期、更能淘汰伪创新的长期赛道。

title: The true meaning of compassion in health care
summary: The most profound lessons in compassion did not come from textbooks or training. They came from the patients who invited me into their stories. “Will you stay for a little while?” A patien...
full_content:
The most profound lessons in compassion did not come from textbooks or training. They came from the patients who invited me into their stories.

“Will you stay for a little while?”

A patient asked me this question after receiving news that would change the course of her life. I had no medical solution to offer. I could not take away her fear or change her diagnosis. All I could do was pull up a chair and sit beside her.

So, I stayed.

Years later, I don’t remember every word that was spoken in that room. What I remember is the lesson she taught me: sometimes the greatest act of compassion is not knowing what to say. It’s being willing to stay.

As a hospital chaplain, people often tell me, “You must see a lot of suffering.” They’re right. I sit with patients who are frightened. I listen to families facing difficult decisions. I walk alongside people whose lives can change in an instant.

Yet despite all the heartbreak I witness, what stays with me most is not the suffering. It’s compassion. Over the years, patients, families, and colleagues have taught me lessons about compassion that continue to shape both my ministry and my life.

The gift of being present

When I first became a chaplain, I thought I needed to have the right words. I wanted to offer comfort, wisdom, or answers. But I soon learned that many situations cannot be fixed. No perfect sentence can erase a devastating diagnosis or remove a family’s pain. What people often need most is something much simpler: someone who will stay, listen, and remind them they are not alone.

Compassion is not about having all the answers. It is about being present when there are no answers. People rarely remember exactly what was said during their hardest moments. They remember who showed up, who listened, and who stayed.

Looking beyond the diagnosis

In health care, it is easy to focus on illness. But every patient is far more than a diagnosis. The woman recovering from surgery may be worried about her grandchildren. The man receiving treatment may be wondering whether he will return to the work he loves. The parent sitting at a child’s bedside may be carrying fears too deep for words.

Everyone has a story. When we take time to listen, we begin to see people as they truly are, not simply as patients, but as human beings with hopes, dreams, relationships, and worries. Compassion begins with curiosity and grows when we genuinely want to understand another person’s experience.

Learning to extend compassion to ourselves

This may be the hardest lesson I have learned. Many people who work in health care are very good at caring for others. We spend our days helping, supporting, and comforting. Sometimes we do that so well that we forget to care for ourselves.

We carry grief. We carry stress. We carry memories of patients and families who leave a lasting impact on our hearts. For years, I believed compassion meant always giving more of myself. Now I understand that compassion also means recognizing our limits. Taking time to rest, reflect, pray, and renew ourselves does not make us less compassionate. It makes it possible to continue caring for others over the long journey of a health care career.

Kindness has a ripple effect

One of the most beautiful things I witness in the hospital is the way compassion spreads. A nurse offers reassurance to a worried family member. A physician sits down and takes a few extra minutes to listen. An environmental services team member notices someone struggling and offers a kind word. A volunteer shares a smile.

These moments may seem small, but they matter. A single act of kindness can change the atmosphere of an entire room. When people experience compassion, they often pass it on. One simple act can touch far more lives than we realize.

What gives me hope

After years of serving as a chaplain, I have come to believe that compassion is one of the most powerful forces in health care. Not because it cures disease. Not because it removes every hardship. But because it reminds people that they do not have to face those hardships alone.

Every day, I see families finding strength they didn’t know they had. I see exhausted staff members offering kindness at the end of a long shift. I see patients encouraging one another. I see hope showing up in unexpected places. At a time when the world often feels divided and uncertain, I continue to witness something remarkable: people choosing to care for one another.

A nurse listens. A family member stays by the bedside through the night. A volunteer offers a smile. A physician slows down long enough to truly see the person in the patient. Small moments. Ordinary moments. Yet these acts of compassion quietly change lives every day.

That is why I remain hopeful. My patients have taught me that even amid fear, loss, and uncertainty, compassion continues to show up. It appears whenever one person chooses to care for another. We may not be able to change every diagnosis, prevent every loss, or solve every problem. But we can choose to care. And as long as people continue choosing to care for one another, there will always be reason to hope.

Sheryl J. Nicholson is a spiritual care coordinator.

title: Care orchestration should start in the patient portal
summary: After years of working with numerous health systems and my own experiences as a patient and caregiver, I have come to realize how challenging it can be to manage one’s own care. Care doesn&#8217...
full_content:
After years of working with numerous health systems and my own experiences as a patient and caregiver, I have come to realize how challenging it can be to manage one’s own care. Care doesn’t stop when patients leave a health care facility. It is often just the beginning of a long journey for them. Most often, after a doctor visit or surgical procedure, a patient has an extensive to-do list: products to purchase, medication regimens to follow, follow-up appointments to schedule, and more.

Follow-through takes time, emotional effort, and organization. People have busy lives, and health care diagnoses can be complicated, so it’s not surprising that some of these details fall through the cracks. The challenge can be especially daunting for patients who have just been diagnosed with a serious illness. They have to process the news and how it will impact their life and their loved ones. Then comes the overwhelming part: figuring out how to address all the steps that are required to treat the condition.

It can also be difficult for caregivers who have to carry the load of serving as the central coordinator for the loved one in their care, especially after the loved one has undergone a surgical or a medical procedure. The caregiver ends up juggling multiple duties: They are the personal care assistant, the source of emotional support, the cook, the chef, the cleaner. The list goes on.

A systems problem

It’s evident that the health care system has fallen short when it comes to the care patients receive after they leave a medical facility. The providers who prescribe the to-do lists have no reliable way of knowing whether the tasks they recommend are completed and if the patient even has the resources (the finances, transportation, health literacy, and confidence) to accomplish them.

This blind spot is understandable, given the realities the health systems face today. With staffing and funding shortages, providers are stretched thin and patients’ electronic health care record (EHR) portals currently have limited after-visit visibility. So what can one do?

The health care system is presented with a host of what-ifs. What if it could offer patients more support beyond a curated to-do list and a recurring nudge? What if patients could navigate all their care to-dos from their EHR portal? And what if all their care supplies could be automatically delivered to their door, shortly after their after-visit notes were finalized?

The patient portal becomes the care orchestrator

The EHR portal seems like the logical medium for overall care coordination. Patients are already there: According to the University of Michigan National Poll on Healthy Aging, the share of adults aged 50 to 80 who have used at least one patient portal grew from 51 percent in 2018 to 78 percent in 2023, as patients become more accustomed to using digital tools to manage their health care.

A new class of care-orchestration platforms is emerging that connects provider recommendations to fulfillment partners directly inside the portal. Done well, this creates a complete engagement loop for both patients and providers without making anyone learn new behavioral patterns. Personalized recommendations from the care team connect directly to existing fulfillment partners via the patient portal. Patients gain the ability to complete items on their to-do list and obtain the products and services recommended to them from the comfort of their home. Clinicians gain a source of information they never had, visibility into whether recommendations are acted on.

A well-designed platform in this category would work like this:

  • A care team recommends the use of a particular wellness product for an ongoing treatment, which is recorded in the patient’s EHR portal.
  • The platform engine reviews the after-visit summary and identifies relevant wellness products that are applicable to this recommendation.
  • Personalized, brand-agnostic options for the product appear alongside the patient’s after-visit summary.
  • The patient or their caregiver selects one of the recommended product options and, with a one-click checkout, purchases the product right from the portal.
  • A third party delivers the product to the patient, with fulfillment partners handling coordination end-to-end.
  • The care team receives purchase confirmation and the added assurance that the patient is following up on recommendations. This increases the likelihood of a favorable care outcome.

The same paradigm would apply to ordering services like physical or occupational therapy, connecting with community-based channels for social determinants of health (SDOH) support, or requesting follow-up appointments with specialists. Access to this data also poses opportunities for research. How much can a solution like this improve portal utilization? What impact could it have on health outcomes? How could this positively impact hospitals’ finances? The role of suppliers and ancillary service providers in the care continuum needs to be reassessed as well, particularly the importance of staying clinically appropriate, transparent, and free of clinician sales incentives that can impact care delivery.

A continuing quest for better care coordination

Those of us working on the post-care adherence gap know that no single platform is a panacea. But connecting the recommendation to the first action is an important step toward a system that benefits both patients and providers.

Health care is not a hero game; it’s an ecosystem. So, I welcome the thoughts of health system operators and researchers on the work others are doing to address the challenges discussed in this article. If you would like to offer your opinion, I am here for it.

Anne Baskakova is a health care executive.

title: Regulatory T cell reprogramming heads to trial in 2026
summary: Most people have heard of cancer immunotherapy by now. These treatments help a patient’s own immune system recognize and attack cancer. The best-known examples are immune checkpoint inhibitors s...
full_content:
Most people have heard of cancer immunotherapy by now. These treatments help a patient’s own immune system recognize and attack cancer. The best-known examples are immune checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab (Keytruda) and nivolumab (Opdivo). These drugs release certain “brakes” that normally keep the immune system from becoming overactive. Another approach, called CAR-T therapy, is more involved. Doctors remove some of a patient’s T cells, a type of white blood cell, genetically engineer them in a laboratory so they can recognize a specific target on cancer cells, grow large numbers of those modified cells, and return them to the patient. A related form of cell therapy is tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, commonly called TIL therapy. In TIL therapy, doctors collect immune cells that have already found their way into a tumor, expand them outside the body, and send much larger numbers back in.

These strategies differ in important ways, but they share a common theme: Each tries to make the immune system’s cancer-fighting cells stronger, less inhibited, more numerous, or better able to recognize their targets. The therapy described here starts somewhere else. It focuses not on the cells trying to kill the cancer, but on one of the cell populations the cancer uses to protect itself, essentially turning the tumor’s own immune bodyguards into the therapeutic target.

The tumor’s bodyguards

That idea sits at the center of an investigational treatment called CRG-150, developed by CoRegen. In July 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the company’s Investigational New Drug (IND) application, allowing a first-in-human phase 1/2a trial to proceed. The study is registered as NCT07730125 and plans to enroll up to 67 adults with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, metastatic hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer, or metastatic prostate cancer. Enrollment is expected to open late in 2026. As of this writing, no patient has yet received the therapy, and there is no evidence that it works in people. The biology behind it, however, raises a broader question about where cancer immunotherapy may be heading.

To understand why CRG-150 is unusual, it helps to understand a group of cells most people outside immunology rarely hear about: regulatory T cells, usually called Tregs. The immune system must walk a difficult line. It has to be aggressive enough to destroy viruses, bacteria, and abnormal cells, yet restrained enough not to attack healthy tissue. Tregs help maintain that balance. They act as a natural brake, suppressing excessive immune responses and helping prevent the immune system from turning against the body’s own tissues, a problem known as autoimmunity. In a healthy person, that function is essential. An immune system with no brakes would be dangerous.

Cancer has become very good at exploiting those same brakes. Tumors are not just collections of malignant cells. They live inside a complicated neighborhood of blood vessels, connective tissue, signaling molecules, and immune cells that scientists call the tumor microenvironment. Some immune cells there try to attack the tumor. Others end up protecting it. Many cancers are skilled at drawing Tregs into that neighborhood, where their normal immunosuppressive function becomes an advantage for the cancer. A Treg that keeps an immune response from becoming excessive in healthy tissue may perform essentially the same job inside a tumor, except now the cells being protected are cancer cells. A patient may therefore have immune cells capable of damaging a tumor, but those cells are operating inside an environment shaped to suppress them. The bodyguards are doing their job. They are simply guarding the wrong thing.

Changing the bodyguards’ instructions

The obvious solution might seem to be getting rid of Tregs altogether. Biology is rarely that cooperative. Tregs exist for a reason, and eliminating their function throughout the body risks removing an important safeguard against autoimmunity and uncontrolled inflammation.

CRG-150 approaches the problem differently. Researchers collect immune cells from the patient’s blood through apheresis, a procedure that separates specific cell types from circulating blood, and isolate the patient’s own Tregs. They then use the gene-editing system CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt a gene called NCOA3, which produces a protein known as steroid receptor coactivator-3, or SRC-3. The manufacturing process is expected to take approximately 28 days from apheresis to delivery of the product back to the patient, after which the edited cells are infused. CRG-150 is the name of that specific product, which consists of a patient’s own SRC-3-edited Tregs. The broader strategy can be described as Treg reprogramming: altering regulatory T cells so that instead of shielding a tumor, they help organize an attack on it.

SRC-3 is what scientists call a transcriptional coactivator. In plain language, it helps regulate broad programs of gene activity inside a cell rather than acting as a single on-or-off switch. Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine, including the late Bert W. O’Malley, MD, spent decades studying steroid receptor coactivators, including SRC-3, before uncovering its role in regulatory T-cell biology. Work published in 2021 showed that when SRC-3 is depleted or pharmacologically inhibited in human Tregs, the cells lose characteristic features of their identity and much of their ability to suppress the proliferation of other T cells. Disrupting SRC-3, in other words, does not simply dial down one signal. It begins to erode the cell’s regulatory identity.

In mouse experiments, removing SRC-3 specifically from Tregs produced a striking change in how those cells behaved. The altered Tregs no longer acted like conventional immunosuppressive Tregs within the tumor. They proliferated extensively, moved into tumors, and released inflammatory signals that helped cancer-fighting T cells and natural killer cells enter the tumor and function there. Investigators also reported that the altered Tregs could interfere with the suppressive activity of the animal’s own unedited Tregs, meaning a relatively small number of modified cells might influence a much larger immune population. Whether that dominant effect occurs in humans is unknown.

The results in mice were dramatic. In a breast cancer model, a single transfer of SRC-3-deficient Tregs eliminated already-established tumors, and animals that cleared the cancer resisted later tumor challenge, suggesting durable antitumor immunity. The same 2023 study also reported tumor eradication in a prostate cancer model. In 2026, researchers extended the work to mouse models of glioblastoma, melanoma, and lung cancer, again finding substantial antitumor effects. Much of that broader work, however, tested the underlying biology in genetically engineered animals rather than in animals treated with a manufactured cell product. These remain animal experiments, not evidence that CRG-150 will work in humans.

Still, the fact that altering the same Treg program produced antitumor effects across several types of solid cancer is one reason Treg reprogramming is intriguing. It suggests a strategy that may not depend on identifying one particular mutation or marker on the cancer cell, but instead on changing the immune environment surrounding it.

A different strategy from existing cell therapies

This is where the strategy begins to look fundamentally different from better-known forms of cell therapy. In CAR-T therapy, a patient’s cells are given a new targeting system so they can recognize a specific molecule on a cancer cell and attack it. That approach has transformed treatment for several blood cancers, but most solid tumors have proved far more difficult. Not every cancer cell necessarily carries the same target, and solid tumors are often surrounded by physical and immune barriers that make it hard for engineered killer cells to reach them and work effectively.

A regulatory T cell presents an almost opposite opportunity. Tumors are already very good at drawing Tregs in. Ordinarily, that is part of the problem. But if the cell’s instructions can be changed before it is returned to the body, a cell type the tumor already accommodates could theoretically become useful. Rather than forcing another killer cell into a hostile environment, researchers may be able to work with a cell population already well adapted to entering and functioning within the tumor microenvironment.

For years, Tregs in cancer have largely been viewed as cells we need to overcome, suppress, or remove. Treg reprogramming starts from a different proposition. The cell itself may not be the problem. Its programming is.

That distinction becomes clearer when compared with checkpoint inhibitors, which interfere with individual molecular signals used to restrain immune responses. Those drugs produce remarkable results for some patients, but many people do not respond, and some tumors remain immunologically “cold,” meaning few active cancer-fighting cells enter them at all. Disrupting SRC-3 aims at something broader: the overall state of the regulatory T cell rather than a single receptor on its surface. In its IND-clearance announcement, CoRegen states that CRG-150 affects multiple immune checkpoint-related targets, including PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4, LAG3, and CCR4. That does not mean CRG-150 blocks all five checkpoints the way drugs directed against those individual molecules would. Rather, the claim is that changing an upstream transcriptional regulator alters several parts of the Treg’s immunosuppressive program at once.

A familiar protein in an unfamiliar role

SRC-3 is better known to many breast cancer researchers by another name: AIB1, for “amplified in breast cancer 1.” It was identified in the 1990s as a gene amplified in breast tumors and as a coactivator of the estrogen receptor. It has long been studied for its role in hormone-dependent cancer growth inside malignant cells.

That history can make the target confusing, because the same protein can support cancer through two entirely different cellular compartments. Inside a cancer cell, SRC-3 can enhance estrogen receptor signaling and other growth-promoting pathways. Inside a regulatory T cell, it helps maintain the suppressive program that tumors can exploit to evade immune attack. CRG-150 acts only on the second of these, which is especially worth noting because the trial includes patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, a setting in which SRC-3/AIB1 has long been studied within the malignant cells themselves. CRG-150 is not an attempt to knock out a cancer-driving gene inside the tumor. It edits the patient’s Tregs. It does not edit the cancer.

That distinction is easy to lose. CoRegen’s own announcement of its FDA clearance describes SRC-3 as a gene enabling cancer cell immune evasion and states that it is overexpressed in most human cancers before explaining that the therapy disrupts the tumor-protective function of regulatory T cells. Placed together, those statements can invite a reader to conclude that CRG-150 attacks SRC-3 in the tumor. It does not. The target is SRC-3, but the therapeutic target cell is the regulatory T cell. For patients and physicians encountering headlines about “targeting SRC-3 in cancer,” that is the distinction that matters most.

Important open questions

The breadth of what SRC-3 does is both the appeal and the concern. Changing an upstream regulator that influences broad programs of gene activity could create a deeper and more durable effect than blocking a single receptor. It could also produce consequences that are harder to predict. The same concern applies to the Treg itself. These cells help keep our immune systems from attacking our own tissues. The goal is not simply to remove immune suppression. It is to remove the right kind of immune suppression, in the right place, while preserving the body’s tolerance of healthy tissue everywhere else.

That may be the most important question CRG-150 has to answer: Can immune tolerance be turned down inside a tumor without turning it down throughout the body?

The animal studies are encouraging on this point because researchers did not observe the widespread autoimmune disease one might fear from wholesale elimination of Treg function. But humans are not laboratory mice, and genome-edited living cells introduce uncertainties that ordinary drugs do not. A medication can be stopped. The genetic edit itself cannot simply be reversed after the cells have been infused. Reflecting that uncertainty, the clinical protocol includes long-term safety follow-up extending as long as fifteen years, consistent with the FDA’s framework for genome-edited therapies.

Manufacturing is its own challenge. Tregs are a relatively scarce population in blood, and isolating, editing, and expanding them while maintaining a viable, consistent cell population is technically difficult. Researchers working on this program published a study in 2025 developing a process to isolate, edit, and expand SRC-3-knockout human Tregs that could be adapted for current good manufacturing practice (cGMP) clinical-scale production. CoRegen has partnered with Lonza to manufacture CRG-150 for the first-in-human study. Producing consistent, well-characterized batches across patients will be an important practical test of the platform.

There is another unusual feature of CRG-150 worth noting. Many existing cell therapies require patients to first receive chemotherapy that temporarily depletes large parts of the immune system, a process called lymphodepletion. The goal is to create space and a more favorable environment for the engineered cells. CRG-150 takes a different route. No lymphodepleting chemotherapy is planned. The edited Tregs are not meant to be the main cancer killers. Their role, based on the preclinical model, is to reshape the tumor environment and recruit the patient’s existing effector immune cells into the fight. At least in theory, depleting a large portion of those lymphocytes beforehand could work against the mechanism the therapy is designed to use.

That is a real potential advantage. It is also a real potential weakness. To enroll, patients must have metastatic disease that has progressed after multiple prior classes of systemic therapy. Their immune responses may already be compromised or substantially altered by advanced disease and prior treatment. A strategy that depends on mobilizing the patient’s remaining immune response will therefore be tested first in exactly the population where that response may be most depleted.

What the first trial will and will not tell us

Expectations should be set accordingly. The first phase is designed primarily to establish safety and identify a dose. The expansion phase plans roughly ten patients per tumor type. Ten patients can reveal a signal worth pursuing. Ten patients cannot establish that a therapy works. Investigators will also track how long the edited cells persist in the body, which may prove as informative as any early response data. If the cells fail to expand or persist without lymphodepletion, that would raise a real question about whether the strategy can work as intended.

Tumors disappearing in mice make compelling headlines. They do not constitute a cancer cure, and many approaches that looked powerful in preclinical studies have failed when confronted with the complexity of human disease. CRG-150 may fail too.

But the significance of an experimental therapy sometimes lies less in whether that particular product succeeds than in the question it forces the field to ask. CAR-T changed our idea of what a medicine could be: a patient’s own living cells, modified and returned as treatment. Checkpoint inhibitors showed that cancer could be attacked not by poisoning the malignant cell directly, but by interfering with the conversations it was having with the immune system. Treg reprogramming raises a further possibility. Cells we have classified as part of the tumor’s defenses may not always need to be eliminated. Perhaps they can be reinstructed.

Cancer is extraordinarily adaptive. It hijacks normal biological processes such as blood vessel formation, metabolism, wound healing, and immune tolerance, then turns them toward its own survival. Regulatory T cells are part of that story. Their purpose is protective. Cancer simply learned to make that protection work in its favor.

Whether that relationship can be reversed in a patient rather than a mouse is now, finally, a question with a trial attached to it.

Laurel A. Coons is a scientist with a background in genomics and biomedical research. She completed her doctoral training in pharmacology and cancer biology at Duke University and conducted research at the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. Her work has focused on genomic regulation, endocrine signaling, and translating complex scientific data into insights relevant to medicine and patient care.

She shares professional updates on X at laurelcoons.

title: 落地临床、抢滩院外，AI康复机器人下一步竞争拼什么？
summary: 具身智能向医疗场景渗透，康复机器人站上新产业节点。技术变化带来新问题，安杰莱科技创始人李鲁亚、希润医疗总经理孟铭强等嘉宾拆解了AI康复机器人产业路径。传统康复机器人技术竞争集中在机械性能，但临床中评价体系正失效。安杰莱搭建“大脑-机器人-人体”闭环系统，通过脑机接口捕捉运动意图，形成完整回路，转动“数据飞轮”。康复另一挑战是设备如何更好适应患者身体，希润医疗转向柔性软体机器人，更适合居家场景，但工...
full_content:
具身智能的热潮正在向医疗场景加速渗透，康复机器人也站上了新的产业节点。

 

过去，康复机器人更多围绕机械结构、驱动能力和运动自由度展开竞争；如今，脑机接口开始进入康复系统，人工智能参与运动意图解码和训练方案生成，机器人则成为执行和反馈的载体。与此同时，康复设备的应用边界也在向社区、养老机构和家庭延伸。

 

技术变化正在带来一连串新的问题：脑机接口究竟能为康复带来什么？院外市场如何建立商业闭环？当设备持续产生数据，一家康复器械公司的价值将被如何重估？

 

在动脉网联合微解药举办的《中国创新医疗资产会客厅》交易圆桌派第二十七期中，安杰莱科技创始人&CEO李鲁亚、希润医疗总经理孟铭强、恒旭资本董事总经理殷悦焓三位嘉宾，从产业与投资两个维度，拆解了AI康复机器人从实验室走向临床、从院内走向院外的产业路径。

 


很长一段时间，康复机器人的技术竞争集中在机械性能：扭矩大小、自由度多少、结构是否坚固。但在临床真实场景中，这套评价体系正在失效。

 

李鲁亚认为，传统康复很大程度上仍是被动训练：机器或者治疗师带动患者完成动作，患者自身的运动意图没有充分进入训练闭环。而神经康复的核心之一是神经重塑，如果能够让患者的大脑主动参与训练，康复逻辑就可能进一步改变。这也是脑机接口进入康复场景的意义。

 

安杰莱搭建的“大脑-机器人-人体”闭环系统正是为了解决这一问题：通过脑机接口捕捉运动意图，AI结合患者健肢运动数据生成个性化运动方案，再由机器人执行并反馈给人体，形成一整套完整回路。

 

每一台投放至医院的设备，同时也是神经数据采集终端，源源不断地沉淀脑电与运动对齐数据。设备越多，数据样本越丰富，解码算法越精准，产品的适配能力持续迭代，由此转动起“数据飞轮”。

 

脑机路线解决的是“如何读懂大脑”的问题。但康复还有另一层挑战——设备本身如何更好地适应患者的身体？

 

这正是柔性机器人切入的方向。希润医疗早期从上海交通大学成果转化而来，2019年从刚性外骨骼转向柔性软体机器人。孟铭强解释，核心原因是在医院调研中发现，患者的康复周期远长于住院周期，社区和家庭需要更长期的训练支持，而传统刚性设备体积大、重量高，不适合院外使用。

 

柔性机器人因此成为更适合居家场景的路径，但工程难度并没有降低——柔性机器人既要保持柔软，又要实现足够的控制精度；既要通过压力、姿态等传感器感知患者动作，又要保证驱动器长期工作的可靠性。

 

与此同时，产品还要解决大量临床使用中的细节问题：患者能否快速穿戴、行动不便的人能否自行操作、治疗师能否降低操作负担。这些看不见的工程打磨，恰恰是拉开产品体验差距的关键。

 

不过，脑机康复和柔性机器人虽然技术路线不同，但最终都在回答同一个问题：康复机器人真正的竞争力，不是堆叠多少硬件参数，而是能否围绕患者的康复需求，把感知、决策和训练真正连接起来。

 

 


技术路线之外，资本对康复机器人的判断也正在发生变化。

 

具身智能热潮之下，人形机器人吸引了大量关注。但在殷悦焓看来，医疗康复机器人与通用具身智能之间存在一道天然的分界线：医疗场景首先要求安全和疗效，其次才是机器人能力。

 

对于神经损伤患者而言，机器人与人体之间的每一次交互都涉及安全风险。机器人必须具备更加严格的力控、感知和安全冗余能力；进入临床后，还需要经历医疗器械注册、生产体系以及临床评价等完整流程。

 

正是基于这些医疗属性，恒旭资本内部形成了一套“三看一验”的判断框架，跳出单纯看硬件参数的惯性思维：

 

一看临床闭环：产品是否进入三甲医院，有没有可量化的临床获益数据；二看数据飞轮：数据是高质量结构化标注的，还是一堆杂乱原始信号，隐私合规是否到位；三看注册证壁垒与适应症拓展空间。最终再验证商业化路径能否复制——无论是医院集采还是康养机构、居家模式，必须跑通付费模型。

 

这个框架的背后，是殷悦焓观察到的市场变化：资本正在从销售收入导向转向“数据资产+注册证”导向，硬件制造本身的估值溢价正在让位于AI算法和闭环能力，纯硬件企业容易陷入价格竞争，纯算法企业又缺少一手数据入口。

 

结论指向一个方向：能够把数据采集、AI解码、机器人控制和效果反馈完整串联起来的软硬一体化企业，才可能形成最深的长期壁垒。


但前提是数据真正具备训练价值——装机量能否支撑模型迭代，数据是否结构化、可标注，治理和合规是否到位。没有这些，所谓“数据飞轮”就只是概念。

 


康复机器人另一个正在发生的变化，是应用场景的外移。

 

孟铭强在调研中发现，患者的住院周转很快，出院后的康复周期却漫长得多。刚性设备无法跟随患者走出医院，这恰恰是柔性技术被推到台前的原因，不是因为它“更先进”，而是因为它能进入医院到不了的地方。

 

顺着这个逻辑，安杰莱推出“嵌入式全民康复”模式，将整套神经康复能力下沉到养老院、社区康复中心、特殊教育学校，实现院内院外同等质量的康复服务。李鲁亚观察到，随着十五五阶段养老支付券政策落地，机构端的支付链路正在逐步打通，To B机构市场已经成为当下确定性最高的方向。

 

“院内是根据地，院外居家是放大器。”殷悦焓如此概括三者关系。

 

院内承担着临床验证、学术背书、医保准入和原始数据积累的核心使命。没有院内的临床验证做基础，居家产品就缺少信任根基。但仅仅固守院内，赛道的天花板会被牢牢锁死。社区和养老康养机构，是从医院通往家庭之间最关键的过渡场景。

 

而真正走向C端居家，仍绕不开几座大山。

 

孟铭强总结了行业普遍痛点：第一是合规，家用医疗器械的电磁兼容、安全标准比院内设备更加严苛；第二是患者依从性，康复是长期训练、见效慢，很像健身，用户很难坚持；第三是付费意愿，大众尚未形成居家康复的消费认知，现阶段个人付费动力不足，更多要依靠长护险、民政助残、家庭病床等政策工具的逐步落地。

 

因此，行业共识是企业要走双轮路线：依靠院内和机构市场完成生存、数据积累与产品打磨；静待政策和用户认知成熟，再逐步释放居家C端的巨大潜力，构建“医院-社区-家庭”三级联动的康复服务体系。

 


如果沿着这条路径往前走，康复机器人最终会变成什么？

 

李鲁亚认为，未来康复机器人会从单一设备变成融合意念感知、智能决策、精准执行和数据进化的“神经一体化”康复平台，商业模式也将从硬件销售走向软硬件、服务与数据结合。

 

孟铭强则把行业机会概括为“顶天”和“立地”：“顶天”意味着继续攻克闭环脑机接口、神经调控等前沿技术，让神经重塑效率进一步提升；“立地”则意味着把产品做到足够轻、足够便宜、足够易用，真正进入家庭，覆盖庞大的长期康复需求。

 

在殷悦焓看来，未来3-5年最有机会跑出来的企业，大致也会落在两个方向：要么拥有足够前沿的技术和扎实的数据基础，要么能够把产品真正做成规模化、可复制的商业模式。

 

三种表述，指向同一个核心：康复机器人竞争的天平，正在从“谁的机器人更强”转向“谁能把医疗闭环跑通”。

 

技术只是起点。真正决定企业价值的，是能否进入临床，拿到注册证，积累真实数据，形成疗效，再把院内验证过的能力延伸到社区和家庭。这段路的终点，或许不再是一台机器，而是一套能够持续产生疗效、数据与收入的康复系统。

 

谁先建成这套系统，谁就可能在下一阶段的竞争中占据主动。

title: 半年涌入80亿美元！高不确定性下的资本豪赌开始了
summary: 今年以来，在AI重构浪潮冲击下，国内医药投资逻辑发生显著转变，资金从偏好临床数据与稳定现金流，转向押注极早期高不确定性项目。其中，口服环肽赛道成为资本焦点，短短半年内吸金超80亿美元。跨国药企（MNC）与顶级投资机构主要采取“买平台”与“买管线”两大策略：诺华、阿斯利康等巨头通过高额首付款及里程碑支付，获取Unnatural Products、元思生肽等企业的AI驱动大环肽发现平台使用权；同时，峰...
full_content:
一段时间以来，投临床数据、投稳定现金流，甚至投BD的可能性，几乎成为国内医药投资人的共识。

 

不过，今年以来，随着AI重构一切的浪潮兴起，这种认知开始动摇。资金密集地从头部逐步流向极早期的高不确定项目。动脉网此前文章分析的AI虚拟细胞是一例，今天打算聊的口服环肽，则是另外一例。



过去短短半年间，口服环肽赛道的融资事件和BD交易呈现爆发的态势，超80亿美金瞬间涌入这个垂直领域。MNC和顶级投资机构用这一大笔钱紧急做了两件事，买平台和买管线。

 

先看买平台。面对一向颇早期的颠覆性技术， MNC选择押注的能持续产出分子的平台能力。2月，诺华与Unnatural Products达成合作，首付款1亿美元、总额超17亿美元，获得其AI驱动的大环肽发现平台使用权。次月，国内口服环肽明星企业元思生肽，宣布阿斯利康达成总额约34.75亿美元的授权合作，后者将获得元思生肽Synova™原创技术平台的使用权，共同开发针对慢性疾病的全球首创大环肽类药物。这笔交易同样围绕平台展开。4月，元思生肽完成1.5亿美元B轮融资，阿斯利康还以原有股东身份在B轮继续跟投。

 

机构同样重押平台。成立仅2年的峰肽药业，也超额完成了8900万美元的B轮融资。这家由奥博资本和启明创投共同孵化的Biotech，尝试运用专有的AI结合物理模拟技术平台开发口服多肽疗法。在B轮融资中，峰肽药业还引入了LAV、Foresite Capital、汉康资本、RA Capital Management等顶级投资机构。此外，被诺华选中的Unnatural Products，也在3月完成4500万美元B轮。MNC和资本，几乎在同一时间站上起跑线，鸣枪开跑。

 

相对来说，买管线的选择比较单一。 6月，翰森制药与Avere Bioscience签署独家许可协议，将口服IL-23环肽资产AVR-001的海外权益授权给Avere，获得1.2亿美元首付款、最高21.8亿美元里程碑付款。就在拿下AVR-001管线权益后的次月，Avere宣布与纳斯达克上市公司NextCure达成全股票合并协议，同步完成3.2亿美元私募融资。

 

 

“热度很高，而且是‘产品上市获批+BD’共同驱动的实质性升温。”沂景资本董事总经理沈琴博士指出，“不是单纯概念炒作，临床产品和大额BD交易都有具体的印证。”

 

此前，默沙东的口服PCSK9环肽抑制剂Enlicitide，和强生的口服IL-23环肽抑制剂Icotrokinra相继在美国获批上市。前者用于降低成年高胆固醇患者的低密度脂蛋白胆固醇，后者中重度斑块银屑病一线全身治疗。作为高发慢病患者等待已久的口服剂型，Enlicitide和Icotrokinra都以近乎高维打低维的方式，迅速打开市场。据强生Q2 2026 业绩电话会议，自Q2上架销售以来，至7月15日，Icotrokinra已经为约11000名患者开出约18000张处方。



值得注意的是，作为一项前沿的制药技术，口服环肽本身还十分早期，相关管线、技术平台的不确定性仍很大。在传统的投资框架中，这属于不确定性极大的项目。

 

一方面，Enlicitide和Icotrokinra身后，几乎没有对手，大多数口服环肽管线的临床进展断档明显。国金证券在一份研报中指出，据insight数据，2021年至2026年间，全球口服环肽在研管线从72项增长至93项，并且管线结构发生质变，后期项目占比显著提升，表明环肽技术已跨越概念验证阶段，进入全梯队推进的成熟期。 在93项在研口服环肽管线中，以IL- 23R为靶点和以PCSK9为靶点的管线分别有6项和5项，属于最热门的靶点。

 

但靶向IL- 23R的口服环肽管线，除了已上市的Icotrokinra和翰森制药授权给Avere的AVR-001外，均处于临床前研究阶段，而靶向PCSK9管线，则除了已上市Enlicitide外，均处于临床前研究阶段。实际上，尽管元思生肽、峰肽药业均布局了大量管线，但大多数尚处于临床前研究阶段，或者早期临床试验阶段。

 

“这两个靶点都属于胞外靶点，适配大环肽的作用模式，是技术优先落地的优选方向，但新药研发链条长，临床、安全性都存在不确定性，最终研发能否成功，也存在偶然因素。”沈琴博士指出。

 

具体来说，当前的口服环肽管线，最大的技术难题，仍在于口服生物利用度太低，即药物吃下去后，真正能进入血液发挥作用的比例极低，通常只有1%~5%。为了达到和注射同样的疗效，口服剂量往往要翻几十甚至上百倍。最典型的例子就是司美格鲁肽，注射版每周1mg就够，口服版却要每天14mg，还得严格空腹、餐前半小时、只用半杯水送服，多喝一口水血药浓度都可能波动。

 

而优化口服生物利用度之所以这么难，是因为几个关键要求互相矛盾。想和靶点结合得好，分子就得大，但肠道只放行小而柔性的分子。想延长半衰期，结构就得"非天然"，但又容易引发免疫反应。想提升吸收，就得用促进剂"开闸放水"，但无差别开门会带来巨大的个体差异。再加上胃酸和消化酶会降解多肽、肠道外排蛋白会把药物泵回去、肝脏还会"过海关"代谢掉一部分。这些物理化学层面的障碍环环相扣，几乎构成了整个赛道共同的天花板。

 

另一方面，Enlicitide和Icotrokinra的成功本身，很难被复制。以默沙东Enlicitide为例，它走了一条和传统完全不同的技术路线。传统环肽合成靠化学拼接，步骤多、收率低，靠逐步优化提升效率。而默沙东用的是酶法级联合成，把分子切成三段，用7种定制酶像流水线一样自动组装，步骤少、效率高。

 

也就好比，传统做环肽就像手工缝衣服，一针一线把氨基酸缝起来，每一步都有损耗。但默沙东则是造了一台专用缝纫机，布料放进去，机器自动缝好。而这台缝纫机，很难被模仿，零件是定制的，7种定制酶是从微生物里筛出来、改了几十万次才适配这个分子的专属酶；组装是复杂的，从合成生物学、酶工程，到蛋白质结晶，每个步骤都是从头就在不断配合、磨合。最重要的是，默沙东的技术和工艺，经过了量产验证。

 

所以，资本的热度与技术的难度之间，横亘着一道尚未填平的鸿沟。 这也正是资金向头部集中的根本原因，只有拥有平台级能力、能持续迭代分子的公司，才可能在这道鸿沟上架起桥梁。



当然，口服环肽面临的困境，毕竟属于新药研发中的共性问题。而这个赛道之所以在资本趋于冷静的大环境下生物，在于其独特的确定性。

 

一方面，口服环肽的创新点在于制剂，而非靶点，在存量市场上具有一定的确定性。“口服环肽可以专攻成熟的靶点，商业化前景的确定性高。”一位从业者告诉动脉网，已获批的两款口服大环肽药物背后就是这个逻辑。Enlicitide以PCSK9靶点，对应的抗体药物早已上市，年销售额超10亿美元，降脂市场已被验证；Icotrokinra选择的IL-23靶点，抗体药物市场同样成熟，对应的重磅药物年销售额峰值甚至超百亿美元，银屑病、克罗恩病市场已被验证。

 

这样的开发策略带来了一些共性的可确定未来，疾病机制清楚、患者人群明确、市场教育已经完成、临床终点现成。口服环肽入场即可弯道超车。即使口服版本只切走抗体市场的一小块，也足以支撑可观的商业价值。更何况口服的依从性优势，还能把一部分"怕打针"的患者拉进治疗人群，把蛋糕做大。

 

另一方面，通过短期做胞外靶点、长期做胞内靶点，口服环肽在增量市场上，也有一定的确定性。 这背后的逻辑在于你，PCSK9、IL-23等胞外靶点机理已被抗体验证、大环肽天然适配、临床路径成熟，确定性高，但竞争者多、商业上限相对明确。而对于转录因子、蛋白-蛋白相互作用界面这类胞内靶点，小分子够不着、抗体进不去，口服环肽是少数有机会触及的模态，一旦突破就是FIC、独占市场，但递送难度最大、失败风险最高。

 

“短期和中长期按照企业优势分批布局，短期风险低，中长期风险高。不建议初创企业在没有验证基础的情况下直接押注高难度远期靶点，可以先用短期靶点完成平台与临床概念验证，再逐步向中长期高价值靶点延伸。”沈琴博士指出。这样一来，胞外靶点的失败不会拖垮平台，分子可以换、靶点可以调，胞内靶点的失败也不会拖垮公司，基本盘在胞外。


 


所以，口服环肽的确定性其实比想象中大，这或许是产业资本、投资机构纷纷涌入的深层逻辑。



另一个有意思的点在于你，AI制药是过去几年医药行业最明确的趋势之一，而口服环肽是这一趋势下的典型样本。一个技术门槛极高的领域，恰好撞上了AI最擅长的环节。

 

对于口服环肽而言，AI的价值，在于多参数优化。多肽药物设计的关键挑战，是在多个参数之间寻找平衡点，即亲和力要够高，半衰期要够长，口服生物利用度要足够，渗透性要能过肠道，同时还要避开酶降解和转运体外排。传统药物化学手段靠大量实验筛选，成本高、周期长。基于深度学习的分子生成模型，可以在广阔的化学空间中快速探索，预测分子的构象、结合界面和渗透性，从而缩小实验验证范围。

 

这解释了为什么大量资金流向有AI平台能力的公司，Unnatural Products与诺华的合作、元思生肽和峰肽药业的技术平台，核心卖点都指向AI加速多肽发现。AI不是万能药，但确实能在这个高难度的筛选过程中节省时间和成本。

 

当然，AI的作用边界同样清晰。多肽的数据量远小于小分子药物，小分子有数十年积累、数百万级别的化合物-活性数据库，多肽的公开数据量远低于此，直接限制了模型训练深度和预测准确性。“AI是很好的辅助工具，能够减少筛选工作量，但高质量多肽实验数据不足是一个问题，现阶段AI还无法独立解决口服大环肽全部成药性卡点。”沈琴博士表示。

 

AI生成的多肽候选分子，最终成药性验证仍需要大量湿实验来完成。它能加速筛选，但无法绕过生物利用度的物理化学限制；它能预测构象，但无法弥补实验数据的缺失；它能提高效率，但无法替代临床验证的漫长周期。


或许从某种意义上讲，并非医药投资人又开始看不确定性高的项目，而是在新的技术范式下，创新药背身的投资逻辑正在发生深刻变化。

title: The case against for-profit health care on Wall Street
summary: The American health care system, as I see it, is undergoing a quiet, clinical decapitation. At the root of this crisis is a fundamental, irreconcilable conflict of interest: the presence of health car...
full_content:
The American health care system, as I see it, is undergoing a quiet, clinical decapitation. At the root of this crisis is a fundamental, irreconcilable conflict of interest: the presence of health care companies on the public stock market. While we like to believe our medical institutions are guided by the Hippocratic Oath, the reality is that once a company goes public, the Oath is replaced by a fiduciary duty to the shareholder. Some will find that argument offensive. Those profiting from the current arrangement certainly will.

In the high-stakes theater of the NYSE and NASDAQ, patient wellness is no longer the product. It is merely the raw material used to manufacture quarterly earnings.

The EPS trap: managing optics, not illness

In a private firm, the path to profit is simple: provide a service so valuable that customers pay for it. In the public market, that logic is inverted. Executives are no longer compensated for long-term clinical outcomes; they are rewarded for the optics of growth. When an executive’s net worth is tied to earnings per share and stock price volatility, the mission shifts from healing patients to navigating capital flows.

The result is a board of directors that prioritizes financial engineering over medical engineering. They aren’t looking for the next cure; they are looking for the next share buyback.

The efficiency lie: when cost-cutting becomes lethal

Public markets demand “efficiency,” a term that has become a dangerous euphemism in a hospital setting. To hit the quarterly numbers that analysts demand, public firms engage in a predictable cycle of self-cannibalization:

  • Staffing as a spigot: Nurses and technicians are treated as variable costs rather than essential infrastructure. Layoffs are timed to hit quarterly targets, leaving lean teams to manage heavy patient loads.
  • The ghost of deferred maintenance: Testing, quality assurance, and equipment upgrades are pushed into the next fiscal year to make the current one look profitable.
  • The automation degradation: Human expertise is replaced by low-cost, automated systems not because they provide better care, but because they scale without the burden of benefits and salaries.

Growth on command: the cancer of constant expansion

The most toxic demand of the public market is not just growth, it is continuous, predictable growth. Stable, healthy growth is viewed as a failure by Wall Street. This growth-on-command dynamic pushes health care organizations to roll out new service lines and technologies prematurely and to expand into markets before their clinical systems can support the load.

Private firms can afford the creative risk of a five-year research cycle. Public firms cannot. They avoid any risk that might create earnings volatility, leading to a stifling of actual innovation in favor of rent-seeking behavior and administrative bloat.

A systemic moral hazard

Quality care cannot survive a compensation structure that rewards substance-free optics. When we allow health care to be traded like tech stocks or oil futures, we are accepting a system designed to fail the vulnerable. A stock ticker measures extraction, while a hospital should measure restoration.

If we allow the 90-day fiscal clock to dictate the pace of medical care, we will continue to see the erosion of the patient-doctor bond. It is time to admit that the “invisible hand” of the market has its thumb on the scale, and it is the patients who are paying the price in more than just dollars.

The proposal

What I propose is simple to state and radical in consequence: policy that removes companies delivering health care, in any form, from the public stock market. The reasoning is straightforward. Health care is an ecosystem, and if even one element of that ecosystem becomes geared toward sheer profit-seeking, the incentive seeps into everything downstream, as it already has.

Health care is a public good, and applying a growth-on-command model to a public good inevitably degrades the good itself. To preserve the basic ethic of medicine, we must be willing to change the ownership structure of health care, from its most elemental services to its most complex systems, if we truly want a system designed to deliver health outcomes rather than earnings.

Yodhin Aggarwal is a health policy student.
