title: How health insurance middlemen delay patient care
summary: A friend I am calling “M” to protect her privacy was diagnosed with breast cancer two months ago. When we met in 6th grade science class, she had a bustling eBay business selling Beanie Ba...
full_content:
A friend I am calling “M” to protect her privacy was diagnosed with breast cancer two months ago. When we met in 6th grade science class, she had a bustling eBay business selling Beanie Babies.

Now she has three young boys, including a two-year-old, and has been a public-school teacher for 19 years. She receives health insurance coverage through her job, and until two months ago she said she loved her insurance. When her cancer diagnosis came, things changed.

Breast cancer rates are increasing among young women, and new research shows that young women diagnosed within three years of childbirth may face even more aggressive disease. With her health insurance, she thought the next steps were going to happen quickly and be straightforward.

But after her diagnosis, she immediately called her health insurance company to ask for breast surgeons in her network, and was told they couldn’t give her that information. She needed to call their “delegate,” an independent group they paid to manage a network of doctors and her care.

The delegate also declined to give her a list of surgeons and told her to have her doctor request it. Hearing this, and being a physician myself, I called. After nearly an hour on the phone, they eventually gave me a short list of surgeons that I passed along to her.

Friends, family, my patients, and even me, an English-speaking, highly educated physician, have difficulty navigating this complex system of sometimes inscrutable requirements, waiting periods, and specialist referrals.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau, in 2024, 92 percent or 310 million Americans had health insurance for some or all of the year. That same year, 66.1 percent held private health insurance coverage, while 35.5 percent had public coverage, under Medicare and Medicaid.

This is a concern as health insurance premiums are on the rise. On July 31, the 2027 rates for health insurance premiums for all states will be released, with the states released so far showing a median increase of 14 percent, up to a high of 22 percent in Washington state.

In May, Lending Tree released a study showing 36.8 percent of Americans were covered by public health insurance in 2024, with Medicare accounting for $1.1 trillion and Medicaid accounting for $931.7 billion of all U.S. health expenditures that year.

For both public and private health insurance, insurance plans are supposed to be a middleman between patient and health care treatment, a broker working to connect people to the care they need and to make sure that care gets paid for. But insurance companies often rely on a second, or even a third layer (more middlemen) to help them do this.

This is costly, complex, and difficult to navigate, even for an insider like me. Why so many layers? Health insurance companies often pay other groups to handle their administrative functions. While this has been happening for many years, more people are sharing their experiences on social media and awareness is spreading.

Many health insurance plans delegate the responsibility for managing which doctors a patient can see or which services or prescriptions are paid for, essentially introducing a second middleman. Although the ultimate responsibility to manage M’s care still falls to them, her insurance company told her to call the delegate to get information about available breast surgeons.

This experience can be confusing and frustrating to patients trying to get answers, especially with a difficult and time-sensitive diagnosis. And, though delegation has been hailed as a model for more than a decade for cost savings and praised for shifting control back to doctors, there has also been increasing scrutiny on this process. Health plans have incurred fines or sanctions for not adequately overseeing delegates.

Additionally, health insurance companies’ use of vendors is being more closely examined. Health insurance companies may use vendors to determine which care, tests, or medications get approved and paid for, a function called utilization management.

These vendors are an intermediary between the patient and the insurance company and are paid to perform these and other functions. Though the ultimate responsibility of paying for care falls to the health plan, the decision-making happens by another entity.

The vendors are theoretically supposed to be neutral, using evidence and pre-determined care pathways to make determinations. However, the vendors also are paid and make a profit off of the work they do, sometimes making money if they save the insurance company money. So in this way there may be perverse incentives.

While there is some evidence to support the cost savings that occurs with these administrative layers and they are lauded as a way to utilize specialized expertise, the personal experience of navigating health decision-making through these added layers suffers from this complexity. These administrative layers make things more costly for the country’s health care system as a whole. Over 25 percent of all health care costs in the United States go toward administrative functions, wasted. These dollars don’t heal patients.

Though underutilized, pathways exist to help people navigate and advocate for themselves when they find this complex system is not serving them or they’re getting lost between the layers. Patients can file appeals to health insurance companies, their delegates, and even regulatory organizations. Unfortunately, few people take advantage of these pathways for many reasons. They may be unaware, find the process confusing, or simply don’t think it will make a difference.

Plus, significant disparities exist for those who utilize these processes. People with lower incomes and those who identify as Asian, Hispanic, and Black are less likely to use them.

But for the small portion of patients who do appeal to their insurance company, the majority end up getting their care paid for.

I’m keeping my fingers crossed since helping M file an appeal about her care, which is the absolute last thing she needs to think about as she starts chemotherapy soon.

Barbara Rubino is an internal medicine physician.

title: What patients don’t say in the dental chair
summary: There is a question I have learned to ask that almost never appears in any clinical protocol. Not “Where does it hurt?” or “How long have you had this problem?” But something m...
full_content:
There is a question I have learned to ask that almost never appears in any clinical protocol. Not “Where does it hurt?” or “How long have you had this problem?” But something much quieter: “Is there anything else you’d like me to know?”

The answers to that question have taught me more about patient care than I expected. Over time, I’ve realized that patients rarely come into the clinic carrying only a dental problem. They often arrive with fears, assumptions, financial worries, embarrassment, and experiences they haven’t mentioned yet. Not because they are trying to hide information, but because they are unsure whether it matters. Understanding what patients don’t say is often just as important as understanding what they do.

The timeline is usually longer than they admit

A patient says the pain started last week. Then, as the conversation continues, they mention that they’ve been taking painkillers for months. Or that the tooth has bothered them on and off for a year.

I’ve learned that many people negotiate with discomfort for a long time before seeking help. They convince themselves it will get better. They adapt. They postpone. Until one day, they can’t. By the time some patients arrive at the clinic, the problem has often been present much longer than the initial story suggests.

Fear doesn’t always look like fear

One of the biggest surprises for me was learning how many patients are afraid. Not everyone says it openly. Some patients walk in smiling. They answer questions comfortably and appear relaxed. Then the moment a dental instrument comes close, their hands tighten around the chair. Their breathing changes. Their shoulders tense. The fear was there all along.

Dental anxiety is one of the most common reasons people delay treatment, yet many patients never mention it. Some are embarrassed. Others believe they should simply be brave. When fear goes unacknowledged, it affects everything: communication, cooperation during treatment, and whether a patient returns for future care.

Patients often arrive after trying everything else

Before many people reach a dental clinic, they have already tried to solve the problem themselves:

  • Salt water rinses
  • Clove oil
  • Painkillers
  • Herbal remedies
  • Advice from family and friends

Some patients tell us immediately. Others don’t mention it unless they’re specifically asked. These details matter because they help us understand how long the problem has existed and what the patient has already been through before seeking professional care.

Money is often the quietest concern in the room

Not every patient who delays treatment is avoiding care because they don’t value it. Sometimes they’re worried about cost. The challenge is that financial concerns are often difficult for people to discuss openly. Patients may say they’ll “come back later.” They may ask for time to think. They may disappear after agreeing to treatment. Behind many of these decisions is a simple question: “Can I actually afford this?” When health care professionals create space for those conversations without judgment, patients are often relieved.

Oral hygiene habits are not always what they seem

Many patients tell us they brush regularly. The interesting part is that “regularly” means something different to everyone. For one person, it means brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. For another, it means brushing once a day whenever they remember. Most patients aren’t being dishonest. They’re describing their habits according to their own understanding. The same applies to smoking, tobacco use, and other lifestyle habits. People often disclose these things only after trust has been established.

Sometimes the real problem isn’t clinical

A patient comes in asking about whitening. Another wants a routine cleaning. But beneath the appointment request is often something much deeper.

I remember a friend from secondary school who never smiled with his mouth open. He had heavy calculus buildup and, somewhere along the way, had convinced himself that his teeth would always look that way. It wasn’t until I started studying oral health care that I learned the truth: The problem was treatable. A simple scaling and polishing session could have changed everything. Instead, he spent years hiding his smile over something that wasn’t permanent at all.

I think about him often because many patients carry similar stories. Not all oral health problems cause pain. Some affect confidence. Some affect relationships. Some affect the way people see themselves.

Patients don’t always know what’s relevant

I’ve also noticed that patients frequently leave out important medical information: diabetes, hypertension, pregnancy, medication use, and bleeding disorders. Usually, it isn’t intentional. Many people simply don’t realize these conditions can influence oral health and dental treatment. To them, the mouth feels separate from the rest of the body. As health care professionals, we often have to bridge that gap.

What this has taught me about patient care

None of these experiences have made me believe patients are dishonest. If anything, they’ve taught me the opposite. Most patients want help. Most patients want to be understood. Most patients want to do the right thing. What prevents them is often fear, embarrassment, financial pressure, misinformation, or simply not knowing what matters.

The more I work with patients, the more I realize that good health care isn’t only about diagnosis and treatment. It’s also about creating an environment where people feel safe enough to tell the full story. Sometimes the most important information isn’t the answer to the first question. It’s the answer that comes after: “Is there anything else you’d like me to know?” And when patients finally answer that question honestly, we are often able to care for them much better.

Mariam Olayode is a dental surgery assistant in Nigeria.

summary: 8月28日，蚂蚁健康与威科集团达成战略合作，整合威科权威医学内容与蚂蚁阿福AI技术，为医生提供即时、可信赖、基于循证的临床洞见。首期成果是威科旗下28本顶尖医学期刊入驻阿福医生版，覆盖17个二级学科，内容全球同步更新。8月，蚂蚁阿福医生版正式上线，定位为医生AI工作站，聚合超6000万篇专业资源，提升循证支持效率和质量。未来，双方将围绕医生需求探索立体化服务升级，计划基于UpToDate打造融合本...
full_content:
从海外到中国，全球临床医生正加速将AI工具融入日常工作流。为切实帮医生减负提效、辅助诊疗，8月28日，蚂蚁健康宣布与全球领先的临床信息和决策支持解决方案提供商威科集团（Wolters Kluwer）（以下简称“威科”）达成战略合作。双方将通过整合威科的权威医学内容与蚂蚁阿福的AI技术和平台能力，为全国数百万医生提供即时、可信赖、基于循证的临床洞见。

 

作为双方合作的首期成果，威科旗下28本具备行业标杆意义的顶尖医学期刊即日起入驻阿福医生版，为全国医生提供可信赖的文献。这28本期刊覆盖17个二级学科，囊括引领全球肿瘤学研究方向的《临床肿瘤学杂志》（Journal of Clinical Oncology）、外科领域引用率最高的《外科年鉴》（Annals of Surgery）等权威刊物，且内容更新与全球保持同步，确保医生能第一时间获取国际前沿医学证据。

 

 

 图：威科旗下多本医学期刊上线阿福医生版

 

今年8月，蚂蚁健康旗下面向医生的应用“蚂蚁阿福医生版”正式上线，定位为国内首个覆盖在线问诊、患者管理和科研全场景的医生AI工作站，为医生配备“AI医学助手”和“AI分身助手”两大核心功能，并与蚂蚁阿福App实现打通，全球范围内率先实现医患双端布局和深度联动。

 

目前，阿福医生版已聚合超过6000万篇循证文献、医学指南、14万份药品说明书等专业资源，其中也包括威科旗下相关医学期刊的阅读权限。在临床决策和科研检索中，无论是针对不同人群的用药方案还是各类循证指南等，医生均可通过阿福医生版查询，还能让AI实时翻译英文指南文献等，循证支持的效率和质量显著提升。

 

期刊上线只是第一步，蚂蚁健康与威科还将围绕医生真实临床需求探索立体化的服务升级。

 

围绕国内医生工作流，蚂蚁健康、威科计划基于UpToDate，为中国医生打造一个融合本土化指南共识、药品说明书等内容的临床决策支持资源。威科UpToDate被誉为“循证医学金标准”，是全球180多个国家和地区、44900家医疗机构的医疗专业人士首选的临床决策工具。双方将进一步探索将这一工具嵌入医生日常诊疗全场景；此外，依托阿福医生版的个性化定制能力，双方还将结合威科顶刊医学知识为每一位医生配备“更懂自己”的专属AI助手。

 

对于此次合作，威科集团副总裁、威科医学国际市场总经理 Christian Cella表示：“中国正加速成为全球最重要的医疗健康AI市场之一，中国医疗机构也在积极探索AI技术的应用。当前，医生对AI的需求，正从信息检索逐步拓展为临床辅助决策、个性化治疗方案、患者全流程管理等多元场景。威科拥有权威医学资源，蚂蚁健康具备强大的AI能力和平台优势。未来，双方将形成合力，助力每一位中国医生‘强技在身’。”

 

蚂蚁集团副总裁、蚂蚁健康事业群总裁张俊杰表示：“蚂蚁健康深耕医疗健康领域十余年，已连接超5000家医院和30万真人医生，并在全国超40城上线‘数字家医’服务。在与医院和医生的长期沟通中，我们深刻体会到，医生群体对提升工作效率、拓宽服务边界有着迫切期待。为此，我们为三甲医院和基层医疗机构等不同场景的医生群体提供了定制化AI能力，希望真正帮医生减负提效，共同服务好广大患者。与威科的合作是一个新起点，未来，蚂蚁将携手更多伙伴，在AI辅助临床决策、全周期健康管理等方向持续深耕，不断探索更贴合医生需求的好服务。”

title: 财报季 | 欧康医药上半年净利润536.13万元，外销收入下降31.11%
summary: 欧康医药2026年上半年营收1.33亿元微降2.81%，但净利润达536.13万元，同比大增74.02%。利润增长主要得益于增值税加计抵减及关税返还款带来的其他收益激增，以及新建产线工艺磨合后槲皮素等产品收率提升、成本管控见效。业务结构上，内销收入增长9.68%，受益于芦丁及黄连素订单增加；外销收入则因客户验证延迟及去库存大幅下滑31.11%，拖累整体营收。产品方面，槐米系列随销量增加而微增，枳实...
full_content:
2026年8月27日，欧康医药披露2026年半年度报告。上半年，欧康医药实现营业收入1.33亿元，同比下降2.81%；归属于上市公司股东的净利润536.13万元，同比增长74.02%；扣非归母净利润355.36万元，同比增长78.93%。基本每股收益0.05元。可以发现，欧康医药上半年的营收基本持平，但净利润增长超七成。

欧康医药营收情况概况统计

 

欧康医药净利润概况统计

 

利润增长的主要驱动因素有二。其一，先进制造业增值税加计抵减政策红利落地，叠加美国子公司收到2025年度支付的关税返还款，共同推高了其他收益。上半年其他收益342.18万元，同比增长265.37%。报告期内公司合计非经常性损益为180.77万元，其中计入当期损益的政府补助为200.73万元。其二，新建产线经过持续工艺磨合，槲皮素和鼠李糖产品收率提升，单位生产成本得到有效管控。

 

从产品结构来看，三大系列表现分化。槐米系列实现营收5094.64万元，同比增长1.27%。公司方面解释，主要因槲皮素和芦丁销量增加。枳实系列营收5468.98万元，同比下降7.13%，主要受查尔酮类产品受市场原因而量价齐跌的影响。综合系列营收2699.84万元，同比下降2.62%。枳实系列占营业收入的41.07%，槐米系列占38.26%，综合系列占20.28%。

 

从区域分布看，内销收入1.03亿元，同比增长9.68%，主要受益于芦丁客户订单增加及黄连素国内采购量提升；外销收入2961.96万元，同比下降31.11%，主要因EP芦丁客户因复审验证延迟订单，以及美国子公司客户清库减少采购。外销下滑对整体营收形成了拖累。

 

费用端，上半年欧康医药的期间费用为1763.67万元，同比减少175.71万元，期间费用率为13.25%。其中销售费用同比下降54.2%，管理费用同比下降7.24%，研发费用同比增长13.86%，财务费用同比增长222.39%。销售费用大幅压缩，研发投入增加，公司在控制运营成本的同时维持了对技术创新的投入力度。经营活动现金流净额2137.66万元，同比下降6.13%，基本保持稳定。

 

在资质认证方面，报告期内公司取得曲克芦丁CEP证书，完成地奥司明WC证书更新、芦丁CEP证书更新等多项海外注册申报工作，地奥司明全新工艺的CEP申报已获受理。曲克芦丁的获证和地奥司明新工艺的申报受理，为公司拓展欧盟市场提供了合规基础。公司产品远销北美、欧洲、日本、澳洲等地区，为海内外知名保健品、医药、食品、化妆品企业供应核心原料。公司加速国内市场布局，逐步开拓国内食品添加剂、医药原料赛道，同步推进化妆品原料、饲料添加剂、药食同源等产品品类国内资质申报与市场拓展。

 

在市场拓展方面，报告期内公司开发新增18家客户，覆盖国内外制药、食品、膳食补充剂、日化领域，产品DBP07、DBP13、DBP14已进入用户注册阶段。部分头部企业开始关注EMIQ等产品，其中部分中小型香精香料公司进入试用阶段，市场开发初见成效，有助于公司降低对美国单一市场的依赖。公司依托Vitafoods、CPHI、FIC等行业展会增加海外意向客户批量储备及开发。

 

在产能建设方面，随着募投项目陆续投产运行，新厂区的积实类（查尔酮类）和槐米类（芦丁、槲皮素等）生产线产能稳步爬坡；老厂区地奥司明产线已完成技术升级改造，实现产能释放。公司拟通过优化工艺参数、细化产品规格排产、调整高附加值产品占比以及强化单耗成本管控等举措，逐步提升产线利用率和运营效率。


作者：武瑛港 崔笑语

title: 刚刚，映恩生物ADC平台超10亿美元出海
summary: 2026年8月28日映恩生物与罗氏旗下基因泰克达成全球合作，依托DUPAC™平台开发下一代ADC药物。映恩生物获4500万美元首付款，潜在里程碑付款超10亿美元，将主导药物发现及早期临床开发，基因泰克获全球独家许可，负责后续开发及商业化。这是映恩生物又一重磅跨国合作，印证中国创新药企在ADC领域的源头创造能力。当前全球ADC产业处于技术迭代关键期，肿瘤耐药等问题凸显，DUPAC™平台是映恩生物针对...
full_content:
2026年8月28日，映恩生物发布公告，已与罗氏集团旗下基因泰克（Genentech）达成全球合作与许可协议。双方将依托映恩生物专有的 DUPAC™新型载荷抗体偶联平台（DualityBio Unique Payload Antibody Conjugate Platform），开发下一代抗体偶联药物（ADC）。

 

根据协议条款，映恩生物将获得4500万美元首付款，并有资格就所有合作项目收取总额超过10亿美元的潜在开发、监管及商业化里程碑付款，同时按获批产品年度净销售额收取分层特许权使用费。

 

研发分工上，映恩生物将主导合作项目的药物发现及全球早期临床开发；基因泰克将获得合作ADC的全球独家许可，在1a期临床开发完成后，独立负责后续临床开发及全球商业化。

 

这是映恩生物达成的又一重磅跨国业务发展合作，也是国产ADC技术平台出海的又一里程碑。继此前与BioNTech、GSK等全球药企达成多项产品授权之后，映恩生物再次凭借底层技术创新获得顶级药企认可，印证了中国创新药企在ADC领域的源头创造能力，正逐步跻身全球第一梯队。

 


当前，全球ADC产业正处于技术迭代的关键关口。

 

以拓扑异构酶抑制剂为代表的载荷ADC，已在多个实体瘤适应症中证实了临床价值，并逐步向更前线治疗推进。但随着临床应用的普及，肿瘤对经典载荷的耐药性、部分肿瘤对传统ADC应答有限等问题日益凸显，成为制约ADC疗效进一步提升的核心瓶颈，也驱动着下一代ADC技术的研发方向。

 

DUPAC™平台正是映恩生物针对这一行业痛点打造的新一代载荷技术平台，也是该公司四大专有ADC技术平台之一。该平台专注于开发具有新型作用机制的差异化载荷，核心目标就是突破现有获批ADC载荷的耐药限制，拓展ADC可覆盖的肿瘤生物学范围。

 

在技术设计上，DUPAC™平台涵盖DUP5、DUP9、DUP10等多种载荷，每种载荷均基于独特的抗肿瘤机制设计，并搭配经过优化的适配型连接子技术，兼顾全身循环稳定性与肿瘤部位特异性释放。

 

整套平台的载荷设计遵循统一的高标准：既保证高效力与广谱抗肿瘤活性，又具备较短的全身半衰期以实现快速清除，同时还能针对异质性实体瘤发挥旁观者效应，从而覆盖对传统拓扑异构酶抑制剂载荷应答不佳的肿瘤类型。

 

目前，基于DUP5及DUP9载荷的ADC已产出扎实的临床前数据：在对拓扑异构酶抑制剂载荷相对不敏感的肿瘤模型中展现出明确抗肿瘤活性，同时在非人灵长类动物中表现出良好的耐受性。相关研究成果已先后在AACR 2025年年会、AACR-NCI-EORTC国际会议、AACR 2026年年会等多个全球顶级学术场合公布，获得行业广泛关注。

 

DUPAC™平台并非孤立的技术点，而是映恩生物ADC技术矩阵的核心组成部分之一。

 

经过多年深耕，映恩生物已构建起四大差异化专有ADC技术平台，覆盖不同技术路径与应用场景，形成了互补的技术壁垒：

 

DITAC（映恩免疫毒素抗体偶联平台）是该公司最成熟的技术平台，基于拓扑异构酶抑制剂载荷设计，已支撑起七款临床阶段资产，在全球超过3200名患者中验证了良好的耐受性与更宽的治疗窗口；

 

DIBAC（创新双特异性抗体偶联平台）是全球为数不多的BsADC技术平台之一，通过双靶点结合提升肿瘤选择性，实现载荷精准递送，发挥协同抗肿瘤效应；

 

DIMAC（免疫调节抗体偶联平台）主打自身免疫疾病赛道，通过智能靶向递送免疫调节载荷，降低全身暴露水平，相比传统免疫治疗方案副作用更优，为自身免疫疾病提供全新治疗路径。

 

四大技术平台共同支撑起映恩生物丰富的产品管线，目前该公司已拥有13款自主研发的ADC候选药物，覆盖肿瘤、自身免疫两大治疗领域，其中多款产品处于全球临床领先梯队。

 


作为全球ADC赛道的核心创新力量，映恩生物近年来持续推进全球化商业布局，已与多家全球顶级药企达成多项重磅许可合作，累计交易总价值超过60亿美元，成为国产创新药技术出海的代表性企业。

 

在此之前，映恩生物已与BioNTech达成三项战略合作，分别针对DB-1303（HER2 ADC）、DB-1311（B7-H3 ADC）、DB-1305（TROP2 ADC）三款核心产品。合作模式上，映恩生物保留大中华区开发与商业化权益，BioNTech负责海外市场的临床开发与商业化。其中DB-1303已在中国提交上市申请，成为国产ADC出海的标杆案例。

 

除此之外，映恩生物还与百济神州就B7-H4靶向ADC达成全球合作，与GSK就CDH17靶向ADC达成独家选择权协议，与Avenzo就EGFR/HER3双抗ADC达成全球授权合作，多条管线同步推进海外临床开发。

 

与上述单产品授权不同，本次与基因泰克的合作，是映恩生物实现技术平台级别的对外授权，标志着公司的技术输出从单个产品层面，升级到底层技术平台层面。

 

放眼全球ADC赛道，技术迭代正在重构产业竞争格局。第一代以经典化疗药物为载荷的ADC已逐步进入成熟阶段，耐药性、适应症拓展的瓶颈日益凸显；下一代ADC的竞争核心，正在向新型作用机制载荷、双特异性递送、免疫调控ADC等方向延伸。

 

未来行业的竞争，将不再是单个分子的比拼，而是技术平台体系、管线迭代能力、全球商业化能力的综合较量。拥有全链条技术平台、能够持续产出差异化候选分子的企业，将在新一轮竞争中占据先机。映恩生物持续落地的跨国合作，正是中国创新药产业升级的一个缩影。

title: ​国内AI虚拟细胞首登《Cell》主刊！腾讯突破AI制药能力瓶颈
summary: 腾讯AI for Life Sciences实验室与中南大学合作构建了全新AI框架UniPert-G2CP，相关论文被《Cell》收录。该模型整合多模态分子扰动因子表征，实现从遗传到化学扰动表型的迁移学习，连接遗传与化学筛选，更准确预测扰动、发现机制，并实现高效计算机辅助药物筛选。其开创性在于回答了同一化合物在不同遗传、细胞背景下响应不同的问题。此前AI在药物研发领域成果显著，但存在共同盲区，即几...
full_content:
用AI模拟细胞对各种干预的反应，是AI虚拟细胞（AIVC）的长期愿景。

 

但现实中，基因筛选和化学药物筛选这两类最重要的扰动数据长期割裂，难以统一建模。

 

面对上述行业挑战，腾讯AI for Life Sciences实验室与中南大学李敏团队合作，构建了一个名为 UniPert-G2CP 的全新AI框架，近日相关论文被《Cell》收录。

 

该模型通过整合多模态分子扰动因子（原因）表征，并实现从遗传到化学扰动表型（结果）的迁移学习，从而连接遗传筛选与化学筛选，从而更准确地预测扰动、发现作用机制，并实现高效的计算机辅助药物筛选。

 

作为国内首个在《Cell》主刊发表的AI虚拟细胞研究成果，它的开创性在于找到了一个新的切口，得以回答问题：同一个化合物，在不同遗传背景、不同细胞背景下的响应，成效为何如此不同？

 

 

过去十年，AI在药物研发领域催生了一系列里程碑式的成果。AlphaFold解决了蛋白结构预测的问题；分子生成模型可以在化学空间中凭空生成新分子；QSAR与ADMET预测能够基于分子结构推算理化性质；DiffDock等AI模型可以预测化合物如何结合到给定靶点。

 

但所有这些成果有一个共同的盲区，即建模的对象是化合物或化合物－单一蛋白靶点，几乎不考虑化合物进入真实细胞后的下游效应。

 

无法模拟细胞的变化，意味着实验室中的优异结果，可能在临床使用中存在显著有效性偏差，

 

真实世界中一个被AI预测为“高亲和力+良好ADMET+类药性优秀”的化合物，仍然可能在BT474乳腺癌细胞里完全无效，在MCF7中却产生显著的转录组扰动。因为这两类细胞的下游通路、基因表达谱、突变背景完全不同。

 

计算结果无法复现，药企往往会承担极大损失。Tufts等多项研究指出，一个新药从立项到上市的平均成本约26亿美元，研发周期10到15年，而临床二期的成功率长期低于30%。大量在分子层面“看起来很好”的化合物，到了细胞和病人身上就失效了。

 

目前的失效成本主要集中在临床前至临床的细胞/动物层面验证阶段。计算建模不覆盖到细胞变化，AI便难以兑现其期望的价值。

 


腾讯与中南大学联合团队提出的UniPert-G2CP，正是针对上述困境设计的解决方案。它是一个两阶段深度学习框架，从基因层面的扰动信息出发，去预测化合物在特定细胞背景下的表型响应。

 

UniPert是一个基于对比学习的多模态分子表征模型，目标是把功能相似的基因、同机制的药物，以及作用于同一通路的基因－药物对，都拉近到同一个语义空间里。

 

针对化学分子，使用SMILES字符串并通过ECFP（扩展连接性指纹）进行子结构特征化；针对遗传扰动，以蛋白质序列为基础输入，整合蛋白质语言模型（ESM）、多序列比对（MSA）和图神经网络（GNN）等多重编码手段。

 

在此基础上，UniPert利用先验生物网络信息和对比学习，将两者映射到共享语义空间，拉近功能相似的跨域扰动分子。

 

论文数据显示：在药物作用机制（MoA）分类任务上，UniPert的类内语义可分性相较传统ECFP方法从1.61提高到1.85，准确率提升14.4%；在35个蛋白药理类别（PCL）上，聚类ARI和NMI分别提高了76.3%和47.0%。

 

 

完成基因筛选和化学药物的统一建模，G2CP（跨域表型迁移学习）开始接手处理数据。

 

它先在基因扰动数据集上预训练模型，让模型学习细胞在不同基因扰动下的基本响应模式；再在有限的化学扰动数据上进行微调，将遗传学知识迁移到药物研发领域。

 

基于这一策略，G2CP有效弥补了化学筛选数据的不足，显著提升了模型在未见化学扰动下的泛化预测能力。

 

两个阶段融合之下，UniPert-G2CP成功将基因和药物的响应规律转化为统一语言，然后将遗传学知识迁移应用到药物研发领域。

 

论文数据显示：在LINCS数据集（跨五种癌细胞系，覆盖4994个基因和7860个小分子）的验证结果中，UniPert-G2CP在仅用20%化学训练数据时，预测精度提升375.4%。

 

此外在ESR1（雌激素受体）案例中，模型成功还原了乳腺癌耐药突变带来的表型偏移，并识别出耐药相关基因和通路。这意味着，UniPert-G2CP已经突破了传统模型“预测”能力的局限性，成功对变化进行了“分析”，完成了生物学解释闭环。

 

 


UniPert-G2CP的突破并非偶然。自2022年开始，腾讯生命科学实验室便开始尝试用统一语言描述生命系统。此后数年，实验室先后发布scBERT、scPROTEIN、scTranslator等模型，均有成果被顶刊收录。

 

这一步调与腾讯健康总裁吴文达强调的步调一致，“科技向善”的核心理念之下，腾讯持续投入蛋白质结构预测、虚拟筛选、分子设计优化、活性预测、ADMET成药性预测、耐药性预测等六大方向，有力推进了全球生命科学的发展。

 

回到UniPert-G2CP。成果验证后，腾讯的研究团队计划将 UniPert–G2CP 作为核心基础能力，集成至即将发布的AI生命科学Agent平台中。这将使虚拟细胞能力以Skill的形式，直接服务于实验科学家的真实科研工作流。

 

从药物靶点的发现与验证，到候选化合物在特定细胞背景下的疗效评估，再到耐药机制的解析。腾讯的目标是让药物研发的关键环节获得可计算、可预测的智能支撑，最终打通从靶点发现到效果评估的虚拟药物研发全链路。

 

由于UniPert–G2CP 提供的是虚拟细胞的基本计算单元，其意义如同GPU之于深度学习。此类计算单元被规模化、模块化并Agent化后，数字孪生诊室将不脱离实验室，真正成为现实。

 

至那时，医生可在云端即可实时构建该患者的数字孪生细胞群，对多种候选治疗方案进行虚拟试验，并基于反馈结果为患者制定最优的组合治疗方案。

 

更快的效率与更小的试错之下，我们或能看到更多患者在付出更少代价的前提下康复，真正实现科技向善。

title: 4人20分钟→单人5分钟搞定！纽智医疗重构核素敷贴制备
summary: 纽智医疗2026年将完成核素敷贴制备系列产品的商业化落地，其核心产品是全球首台套CDS自动核素敷贴制备机，应用于增生性瘢痕等三大疾病治疗。我国相关疾病治疗人群庞大，核素敷贴因无痛、复发率低等特点成首选，但手工制备模式存在诸多问题：人力成本高、效率低，四名医护人员协作需20分钟完成一例简单疤痕敷贴制备，导致医护人员精力被占用、医院运营成本增加、周转效率降低，国内仅216家医疗机构开展相关治疗，患者面...
full_content:
2026年，纽智医疗核素敷贴制备系列产品完成商业化落地，正式面向国内临床场景开展市场推广，为同位素敷贴制备带来了新的智能自动化解决方案。 


 

据创始人马贺透露，这是全球首台套CDS自动核素敷贴制备机，也是纽智医疗现阶段的核心产品，主要应用于增生性瘢痕、瘢痕疙瘩、血管瘤三大疾病的核素敷贴治疗场景。

 

然而，在临床中，这三大疾病的治疗方式十分丰富，除核素敷贴外，还有激光、手术切除、药物注射等数种选项。在此背景之下，为什么纽智医疗还是锚定在了核素敷贴赛道，并致力于探索自动化、智能化技术在其中的应用？

 

故事的开篇，还要从一场对话讲起。

 


2020年，机缘巧合之下，马贺与苏州某医院的核医学科主任有了一次深入交流。

 

正是这次交流，让马贺得以窥见核素敷贴自动化制备这一蓝海市场机遇。

 

一方面，这是一个具有相当体量市场规模的赛道。在我国，由手术或创伤导致的增生性瘢痕的治疗人群每年约有500万人次；而瘢痕疙瘩和皮肤毛细血管瘤的治疗人群每年约为450万人次和50万人次（数据由企业后续测算所得）。而在其中，因无痛、复发率低、性价比高等特点，核素敷贴成为众多患者的治疗首选。

 

然而，这一治疗方式在临床应用，却因手工制备模式而备受桎梏。

 

手工制备模式下，敷贴在临床应用最先面临的问题便是人力成本较高、效率较低。据悉，完成一例简单疤痕的敷贴制备，就需要四名熟练医护人员流水线协同作业20分钟。而这，又会衍生出三大困境。

 

其一是对于医护人员而言，工作时间和精力不得不被裁剪滤纸、滴加核素药液这类重复性劳动占用，导致其难以专注或投身于更高价值的临床实践或科研工作中，着实可惜；其二是对于医院而言，较高的人力成本和效率在一定程度上推高了科室的运营成本，也拉低了周转效率。由此导致部分医院直接不提供相关服务，并由此导致我国相关服务供给有限。


据《2024全国核医学现状普查简报》统计数据，国内仅有216家医疗机构开展核素敷贴治疗。而这，对于那些有意选择这一治疗方式的患者而言，显然也造成了不便。他们或要另寻提供相关项目的医院，或要面临较长的等待周期。

 

但是，人力与供给的矛盾，还并非手工制备模式带来的全部难题。

 

据马贺介绍，手工制备模式下，敷贴的治疗效果还仰仗医生个人经验手感。面对形态复杂、面积庞大的疤痕病灶，敷贴裁剪尺寸、编号整理可能会出现错乱。一旦裁剪尺寸把控失当，偏大的敷贴会灼伤病灶周边健康皮肤，若是尺寸不足，又无法完整覆盖病变区域，最终直接拉低实际治疗效果。

 

与此同时，手工制备带来的职业伤害同样不容忽视。拓印疤痕轮廓、裁剪耗材、滴加放射性同位素药液，整套流程中医护人员都需要近距离接触放射源。经年累月的反复作业，不少医生出现手指反复脱皮、难以愈合的职业损伤，医务人员的职业健康持续承受着隐形威胁。

 

对此，这位本科毕业于东北大学计算机科学与技术专业、博士就读于新加坡国立大学计算机科学专业，尔后又长期深耕医工交叉领域的创业者，意识到，这是可以利用工程思维和能力解决医疗问题的典型案例。而这也正是他一直想做的事。

 

由此，纽智医疗得以诞生，并开启了CDS自动核素敷贴制备机的研发工作。并且，该产品在样机阶段便得到了前述科室主任的高度赞誉。

 

单人耗时5分钟即可完成，人均产值有望提升10-20倍


从提升效率到降低成本，从提升治疗精度到辐射防护，前文所提及的核素敷贴临床痛点，纽智医疗均有解决方案。

 

进一步而言，在效率提升和成本降低方面，纽智医疗CDS自动核素敷贴制备机可将传统手工制备模式下四人二十分钟的制备流程，压缩至单人耗时5分钟，大幅提升作业效率的同时，也有望将科室人均产值提升10-20倍。

 

与此同时，基于纽智医疗自研的AI算法和精准柔性切割技术，该设备可有效提升治疗精度。


 

具体而言，其自研的AI图像识别-分割算法，可实现疤痕与正常皮肤边界的精准识别，进而可有效规避因边界模糊而导致敷贴尺寸不匹配的问题；在此基础上，在AI算法与柔性切割技术的配合下，该设备还可实现针对多种敷贴材料的精准切割（柔性切割精准度达到98%），并兼顾病灶适配性与耗材利用效率；最后纽智医疗的AI算法还可完成核药给药点位测算，保障核素药液在敷贴内部均匀扩散。


 

从“病灶区域”的精准识别到敷贴的精准切割再到给药点位的精准预测，纽智医疗的AI能力贯穿敷贴制备的全流程，也在各个关键环节协同发力，共同实现治疗精准度的提升。

 

而除此之外，纽智医疗亦十分重视医护人员的辐射防护。据马贺介绍，该设备配置全封闭负压防护结构，有机玻璃+铝铅复合外壳在不触发韧至辐射的情况下对原生Beta射线防护率达99%；同时，背部接入医院废气管道的负压发生器能够有效避免潜在的核素气凝胶向外溢出。


不仅如此，纽智医疗还研发了“三明治”辐射防护耗材结构。其中，封闭层为完全透明、防水气密的医用级PU膜，可把核素牢牢锁在内部；载药层则为定制的高吸附性滤纸，可确保磷32核素瞬间吸收并实现绝对均匀分布；屏蔽层则为厚度仅0.5毫米的无铅稀土软胶防护巾，可实现超过99.8%的Beta防护。这意味着，纽智医疗在完成治疗支持的同时，也保护患者、保护医生，以及他们的身边人。

 

通过设备的全封闭负压防护和耗材的“三明治”防护结构，纽智医疗彻底消除医护人员近距离接触放射源和传统重金属致癌材料带来的职业损伤风险。

 

不仅如此，在提升患者舒适度方面，纽智医疗也有自己的巧妙设计：通过前述三层复合材料与外部医用胶带的结合，可自然形成持续的加压效果，相较于传统治疗的“纽扣+弹力绷带”的固定法，可极大提升患者舒适度并提升医生操作效率。

 

截至目前，纽智医疗的CDS自动核素敷贴制备机已能应用于磷32、锶90、SRT治疗；人体定位贴、射线防护巾等耗材也已完成一类医疗器械备案、进入国家医保库并开启全国挂网。


在产品开发完成后，纽智医疗也制定了清晰的商业模式与推广计划，并已取得阶段性成绩。

 

已落地30余家医院，将重点发力核医学智能基础设施建设


“设备+耗材”双轮驱动是纽智医疗目前主要的商业模式。


与此同时，纽智医疗也在布局小程序平台以作为增值服务和数据价值载体，进而构建“设备‑耗材‑平台”三位一体的未来商业生态。

 

进一步来看，在设备方面，针对不同医院的预算现状，纽智医疗开放了销售与租赁两种形式；而在耗材方面，纽智医疗则选择将其与自身设备形成强绑定，以达到更优的应用效果。


并且，依托小程序平台，企业可实现患者治疗全生命周期管理，沉淀C端患者资源，打通院前科普、诊前预约、诊时跟踪到预后随访全链路，让就诊患者自然纳入平台生态。


该生态既可为医院导流、承接预约、健康宣教、随访管理等部分临床流程，沉淀汇总多中心临床数据，也可基于随访场景延伸医美相关药品与服务的商业化机会。

 

据马贺透露，截至目前，已有30余家医院与纽智医疗达成明确合作意向，且部分机构已经完成设备装机，正式投入科室临床使用。

 

在接下来的一段时间里，纽智医疗一方面将持续拓展设备及耗材在更多医院的落地使用；另一方面也在积极寻求千万级融资以扩大生产、拓展市场和建设产业生态。

 

而在更为久远的将来，纽智医疗还会持续立足核医学领域，推出创新产品并完成身份跃迁。

 

具体而言，纽智医疗并不希望只成为单一硬件设备供应商，而是希望成长为核医学领域智能化基础设施提供商，即以AI大模型作为技术内核，提供覆盖诊断‑规划‑治疗‑随访的完整智能解决方案，并在多设备协同联动的基础上搭建起科室级AI辅助决策生态，以此推动核医学科室整体诊疗流程的迭代升级。

 

行文至此，我们已了解到纽智医疗及其产品的特点与优势。而站在产业视角，还有一个值得探讨的问题：同核医学其他细分赛道相比，核素敷贴自动化制备是否存在壁垒不足的隐忧？

 

对此，马贺给出了否定的回答——这一赛道对企业能力提出了综合性要求。它要求企业同时具备AI算法应用研发能力、先进新材料的制备加工能力以及适配临床真需求设备的快速开发能力等。


而纽智医疗组建了一支涵盖人工智能、2C互联网产品、机器人技术、精密机械加工、新材料研发等医工交叉复合型背景的核心团队，能够支撑其完成适配临床需求且横跨多技术领域的医疗设备研发工作。




同时“纽智医疗积累的数十项专利储备、对临床痛点的深度理解、医工交叉复合型人才团队，叠加CDS自动核素敷贴制备机的首证效应，将支撑我们在未来2-3年持续保有核素敷贴自动化制备赛道的先发优势。”马贺总结道。

title: Supporting Thailand’s next generation of AI startups
summary: OpenAI and Thailand’s MHESI launch an eight-week accelerator helping 10 health, wellness, and education startups turn AI prototypes into trusted products....
full_content:
Today in Bangkok, OpenAI and Thailand’s Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation (MHESI) announced a new accelerator to help Thai startups turn promising prototypes into products ready for real-world use and growth.

The OpenAI x MHESI AI Accelerator brings together ten startups working across health, wellness, and education. It marks OpenAI’s first public-private partnership with the Thai government focused on supporting local startups, and is being delivered with partners including the National Innovation Agency (NIA), Mahidol University, and Techsauce.

A compelling AI demonstration is only the beginning. Building a product that people can rely on is much harder. It takes careful testing, feedback from real users, strong safeguards, and a business model that can support the product as it grows. That work matters even more in healthcare and education, where the stakes are high and reliability is essential.

Over eight weeks, participating founders will work with mentors from OpenAI and across Thailand’s technology, research, and startup communities to bridge the gap between prototype and deployment.

A fast-growing community of AI builders

Thailand combines strong technical talent with deep expertise in fields such as healthcare and education, supported by a fast-growing community of AI builders.

Our internal data shows that Thailand ranks among the top 20 countries globally for ChatGPT weekly active users. Since the start of 2026, weekly active usage of Codex in Thailand has grown more than 350-fold, also placing the country among the top 20 globally for Codex usage. This momentum reflects how people across Thailand are increasingly using AI to write software, develop products, and get meaningful work done. The next step is to help more of those ideas move beyond early prototypes and become products people can use and trust.

Building for needs that matter locally

The accelerator’s first cohort includes five startups focused on medical and wellness AI, and five working in education.

Both areas are central to Thailand’s long-term development and well suited to solutions that combine AI with deep local knowledge. An ageing population is increasing demand for new approaches to healthcare, prevention, and independent living. At the same time, stronger learning outcomes and preparation for an increasingly digital economy will be critical to the country’s future competitiveness.

The ten participating startups are CARIVA, Wello Food, Dietz, Precisionize, FitSloth, Curico, insKru, Floaino, EasyKids Robotics, and Globish. Selected with NIA, the Ministry of Education, and the MHESI innovation network, the cohort includes teams that participated in the AIAT × OpenAI Codex Hackathon Bangkok earlier this year.

Each company is focused on a specific problem. The accelerator will help the teams combine their domain knowledge with frontier AI capabilities to build products grounded in the needs of people and organizations across Thailand.

How the accelerator works

Throughout the accelerator, the startups will work alongside OpenAI mentors to strengthen their products and prepare for deployment.

OpenAI will provide each team with US$2,000 in API credits, one-on-one technical guidance, and access to OpenAI’s latest frontier models. Each startup will also have a dedicated mentor throughout the program. Weekly sessions will cover product design, engineering, automated testing, evaluation, responsible AI, privacy and security, cost management, growth, and fundraising.

MHESI will connect the teams with Thailand’s research and talent networks, while NIA will link them to the country’s funding and growth ecosystem. Mahidol University will contribute academic expertise and mentors.

Each startup will set a specific product, pilot, evaluation, or commercial milestone for the eight-week program. By the end of the accelerator, teams are expected to demonstrate a working product or substantial upgrade, evidence from representative users, initial evaluation findings, and a credible path to implementation.

From hospital phone lines to classrooms

CARIVA is developing a multilingual voice agent for hospital phone lines. Designed to communicate in a patient’s preferred language, it can assist with routine requests such as appointment scheduling and recognize when a caller may be describing a medical emergency.

During the accelerator, CARIVA will work with OpenAI on evaluation methods and steering strategies for its real-time speech model. By Demo Day, the team aims to deploy the first capability in a pilot hospital’s live call flow.

Curico is developing AI-powered learning tools for children, families, and educators.

By Demo Day, Curico aims to pilot its platform in Bangkok Metropolitan Administration childcare centers, with a pathway to reach more than 200 centers. The team also plans to train more than 200 teachers through an AI storybook workshop with the Institute for the Promotion of Teaching Science and Technology; test AI-assisted grading at Chulalongkorn University; develop new school pilots with MHESI and the Ministry of Education; and grow its family learning platform to more than 1,000 monthly active users.

From accelerator to implementation

The accelerator will conclude with a Demo Day in Bangkok in November. Participating startups will demonstrate what they have built, share evidence from users and product evaluations, and present their plans for deployment and growth.

The event will bring together investors, government agencies, universities, hospitals, schools, potential customers, and other organizations that can help move successful prototypes into sustained implementation.

This first cohort is the beginning of a longer-term effort. By bringing together government, universities, startups, investors, and technology partners, we aim to establish a repeatable model that helps Thai founders build trusted AI products and take solutions developed in Thailand to the world.

title: Patient dissatisfaction begins before the doctor walks in
summary: When patients describe a disappointing health care experience, we often assume the problem occurred in the examination room. Sometimes it did. But after years of caring for patients in urgent and emer...
full_content:
When patients describe a disappointing health care experience, we often assume the problem occurred in the examination room. Sometimes it did. But after years of caring for patients in urgent and emergency settings and helping lead a high-volume orthopedic urgent care practice, I have learned that many negative patient experiences begin long before the physician walks through the door.

A patient may arrive in pain and not know how long the visit will take. They may move from registration to an examination room to imaging without understanding what happens next. They may receive excellent medical care and still leave frustrated because nobody explained the process.

That distinction matters. If we treat every patient-experience problem as a physician communication problem, we risk trying to fix individuals when what often needs attention is the system surrounding them.

Patients experience a journey, not an encounter

Clinicians tend to think about visits in clinical segments: history, examination, imaging, diagnosis, treatment, and disposition. Patients experience something different. They experience the front desk, paperwork, waiting room, medical assistant, examination room, imaging department, clinician, discharge process, and follow-up instructions as one continuous encounter. A breakdown anywhere along that journey can influence how they perceive everything that follows.

This is particularly apparent in urgent care. Patients often arrive unexpectedly, in pain, and looking for answers quickly. Meanwhile, the clinical team is balancing unpredictable patient volumes, procedures, imaging, acute injuries, and competing demands.

Small operational problems can quickly become patient-experience problems.

Waiting is not always the real problem

One of the most important lessons I have learned is that patients may tolerate waiting better than they tolerate uncertainty. There will always be days when a medical practice runs behind. An unexpectedly complex patient may require additional attention. Imaging may take longer than anticipated. An urgent case may appropriately move ahead of another patient.

We cannot eliminate every delay. But we can reduce the uncertainty surrounding it. A brief acknowledgment of a delay and an explanation of what happens next can change the experience.

Silence creates its own narrative. A patient sitting alone in an examination room may assume nobody knows they are there. Meanwhile, the clinical team may be reviewing imaging, consulting another clinician, or preparing the next step in care. The work is happening. The patient simply cannot see it.

Closing that information gap may be one of the simplest opportunities we have to improve the patient experience.

Before blaming the employee, examine the process

Health care has another tendency worth reconsidering. When something goes wrong, we often look first for the person responsible. Why didn’t someone communicate the delay? Why did the patient wait so long? Why wasn’t imaging completed sooner? Why did discharge take another 20 minutes?

Sometimes individual performance does need to be addressed. But when the same problem occurs repeatedly across different employees and different days, leaders should ask a different question: Is our system making it unnecessarily difficult for people to do their jobs well?

That question has changed how I approach operational problems as a physician leader. Perhaps responsibilities are unclear. Perhaps information is not reaching the right person. Perhaps two processes unnecessarily duplicate each other. Perhaps staffing does not match patient arrival patterns.

Patient feedback can therefore be more than a satisfaction metric. It can be operational intelligence.

Physicians need to participate in process improvement

Physicians sometimes view operational improvement as something that happens in administrative meetings. I think that is a missed opportunity.

Frontline clinicians see parts of the health care system that dashboards cannot fully capture. We know where patients repeatedly become confused. We see bottlenecks develop. We know which processes look efficient on paper but become cumbersome during a busy clinic.

At the same time, physicians see only one part of the system. Medical assistants, nurses, advanced practice providers, imaging staff, schedulers, front-desk teams, and operational leaders see problems that physicians may never notice. Meaningful improvement happens when those perspectives meet. My experience in physician leadership has increasingly convinced me that improving patient experience requires the same mindset we bring to clinical quality: identify the problem, understand the process, involve the people doing the work, make a change, and determine whether it actually helped.

The goal should not be a better score

Patient-experience scores matter. They can identify patterns and highlight areas that deserve attention. But chasing the number itself can become the wrong objective. A better question is: What is the score trying to tell us about the patient’s experience?

A poor communication score may reveal a communication problem. A poor waiting score may reveal a workflow or capacity problem. Repeated complaints about staff interactions may point toward unclear expectations, inadequate training, or processes that consistently place employees in difficult situations.

The number is the signal. The work begins when we determine what is producing it. That is why sustainable patient-experience improvement cannot belong to a single physician or department. It requires clinical care, operations, communication, leadership, and frontline staff to work toward the same objective.

Patient experience is an operational outcome

The longer I work in urgent and emergency care, the less I view patient experience as a separate category of health care. It is often the visible result of everything happening underneath.

When communication is clear, workflows make sense, teams understand their responsibilities, and patients know what to expect, the experience feels different. Not because someone instructed the staff to provide “five-star service.” Because the system is functioning better around the patient.

That may be the most important lesson physician leaders can take from patient-experience feedback: If we want patients to experience better care, we should not begin by asking how to improve the score. We should begin by asking how to improve the system that produced it.

Manoj Sreedharan is a board-certified family medicine physician and the medical director of Injury Express at OrthoIllinois in Rockford, Illinois. He is also an assistant professor at the University of Illinois College of Medicine Rockford and a practicing emergency medicine physician at MercyOne Clinton in Iowa.

His work focuses on health care quality improvement, patient safety, patient experience, clinical operations, and evidence-based medicine. He is actively involved in clinical research, including biologic therapies for rheumatologic conditions, and serves as a peer reviewer for medical journals. He is passionate about advancing health care through physician leadership, medical education, and continuous quality improvement.

His peer-reviewed work includes a study of blood pressure control among U.S. adults with hypertension stratified by glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist use, drawn from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2017 to 2020. He shares updates on LinkedIn.

title: Hospital peer review needs recusal rules, not assumptions
summary: Hospital peer review is one of medicine’s most important mechanisms for protecting patients and maintaining professional standards. Physicians possess the clinical expertise necessary to evaluat...
full_content:
Hospital peer review is one of medicine’s most important mechanisms for protecting patients and maintaining professional standards. Physicians possess the clinical expertise necessary to evaluate the work of other physicians, particularly when questions involve complex procedures, specialty-specific judgment, or unusual complications.

But this structure creates an unavoidable tension. The physicians most qualified to evaluate a colleague may also be the physicians who compete with that colleague for patients, referrals, operating-room access, call coverage, procedural volume, leadership positions, or hospital resources.

That does not mean competitors are inherently biased. Nor does the existence of competition establish that a peer-review decision is improper. The more useful policy question is narrower: When professional or economic competition exists, what safeguards should hospitals use to preserve confidence in the fairness of peer review?

Expertise and independence are not always the same thing

Consider two surgeons practicing the same subspecialty at the same hospital. Their overlapping expertise may make one an ideal clinical reviewer of the other’s cases. Yet they may also compete for referrals, block time, service-line leadership, equipment, personnel, or procedural market share.

Both realities can be true simultaneously. A physician can possess exceptional clinical expertise while also having interests that could reasonably raise questions about impartiality. Recognizing that possibility is not an accusation of misconduct. It is simply good governance.

Medicine already recognizes conflicts of interest in other settings. Researchers disclose financial relationships. Medical journals increasingly maintain policies governing conflicts involving editors and peer reviewers. Corporate directors may recuse themselves from decisions involving personal financial interests, and judges operate under recusal standards designed to protect confidence in impartial decision-making. Professional review deserves comparable institutional rigor.

What the evidence tells us

Conflict management in medicine is not a new concept. A 2025 scoping review in BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine examined empirical research on conflicts of interest among biomedical peer reviewers and concluded that both financial and nonfinancial interests can affect the integrity of peer-review processes.

A separate 2025 study in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology examined 250 medical journals and found that about 70 percent had conflict-of-interest policies for peer reviewers. Most policies included some form of management strategy, although their comprehensiveness varied considerably. More recent research examining how journals actually implement these policies found that reviewers with identified conflicts were frequently disqualified from reviewing, while substantial variation remained in disclosure, verification, enforcement, and implementation.

These studies involve scientific publishing rather than hospital credentialing, so the two systems should not be treated as identical. But they demonstrate a broader principle: Expertise does not eliminate the need to identify and manage competing interests. Hospital peer review could apply the same principle.

A tiered conflict and recusal framework

Rather than assuming every competitor is biased (or pretending competition is irrelevant), hospitals could adopt a standardized three-tier approach:

  • Low-level conflict (document): Two physicians practice in the same specialty and hospital but have no meaningful financial rivalry, active personal dispute, or direct involvement in the matter under review. Participation may be appropriate, with a documented conflict disclosure.
  • Moderate conflict (disclose and corroborate): Physicians significantly overlap in referral networks, procedural services, call responsibilities, leadership opportunities, or service-line competition. Participation may still be reasonable, but the competing interest should be disclosed, and important clinical conclusions should be independently corroborated.
  • High-level conflict (recuse and obtain independent review): A reviewer directly competes financially with the physician under review, has a substantial personal or business conflict, originated or materially participated in the allegation, or could derive meaningful professional or economic benefit from restricting the physician’s practice. In these circumstances, recusal from final deliberation or voting and independent external specialty review should be strongly considered.

This framework does not presume misconduct. It simply matches the safeguard to the magnitude of the conflict.

Patient safety still comes first

Any reform must preserve the ability of hospitals to respond immediately to genuine patient-safety threats. A surgeon confronting an intraoperative emergency cannot wait for an external reviewer hundreds of miles away. Medical staffs must retain the authority to intervene rapidly when patient welfare may be at risk.

The important distinction is between immediate patient-safety intervention and final professional judgment. A physician with a potential conflict may appropriately provide technical information or participate in an urgent clinical response. That does not necessarily mean the same physician should control the investigation, determine whether a standard was violated, recommend sanctions, and vote on the final professional-review action. Separating these roles may strengthen both safety and confidence in the process.

Federal law already recognizes economic competition

There is an important policy signal within the Health Care Quality Improvement Act of 1986 (HCQIA). HCQIA establishes standards under which qualifying professional-review actions receive protection from damages. Among other requirements, an action must be undertaken in the reasonable belief that it furthers quality health care, after a reasonable effort to obtain the facts, with adequate procedures, and in the reasonable belief that the action is warranted by the known facts. The statute also creates a presumption that qualifying professional-review actions satisfy those standards unless rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence.

Notably, HCQIA’s statutory safe-harbor hearing procedures state that a hearing officer or panel should not be in direct economic competition with the physician involved. That provision does not prohibit every economically competing physician from participating at every stage of peer review. But it demonstrates that Congress recognized direct economic competition as sufficiently important to address explicitly when describing fair hearing procedures.

Courts have also emphasized that HCQIA applies an objective reasonableness standard. In Poliner v. Texas Health Systems, the Fifth Circuit held that subjective bad faith or alleged anticompetitive motive alone does not defeat HCQIA immunity; the key question is whether the professional-review action was objectively reasonable based on the information available at the time.

That makes prospective conflict management even more important. The strongest policy is not one that waits for litigation to determine whether bias occurred. It is one that builds safeguards into the process before consequential decisions are made.

External review as a quality safeguard

External review should not be interpreted as a vote of no confidence in the local medical staff. When substantial conflicts exist, an independent physician from the same specialty can provide a clinical assessment less affected by local referral patterns, economic relationships, leadership disputes, or institutional dynamics.

Hospitals could reduce cost and delay by developing regional peer-review collaborations or maintaining pre-vetted panels of independent specialists available for expedited review. The external reviewer need not replace the medical executive committee. The purpose is to provide an independent evidentiary baseline before consequential credentialing decisions are finalized.

Protecting the credibility of professional self-regulation

Physicians have been entrusted with extraordinary responsibility to regulate their own profession. That authority depends not only on expertise but also on confidence in the integrity of the process.

The question is not whether competitors should ever evaluate one another. In specialized medicine, some degree of professional overlap may be unavoidable. The better question is whether institutions should rely solely on informal assumptions of impartiality when disclosure, corroboration, recusal, and independent specialty review are available.

Peer review is strongest when physicians and patients can reasonably believe that clinical evidence (not economic rivalry, referral competition, institutional politics, or personal conflict) is determining the outcome. Expertise gives peer review its clinical authority. Independence gives it credibility. Medicine needs both.

Babajide Ogunseinde is a Harvard-trained, ABPS board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon, innovator, author, and physician leader with more than fifteen years of experience and over 8,000 spine procedures. He practices as an independent spine consultant. A summa cum laude graduate of Virginia Commonwealth University and valedictorian of Howard University College of Medicine, he completed his orthopedic surgery residency and his spine fellowship at Harvard.

Ogunseinde pioneered the FDA-cleared posteromedial-to-lateral (PML) technique for sacroiliac joint fusion and founded the PML Mastery digital app. He holds a health care leadership certification from Stanford University and is an MBA and Certified Physician Executive candidate. He serves as an ABPS oral board examiner and codirector of its leadership program, and he is a new Distinguished Fellow of the North American Spine Society and an editorial reviewer for the Journal of Spine Surgery.

His scholarship spans sacroiliac joint dysfunction, minimally invasive spine surgery, outcomes in high-BMI patients, and orthopedic trauma, with work appearing in the Journal of Clinical Spine Surgery, the Journal of Spine Surgery, the Journal of Surgical Case Reports, and the Journal of Pediatric Orthopedics. He is the author of four books spanning surgical innovation, sacroiliac joint disease, faith, leadership, weight loss, and preventive health: Faith and Purpose: The PML Story; SI Joint Dysfunction: The Truth Shall Set You Free; Messages From Our Father: Father’s Wisdom; and The Coach Before the Scalpel: A Surgeon and a Coach’s Guide to Preventing Obesity, Chronic Back Pain, and the Surgery You Never Needed. He is a 2026 Global Recognition Award recipient and an international invited speaker.

His books and PML resources are available at ogunseindepml.com, and he shares updates on LinkedIn, Instagram, and YouTube.

title: Medical satire: A wolf can pass as your doctor now
summary: When I was just a Medium-Sized Bad Wolf loping through the forest, I stumbled upon a doctor in a white coat, carrying a bag of supplies. It was Sunday night, and dinner options were scarce, since most...
full_content:
When I was just a Medium-Sized Bad Wolf loping through the forest, I stumbled upon a doctor in a white coat, carrying a bag of supplies. It was Sunday night, and dinner options were scarce, since most other humans were home with their families.

“Where are you going so late, Doctor?”

She sighed. “Another patient who refused the flu vaccine is sick with the flu, so I’m bringing them Tamiflu.”

I tricked her into giving me the patient’s address by saying I had free Ozempic samples. Then I ate her, but she was mostly bones and Monster Energy drinks.

Thankfully, the patient was nice and plump after repeated insurance denials of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s). Licking my lips, I realized I’d stumbled upon a brilliant disguise. A white coat, so much better than a red hood!

Soon I became a Big Bad Wolf working full time as a doctor, and it’s been a truly satisfying career. Especially now that people get medical advice from TikTok influencers, I often don’t even have to do anything very wolfly to get humans to do my bidding.

I started out in the ER, where everyone was still two steps from the ledge after the pandemic. Patients in extreme duress never noticed my big teeth, let alone my eyes or ears. Even if I forgot to wipe all the blood off my mouth, people willingly submitted to my “treatment.”

Like, when someone came in with a life-threatening arrhythmia, BAM! They let me sedate them straight away. One time, after a particularly tasty meal, I got carried away and howled, “WHO’S AFRAID OF THE BIG BAD WOLF!” In the chaos of code blues, nonstop alarms, and patients screaming in pain or shouting at staff, no one so much as glanced up at me.

With all the desperately ill people, including many no one would miss, it was almost too easy. And I was prospering a bit too much, even for my high-capacity stomach.

So I decided to try my paw at primary care, where they were so frantic for anyone to deal with the never-ending unpaid work of responding to AI-written emails that they practically begged me to join. Patients greeted me with the squinty eyes of skeptics who had lots of opinions about ivermectin (which I’m a big fan of, having used it for a gnarly case of mange).

“Doctor, what big eyes you have,” they’d say when I suggested it was time for a colonoscopy. Then when I recommended a vaccine, they’d suddenly notice my large teeth. I’d learned by this point, after one pulled a gun on me, to swallow them whole.

Soon enough, though, this also became too predictable.

Given my passion for gore, I decided to be a surgeon, the kind that does nonemergency “elective” surgeries. This would be a true test of my wolfly powers of deception. Plus, I’d get to run around with a scalpel.

Plastic surgery was the obvious choice, but it was tough to get into. Humans hate vaccines, but they love nose jobs. I was about to give up when I discovered a subspecialty with shockingly little competition: gender-affirming surgery.

The lack of interest was baffling, since I’d heard so much on the news about this field’s potential for huge profits and all the young, impressionable humans who were easy targets. Still, I was practically a lone wolf, frothing with anticipation.

Unfortunately, it turned out that the multimillion-dollar “sex-rejecting procedures” industry included a whole lot of things that didn’t involve any actual cutting. And the tender-fleshed young humans I’d drooled over weren’t getting gender-affirming surgery very often.

On top of that, patients had difficulty getting coverage and often required lengthy evaluations. No apex predator should ever have to submit a prior authorization, and wrangling diagnosis codes made me growl and gnash my teeth.

So there was hardly any surgery, only wasted time and my hungry belly. At one point, I hadn’t seen the OR (or had a meal that wasn’t a rat from the hospital parking lot) for four weeks!

I admit, I got a little sloppy in my hunger and despair. One day in clinic, a patient said, “Doctor, what big hands you have!” and I just said, “Yup.”

Even worse, these patients were shrewd and well connected. Slowly but surely, in online communities and chat groups, they pieced together my tiny missteps: hairs sticking out of my mask, a slip of the tail, those few times I forgot to walk on my hind legs.

Just as they were about to out me publicly with their planned peaceful protest and sit-in, I struck a deal with the feds: I’d out myself as the Big Bad Wolf Doctor in exchange for my protection.

Now I live in a cage that says “Property of the Federal Government.” I’m only allowed out for media appearances, and I’m technically not supposed to eat people anymore, but at least my belly’s not filled with stones.

The good news is that they still allow me to do plenty of shifts in the immigrant clinic. Although they taste plenty human to me, my new boss says they don’t count.

The author is an anonymous physician.

title: Cognitive assessment in primary care almost never happens
summary: In my primary care practice, few moments carry as much quiet weight as when an older patient leans in and says, “Doctor, I’m worried about my memory.” That moment is increasingly com...
full_content:
In my primary care practice, few moments carry as much quiet weight as when an older patient leans in and says, “Doctor, I’m worried about my memory.” That moment is increasingly common, given that an estimated 42 percent of adults who reach age 55 will develop dementia in their lifetime, so nearly every family will face a version of it. It takes courage to say those words out loud, but our health care system too often dismisses memory issues as a normal part of aging, when it doesn’t have to be.

A study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia perfectly encapsulates this widespread challenge. Only 5.4 percent of patients who reported a new memory concern at their Medicare Annual Wellness Visit (AWV) received a cognitive assessment, and just 2.1 percent were referred to a specialist. The AWV already requires clinicians to look for cognitive problems, so these were patients who named the exact issue we are meant to catch. Of the 1,411 patients studied, more than 9 in 10 still walked out without an assessment or referral.

It’s critically important that we as PCPs leverage every tool in our toolbox to address this missed opportunity. A short, AI-based cognitive assessment can find these patients early, right inside the primary care visit, and with early interventions and personalized brain health action plans, we can help change the trajectory of these patients’ lives.

Missed opportunities

PCPs are working in good faith, even under enormous pressures. We are stretched thin, with only minutes per visit and no clear pathway to turn a patient’s memory concern into a cognitive assessment and a plan. That is perhaps one of the reasons why primary care identifies only about 8 percent of the mild cognitive impairment it should be detecting, which leaves more than 7 million Americans living with an early, often treatable condition they know nothing about.

When a memory concern goes unaddressed, delay compounds the harm. A dementia diagnosis arrives on average 3.5 years after symptoms first appear, and the wait stretches longer for younger patients and for people of color. Every month of delay narrows the window when a clinician can still intervene, when lifestyle change carries the most weight, and when families can plan while their loved one still has a strong voice in those decisions.

Waiting also squanders the chance to fix problems outright, because some cognitive impairment traces to reversible causes such as sleep disorders, medication side effects, vitamin deficiencies, depression, or thyroid disease. The economic stakes track the human ones, as dementia now costs the country an estimated $781 billion a year, much of it driven by late-stage care that earlier detection could help reduce.

Lessons from oncology

Two generations ago, medicine faced the same kind of gap in breast cancer, but closed it. Historically, physicians typically waited until a lump appeared, then treated a cancer that had often already spread. Routine mammography rewrote that story, and early large-scale trials reported a roughly 31 percent reduction in mortality among women invited for screening. Finding disease earlier, at scale, changed the outcome.

In dementia, the same opportunity is within reach. Up to 45 percent of cases could be prevented or delayed by addressing modifiable risk factors, the 2024 Lancet Commission estimates. Earlier detection can expand clinicians’ access to proven interventions and offer more time to use them.

Similarly, just as Medicare coverage once made mammography routine, the bipartisan Alzheimer’s Screening and Prevention (ASAP) Act would open a pathway for Medicare to cover tests that detect Alzheimer’s earlier. The Alzheimer’s Association has framed this embrace of early detection as brain health’s mammogram moment. The label fits, given that the tests exist, but insurance coverage is what truly turns them into the standard of care.

Making assessment routine

The clinical tools available appear well-suited for this moment. A short digital assessment captures hundreds of data points beyond the reach of a paper test, from the timing of a pen stroke to subtle patterns in speech, and AI analyzes them in minutes rather than the two to three hours a full neuropsychological evaluation demands. That analysis gives a primary care team specialist-level insight at the point of care, turning a memory concern into clear clinical indicators and a plan to act on, the same day rather than a months-long wait.

Making cognitive assessments part of everyday practice will require deliberate choices by health system leaders. Four steps would move us quickly:

  • Treat a reported memory concern as an actionable finding, with a documented response at the same visit.
  • Build a brief cognitive assessment into the AWV, where federal rules already require attention to cognition.
  • Equip primary care with validated assessments, so detection does not hinge on a scarce specialist.
  • Decide in advance what a positive result triggers: a fuller evaluation, a care plan, or a targeted specialist referral.

Even without a single new discovery, we could close this detection gap today. The assessments are validated and take only minutes, and patients are already speaking up. When an older person summons the courage to voice their concern, our job is to meet them with more than a reassuring nod. We owe them a clear answer and a plan, while there is still time to change the outcome.

Health systems that build readiness now will spare countless families years of avoidable uncertainty and set the standard for brain health for the next generation.

John Showalter is board-certified in internal medicine and informatics and serves as chief operating officer of Linus Health, an AI-driven brain health company focused on early detection and proactive intervention. Linus Health has won Time Magazine’s Best Inventions and Fast Company’s Innovation by Design awards for its work bringing the power of digital cognitive assessments to PCPs.

He practices medicine in Danville, Pa., with a focus on cognitive care and dementia prevention. He can be found on LinkedIn.

title: The Seroquel controversy most doctors have forgotten
summary: Few drugs boast the rap sheet of Seroquel (quetiapine). After the pharmaceutical industry marketed atypical antipsychotics like Seroquel as amazingly superior to older antipsychotics like Thorazine an...
full_content:
Few drugs boast the rap sheet of Seroquel (quetiapine). After the pharmaceutical industry marketed atypical antipsychotics like Seroquel as amazingly superior to older antipsychotics like Thorazine and Haldol (pay no attention to their same tardive dyskinesia side effects), Seroquel became its manufacturer’s second-best-selling drug globally, behind only Nexium and netting $5.3 billion in 2011. Many have forgotten Seroquel’s contested past, including how an early proponent went to prison in a research funding fraud case, how unsealed litigation documents raised conflict-of-interest questions about the drug’s science, and how the drug’s heavy use in the military drew belated scrutiny.

The rap sheet and danger cascade continue. In April, research in the Annals of the American Thoracic Society linked quetiapine to next-day impaired alertness and impaired driving. Last year, a warning about elevated prolactin and a possible association with breast cancer was added to the quetiapine label. Also last year, the drug’s manufacturer resolved a lawsuit over alleged generic-delaying maneuvers with a $51 million settlement that included no admission of wrongdoing. Here is a quick Seroquel history:

  • Richard Borison, MD, former chief of psychiatry at the Augusta Veterans Affairs (VA) medical center and the Medical College of Georgia, and his research partner ran industry-funded drug trials that enrolled patients at the VA hospital and at other sites. Both were accused of diverting more than $10 million from the Medical College of Georgia into privately held companies. Borison pleaded guilty to counts including theft and racketeering and was sentenced to 15 years in prison. His 1996 U.S. Seroquel Study Group research has never been retracted and stands today.
  • Charles Schulz, MD, a prominent early Seroquel proponent, received $112,000 in consulting fees and university grants from the drug’s manufacturer between 2002 and 2007, according to state records.
  • Unsealed litigation documents reported in 2009 showed that Wayne Macfadden, MD, then the U.S. medical director for Seroquel at the manufacturer, acknowledged sexual relationships with women involved in the drug’s research and publications. Plaintiffs’ lawyers argued that the relationships were conflicts of interest that biased the company’s science. The documents did not establish what effect, if any, the relationships had on published results.
  • More than 15 years ago, a West Virginia father whose son died compiled a list of nearly 300 soldiers and veterans who were taking Seroquel and antidepressants and who died suddenly or whose deaths the military ruled suicides. Families identified Pfc. Derek Johnson, 22, of Hurricane, West Virginia; Cpl. Andrew White, 23, of Cross Lanes, West Virginia; Cpl. Chad Oligschlaeger, 21, of Round Rock, Texas; Cpl. Nicholas Endicott, 24, of Pecks Mill, West Virginia; and Spc. Ken Jacobs, 21, of Walworth, New York among those who died suddenly while taking drug combinations that included Seroquel. A warning about cardiac side effects was later added to the label.

Conclusion

In my view, the commercial success and financial tenacity of drugs like Seroquel owe a great deal to “ask your doctor” direct-to-consumer advertising. That advertising encourages fear, hypochondria, self-diagnosis, and uncritical acceptance of pharmaceutical marketing.

Martha Rosenberg is an investigative reporter whose work has appeared in the British Medical Journal (BMJ), Consumer Reports, Public Citizen, the Center for Health Journalism at USC Annenberg, the Nieman Foundation for Journalism at Harvard University, and other outlets. She studied at Rush Medical School and writes on health care, food, medicine, and public policy.

Rosenberg’s reporting has been cited by Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, Public Library of Science Biology, ScienceDirect, the Journal of Pain & Palliative Care Pharmacotherapy, the Journal of Trauma & Dissociation, Britannica, National Geographic, Hastings Law Journal, and Wikipedia. She is the author of several books, including Multidisciplinary Management of Chronic Pain: A Practical Guide for Clinicians, Born With a Junk Food Deficiency, Big Food, Big Pharma, Big Lies, and Food, Clothes, Men, Gas and Other Problems. She publishes on Substack, OpEdNews, and her Amazon author page.

title: 研发花9亿营收2.6亿，礼来亚洲高瓴启明投资的Biotech冲刺A+H上市
summary: 2026年8月，益方生物向港交所递交招股书，此前已于2022年7月登陆上交所科创板，募资20.8亿元。其营收起伏不定，2024年1.69亿，2025年大降78%，2026年H1同比大涨178%。公司由三位海归博士创立，在先灵葆雅和默沙东有丰富药物研发经验，且做药底子扎实。融资过程中，礼来亚洲、高瓴创投等明星机构参与，合计带来14.35亿元资金。目前，益方生物有两款已上市产品贝福替尼和格索雷塞，均授...
full_content:
2026年8月，益方生物再次向港交所递交招股书。


不同于部分初创Biotech，这家公司已经拥有两款对外授权并且获批进入医保的药物。同时在2022年7月已经成功登陆上交所科创板，拿到了20.8亿元的A股募资。只是其营收却起伏不定，2024年有1.69亿，2025年却大降78%，进入2026年H1，又同比大涨178%。


在其融资过程中，不乏有高瓴创投、礼来亚洲、启明创投、奥博资本等明星机构的参与。这样一家受明星机构追捧，已经登陆科创板、手握两款商业化产品的Biotech为何仍要奔赴港交所推进A+H布局？



益方生物的创始团队，来自3位前默沙东、先灵葆雅的海归科学家。


王耀林是三人中的老大哥，赴美完成博士学位和博士后研究后，在先灵葆雅和默沙东工作了近20年，专注于抗肿瘤小分子药物的药理研究与开发，是业内备受认可的资深科学家。2013年他回国创立益方生物，统筹战略方向和重大研发决策。


江岳恒在先灵葆雅和默沙东从事了近15年的小分子新药研究，回国后曾任职于雅本化学，积累了丰富的研发管理和产业运营经验。加入益方后，他负责业务发展和CMC（化学、制造与控制）等核心环节，以及牵头对外合作。


代星博士则在先灵葆雅和默沙东拥有超过17年的药物发现与研发项目管理经验。三位创始人从求学、科研到创业，彼此之间的发展轨迹相似，既有学术上的默契，也有产业上的互补，是益方生物走到今天的重要基石。


一路陪伴这家公司成长的，还有一批生物医药圈的投资机构。从早期轮次到D轮，礼来亚洲、高瓴创投、启明创投、奥博资本等明星机构接连入局，合计给公司带来14.35亿元资金。


这个团队做药底子扎实，但商业化能力稍显不足。目前益方的两款上市产品，贝福替尼和格索雷塞，已经把国内权益授权给其他药企，靠首付款、里程碑、特许权使用费换取收入。公司过往的全部收入，几乎都来自贝达药业、正大天晴这两家合作方。


贝福替尼，一款第三代 EGFR 抑制剂，授权给到贝达药业，药物已经在国内获批上市，顺利进入国家医保目录。格索雷塞，KRAS G12C 抑制剂，授权正大天晴，同样完成获批、纳入医保。


两款产品走完从实验室到申报上市的完整路径，证明了自身具备把自研小分子推到商业化阶段的转化能力。


真正决定益方未来天花板的，是两款还处在注册3期临床的核心候选药物D-2570和D-0502。


D-2570是TYK2变构抑制剂，瞄准银屑病，溃疡性结肠炎、系统性红斑狼疮等一系列自身免疫疾病。它的2期临床试验拿到不错的数据，银屑病面积与严重程度指数改善75%以上的患者比例达到90%，严重不良事件发生率为0。


益方在研管线，图源招股书


另一款核心产品泰瑞司群，代号D-0502，是一款口服SERD药物，用于治疗雌激素受体阳性乳腺癌。它正与现有标准治疗药物氟维司群注射液展开头对头的3期临床。如果成功，意味着这部分乳腺癌患者有望告别每月一次的肌肉注射，改为每天一片口服药。


再往后看，益方手里还握着一批处在临床前的储备项目。包括WRN、KIF18A这类合成致死靶点候选分子，还有STAT6降解剂。同时还在打磨新一代ADC平台，自己设计连接子和有效载荷，为更远期的产品做储备。



把核心管线放回行业坐标里，才能看明白它的机会和风险。


TYK2抑制剂是一个被验证过的蓝海。2022年，BMS的Deucravacitinib获批上市，打开了这扇大门。全球TYK2抑制剂市场2025 年规模约6.85亿美元，2035年可望达到96.3亿美元。中国市场增速更快，2028年到2035年的复合增长率预计达到37.5%。


除了BMS，全球还有6条管线处于3期临床，益方生物的D-2570是其中之一。这个赛道的美妙之处在于，它足够新，竞品不多，且口服剂型天然比生物制剂更受患者欢迎。银屑病患者需要长期用药，能口服、副作用小，本身就是巨大的临床优势。


进度靠前的TYK2抑制剂，图源招股书


在乳腺癌的SERD赛道上，情况类似。全球已有4款口服1款注射液药物获批，中国也有3款进入3期临床。益方生物的D-0502要面对的，不仅是跨国药企的壁垒，还有恒瑞、先声等国内同行的速度竞赛。


已经商业化的格索雷塞所处的KRAS G12C赛道，竞争同样激烈。2025年全球市场当中，索托拉西布、阿达格拉西布已经占据主要份额，格索雷塞拿到3.5%的全球市占率，后续还要持续面对同类产品的竞争。


更现实的挑战来自商业化。益方的两款上市产品，贝福替尼和格索雷塞，都已经纳入国家医保目录。这带来了可及性，也带来了定价压力。2025年收入的断崖式下跌，已经说明了这种商业模式有多依赖合作伙伴的付款节奏。


目前，D-2570在国内银屑病注册性3期、头对头3期正在推进。还同步开展了溃疡性结肠炎UC、系统性红斑狼疮SLE、银屑病关节炎PsA、非节段型白癜风的多项2期临床。未来几年，益方两条核心管线都将迎来重要节点。


核心管线关键节点，据招股书数据制图


海外临床方面，D-2570已经在美国启动单药治疗中重度斑块状银屑病的2期临床。另一核心管线D-0502海外仅完成美国1期临床，此后尚未启动新的海外试验。


结合企业这几年的财务数据，或许能看得更加清楚。


2024年，公司营收1.69亿元。到了2025年，这个数字骤降至0.37亿元。不是因为卖不动药，而是因为那一年没有收到合作伙伴的里程碑付款。2026年H1，商业化特许权使用费入账后，收入回升到0.53亿元。


只是这远远不够覆盖研发开支。2024年研发支出3.843亿元，2025年为3.258亿元。


各管线研发投入情况，据招股书、财报数据制图


到了2026年H1，研发投入达到1.847亿元，其中D-2570资金占比达86.5%，是益方现阶段的首要优先级管线，另一核心管线D-0502本期投入仅占7.6%。有限资源明显向D-2570倾斜，其余管线推进节奏显著放缓。


赛道竞争激烈，临床推进速度本身就是竞争的一部分，无论自主推进海外临床，还是寻找BD合作伙伴对外授权，都需要投入大量资金维持研发节奏。招股书披露的募资用途，也是指向此处。谋求A+H两地上市，正是益方走过下一阶段的自然选择。

title: 打造京津冀协同新基建，一场大赛如何跑通“价值兑现”路径？
summary: 8月15日，2026京津冀创新医学转化与产业促进大赛完成全部复赛，15场复赛密集铺开，266个项目登场。大赛累计征集612个项目，较2025年增长51%，涵盖多医学创新赛道。大赛定位打造“京津冀区域协同新基建”，每场复赛线下路演配套多维赋能活动，用“技术+临床+产业”五维标尺，将概念落地为生态。数据显示，验证与中试阶段项目占总报名数67%，大赛通过“实地考察+多维赋能”提供关键跳板。复赛直接设在医...
full_content:
8月15日，2026京津冀创新医学转化与产业促进大赛完成全部复赛。15场复赛（含12场专业赛道及3场津冀区域专场）在约50天内密集铺开，266个入围项目悉数登场。

 

2026年京津冀创新医学转化与产业促进大赛以“创聚京津冀·医企促健康”为主题，由中共北京市委统战部､京津冀协同发展联合工作办公室指导，农工党北京市委､北京市工商联､通州区政府联合主办｡

 

自4月2日报名正式启动，本届大赛累计征集612个项目，较2025年增长51%，项目来自全国及美、日境外地区，其中京津冀占比超过半数，涵盖AI医疗、创新药、中医药、儿童医学、脑机接口等医学创新赛道。

 

行至第三届，大赛的定位愈发清晰：致力于打造“京津冀区域协同新基建”，打破地域与行业的隐形壁垒，切实回应创业团队对资源要素的渴求，架构起多方资源互通、供需高效交互的基建平台。值得关注的是，本届每场复赛线下路演都配套了实地参访、政策宣讲、产业推介、平台对接、知识产权金融分享等多维赋能活动。

 

当大多数赛事还在比拼PPT时，京津冀创新医学转化与产业促进大赛用“技术+临床+产业”的五维标尺，将“区域医学转化新基建”从概念落地为生态——让临床创新成果不再沉睡，让创业转化与价值兑现高效循环的生态圈。


 


“新基建”的赋能重心，精准匹配了参赛项目的阶段特征。

 

数据显示，本届大赛覆盖从初创孵化到产业化落地的全培育周期，其中验证与中试阶段项目达410个，占总报名数的67%。这意味着，超三分之二的项目已跨越早期研发“死亡谷”，进入临床验证与工艺放大的关键攻坚期。

 

针对这一需求，大赛通过“实地考察+多维赋能”，提供了从实验室走向临床检验的关键跳板，将“新基建”落在实处。

 

复赛直接设在医院里，让创业团队与临床医生面对面。7月24日，心血管临床创新专业赛道复赛走进安贞医院通州院区；7月30日，神经系统与脑机接口专业赛道复赛来到北京天坛医院脑机接口临床与转化病房；8月5日，消化系统与消化健康专业赛道复赛在北京友谊医院通州院区举行。参会专家、参赛团队探访临床转化一线，近距离观摩临床落地应用场景，实现科创团队与临床转化平台深度对接。

 

四大专业赛道为2026年大赛首次新增，专设独立奖项，由四大国家级医学中心——国家儿童医学中心、消化系统疾病国家临床医学研究中心、心血管系统疾病国家临床医学研究中心、国家神经系统疾病医学中心联动脑机接口转化研究中心直接牵头，为医学创新提供了一套临床落地的国家级权威框架——好项目直接可以对接到合适的临床验证平台。

 

复赛也走进国家级大科学装置、产业链工厂。6月25日首场复赛，参赛团队就来到了怀柔科学城，集体探访北京大学多模态跨尺度生物医学成像中心、怀柔科学城创新馆、春风药业北京中药制剂CDMO共性技术中心，近距离接触国家级大科学装置与产业化服务体系。大赛将硬核科研设施与成熟生产平台直接导入赛程，加速对接技术攻关工具箱和中试落地试验田，实现了从“赛场”到“市场”的无缝衔接。

 


对于医学创新项目而言，从一张专利证书到一款上市产品，横亘着资金缺口、工艺开发、商业合规三座大山，导致大量源自病房的“金点子”止步于实验室。本届大赛有246个项目来自全国各级医院及临床机构主体，占比40%，带来了大量源自临床一线的创新需求与成果。

 

如何将这些“金点子”深度嵌入产业链？大赛给出的答案是：推动“医工融合”嵌合路径，构建“产业+金融+资本+平台”的全要素支撑矩阵。

 

针对“缺设备、缺标准、缺渠道”的转化痛点，悦康药业向AI赛道团队推介全链条数字化生产基地，让算法模型有了验证落地的实体场景；春风药业亮出全国首家中药制剂CDMO平台，覆盖从药学研发到中试生产的全周期服务；灵赋生物联合北京市心肺血管疾病研究所共建的实验动物共性技术服务平台，提供特色模式动物与高标准疾病模型构建服务。

 

与此同时，大赛具备产业连接器属性，吸引了诺思格医药、三元基因、福元医药、中科搏锐、赛赋医药、奥托博克、赛翌恒威等产业链上下游的关键角色，参与到对口复赛中。这些企业不以“参赛者”或单纯“买家”身份出现，而是作为“合伙人”寻找优质项目。产业链真实需求的精准匹配，使得大赛现场成为一个高效的要素流转市场。


针对创新项目“轻资产、长周期、难抵押”导致的融资顽疾，民生银行北京分行现场发布了“4+2+16”科创网络布局，推出分层信贷产品，配套跨境、知识产权、产业生态、数字化运营等综合增值服务，构建一套针对创业团队全生命周期的精准支持系统。


首发展创投、中信医疗基金、中关村协同创新基金、海纳有容私募基金、蓝驰创投、纳通集团产业基金等投资机构深度嵌入复赛评审环节。这些具备深厚产业背景的资本方，将大赛视为优质项目源的“前哨站”，在概念验证与成果转化期即建立深度链接。

 

本届大赛首次双向联动北京市国际创新创业标杆平台HICOOL，参赛项目将共享HICOOL的国际资本与产业资源，接入其多层级、多元化的国际创业生态，获得顶级投资人、知名导师及头部企业家的全程辅导。

 


三年大赛不断升级的背后，“赛事即孵化”正在成为医学创新转化的新趋势——政府“搭台子”，强化京津冀“创新转化共同体”联动优势，建成高校找转化出口、资本找项目、医生找工程化伙伴与资金的基建平台。

 

北京发挥临床与策源高地优势。农工党北京市委充分发挥其联系医药卫生界高中级知识分子的界别优势，链接高校科研与临床一线资源，联动北京中医药大学、天津医科大学等顶尖院校，将实验室里的原始创新引入转化赛道。北京市工商联立足京津冀生物医药产业优势，重点发挥“京津冀企业家联盟”的平台枢纽作用，紧密携手津冀工商联，强化三地协同联动，畅通产业资源对接渠道。

 

作为京津冀医学转化的物理承载中枢，北京城市副中心通州区政府加速“一区一带”产业布局落地：政策端，解读《关于北京城市副中心支持医药健康产业发展的若干措施》，叠加“运河英才”计划，为项目落地提供从资金到人才的全周期保障。空间端，中关村（通州）创新医学转化产业园已构建起“验证－孵化－加速”的成熟生态，不仅引入了灵赋生物等共性技术平台，更打造了通州区首家市级创新医疗孵化器。周边集聚的北京大学人民医院、甘李药业等机构，形成了“临床－研发－生产”的闭环生态。

 

天津彰显产业与空间腹地优势。7月14日天津工商联专场，由天津市工商业联合会、天津医科大学、农工党天津市委共同主办，承接大赛“评审+资源”双重优势，深化创新协同。武清区投资促进局重点推介了“智能科技、生物医药双高引领”的6条重点产业链。产业+空间的双重供给，将填补创新项目“中试难、生产难”的空白。

 

河北立足转化与制造基地优势。8月7日石家庄专场，河北省工商联结合河北“京津研发、河北转化”定位，介绍河北医药产业体系、中医药资源、龙头企业集聚优势与营商环境，诚邀优质项目落地。以岭医药研究院等本土龙头的参与，标志着河北不再只是“承接方”，而是以产业体系为京津冀创新提供全链条支撑。

 

深层样本意义在于，大赛试图回答一个行业共性难题：当创新不再是单点突破，而是系统发展、区域协同的“基础设施”究竟该怎么建？从北京副中心的政策空间，到天津武清的产业链配套，再到河北石家庄的制造腹地，三地政府不再单打独斗，而是通过一套赛事机制实现了资源要素的跨区域自由流动。

 

坚持“以终为始”，我们需将“价值兑现”前置为医学创新转化的核心标尺。大赛正是这一理念的践行者：它不再仅是赛事，而是作为“区域协同新基建”的关键一环，致力于成为打通创新链与产业链的精准链接器。

 

当创新不再是孤岛，转化不再靠运气，中国医疗创新的“新基建”才算真正落成。总决赛入围名单将在“京津冀创新医学转化产业促进大赛”公众号发布，敬请关注。


9月，2026年京津冀创新医学转化与产业促进大赛总决赛，我们不见不散！（请扫码报名）

title: 用“数字基座”破解银发难题，东软睿新城市级智慧康养服务平台，从沈阳跑向全国
summary: 东软睿新2026年上半年财报显示，其养老科技与服务业务营收同比增长57.4%，成为集团增长最迅猛板块。这一亮眼数据背后，标志着其智慧康养服务从沈阳试点探索正式迈向全国规模化复制新阶段。面对我国超3.2亿老龄群体带来的服务分散、供需匹配难及监管缺失等痛点，传统单点系统形成的信息孤岛已无法满足需求。随着AI、大数据等技术成熟及政策对“15分钟养老服务圈”的推动，构建统筹机构、社区、居家等多业态的城市级...
full_content:
日前，东软睿新对外披露了2026年上半年财报。财报显示，东软睿新实现收入9.61亿元，期内利润达到2.07亿元。

 

图源：东软睿新2026H1财报


其中，一组数据表现尤为抢眼——东软睿新养老科技与服务业务板块，营收达620.4万元，同比增长57.4%。它也是东软睿新集团业务增长最为迅猛的板块。

 

虽然，620.4万元的收入绝对额较小，但业务快速增长背后的信息仍值得深挖——一方面，随着东软睿新沈阳“盛情康养”平台上线满一年，其运营数据已经跑通；另一方面，以此为起点，东软睿新的智慧康养服务正从试点探索走向规模化复制的新阶段。



让我们先回到当前面临的问题上来——

根据国家统计局数据，2025年年末我国有着超3.2亿老龄群体。庞大的老龄群体，面临的从来不单是服务欠缺的问题，更是服务相对分散、供需匹配难且服务缺乏有效监管等问题。

这导致机构往往各自为战，每家养老院都有着自己的管理系统和服务标准；社区服务碎片化，助餐、助浴、上门护理分属不同主体，数据互不流通；家庭寻找服务时，由于欠缺服务评价闭环，老人和子女很难找到优质服务；而政府层面，难以实现精准补贴发放、难以第一时间应对突发状况……

城市需要的无疑是一套可以更好地统筹覆盖机构及社区养老、居家及助餐服务、适老化产品、健康医疗、老年教育等多元业态的养老数字基座。

而在过去数十年的发展中，养老信息化领域提供了大量单点系统——机构管理系统、民政监管系统、社区台账系统等等。但是，系统之间数据并不互通，信息孤岛的存在导致资源无法得到有效匹配。

近年来，政策端持续加码，民政部“十四五”期间明确提出要在城市建立15分钟养老服务圈、在农村建立县乡村三级养老服务网络。“15分钟养老服务圈”的本质显然并非是如同过去一般建立机构、堆加系统，而是建立起跨机构、跨区域的数字化底座，高效调配资源。

技术端的利好支撑着其成为现实。随着人工智能、大数据、物联网发展进一步成熟，过往数据协同面临的成本高、响应慢等难题得到有效解决，已经可以支撑城市级实时数据调度，为数字基座的打造创造了条件。

在此背景下，“数字基座”就从“要不要建”变成了“如何建好”的问题。而谁能建好养老“数字基座”，也意味着谁掌握了养老产业的“基础设施入口”。

 


2025年6月，东软睿新推出“盛情康养”沈阳基本养老服务综合平台，为沈阳构建起城市级智慧养老“数字基座”。到如今，时间刚好过去一年。

与大众理解的仅仅是提供信息挂网让用户选择不同，它构建起的是一套覆盖政府、机构、社区、家庭的服务体系——


对政府，平台提供实时监管、数据分析和决策支持。民政部门可精准掌握辖区内养老服务的供需状况，哪些区域机构床位紧张、哪些社区助餐点覆盖不足、补贴发放是否精准到人，都可以了解得清清楚楚。


对机构，配合“睿新通”医养护一体化智慧养老系统和智能物联设备，机构可实现服务标准化、流程透明化、运营智能化——从老人入住评估到护理记录，从物资管理到风险预警，都可在数字化轨道上运行。


对社区，平台链接网格员、家庭医生、志愿者等多方力量，把服务送到老人家门口。而这恰好对应了民政部推行的“15分钟养老服务圈”，解决了“服务最后一公里”难题。

对家庭，老人和子女在手机端即可便捷地实现服务查找、下单预约、评价反馈。无论是上门护理，还是助餐助浴、康复护理，均可实现一键触达。


有别于其他平台，东软睿新打造养老“数字基座”想得更为透彻，其背后始终贯彻着“教医养融合”战略。

东软睿新CEO温涛表示，“一个人从年轻到年老，需要的是连续地健康管理，而不是‘教育归教育、医疗归医疗、养老归养老’的碎片化服务。”东软睿新希望通过“教医养”融合，打通健康人才培养、疾病诊疗、养老照护、疗愈康养全链条，最终服务一个人的全生命周期健康管理。

 

在大的生态闭环中，东软睿新进一步完善了针对老龄群体的生态闭环。其中，“教”是底座。在“养老始于防老，教育驱动养老”的理念贯彻下，东软睿新开设了老年大学“东软凤凰学院”。基于打造特色“LIFECARES-乐、养、医、学、为”老年教育模式，目前，东软凤凰学院已构建“三所大学分校+8家康旅分院”，构建起“AI与艺术创作+健康与康复+心灵康旅”的特色内容，帮助长者在数字化时代重构人生、收获健康。截至6月底，东软睿新三所大学凤凰学院仅线下付费课程的学员就有近2000人次。


“医”是支撑。东软睿新旗下睿康心血管病医院、睿康口腔医院已进入稳定运营期，大连睿康康复医院也在稳步推进中。2026年上半年，睿康心血管病医院作为三级心血管病专科医院，是辽宁地区唯一指定承接国家心血管高危筛查项目的定点机构。并且，其“健康生活方式”科室打通“预防-诊疗-康复”闭环，有效实现了患者的生活方式医学干预；睿康口腔医院则加速推动数字化诊疗，2026年上半年完成门诊接待近1.2万人次。睿康之家颐养院入住率持续高达100%。

 

“养”是落地。城市级数字“养老基座”，则作为资源连接器，把教育、医疗、养老服务整合到一个入口。依托东软睿新的“教助医、教助养，医转养、医辅教，养托医、养辅教”的多业态深度协同，实现资源的深度链接。

也是得益于这一独特优势，上线一年，沈阳“盛情康养”平台捷报频频——


-注册用户突破6万人

-累计保障超100万人次的长者公共服务

-汇聚生态合作伙伴1200余家

-上线适老化产品与服务超6000项，覆盖医护上门、助餐助浴、康复护理等30余类核心场景

-平台交易额逾1500万元


行业层面，“盛情康养”作为国家试点标杆案例，入选国际数据公司（IDC）发布的《中国AI+养老产业格局及厂商能力分析，2026》。

值得注意的是，平台GMV超过1500万元，这也说明平台流水已经开始起量。虽然公司从中确认的收入比例仍较小，但这也意味着公司商业化变现路径已经初步跑通，且远未到天花板。


随着单点模式逐步验证完成，接下来的问题是：这一模式能否有效复制？



答案是：可以。

截至目前，东软睿新已有10个城市级智慧康养平台上线，平台模式成功拓展到23个城市。预计到2026年底，将在全国30个城市完成布局。

就在8月21日，随着“康百汇”平台上线，东软睿新在粤港澳大湾区也落下关键一子。

但从沈阳到全国，从来不是简单地把一个系统搬到另一个城市。东软睿新想要输出的绝非一个平台，而是一套城市级智慧康养服务体系——融合人工智能、大数据、物联网，集管理、运营、服务三位一体，为政府提供决策支持，为机构降本增效，为老年人提供教医养一站式服务。

在这个过程中，困难显而易见——系统可以标准化，但运营服务本身很难标准化。这也是部分城市级养老平台折戟的核心原因之一——部分平台在扩张后出现“签约很多、落地很少、用的人更少”的局面。

东软睿新无疑意识到了服务的重要性。东软睿新集团副总裁、东软睿新健康科技公司总裁王星辉提出过三个底线：“数据安全不越界、服务品质不妥协、长者权益不让步。”它们指向的是在规模化扩张中强调坚守服务质量的红线。

而东软睿新的解法，还是需要回到“教医养”融合中去。



温涛明确指出，“我们的三所大学是人才供给端、科研端和教育科技输出端；医院是临床数据端、医疗服务端和专业标准端；医养院和康养设施是场景端、服务端和模式验证端。三者融合之后，人才有地方实践，临床有数据沉淀，养老有专业支撑，疗愈有场景验证。这不是简单的1加1加1等于3，而是产生了‘乘数效应’，1加1加1远大于3。”


例如，睿康之家颐养院面向三所大学“老年保健与管理”专业学生开设“睿康颐智实验班”，将五级养老机构的运营标准、服务流程、岗位能力模型直接转化为大学课程内容，让一线管理者走上讲台，把场景搬进课堂，实现“教医养”生态的联动。这也是东软睿新区别于其他公司之处，SaaS企业可以输出系统，但是输出不了具备实战经验的人才；而东软睿新则可以通过自身教育禀赋，批量化输出行业所需各类人才与标准。


招股书显示，作为东软睿新核心业务的学历高等教育服务，在上半年实现营收7.96亿元。而为了更好地服务“教医养”一体化战略，东软睿新还在加大HT类学科专业建设，开设诸如智能医学工程、医学信息工程、医学影像技术、健康服务与管理、老年保健与管理等专业。而教育科技与服务方面，东软睿新通过对人工智能等技术的融合应用，不断对外输出教育资源；东软睿新线上教育平台“东软教育在线”累计注册用户更是达到了236.1万人，不断夯实着健康人才的培养。


根据头豹研究院，预计到2035年，中国银发经济规模将达到30万亿元。面向万亿级银发经济市场，城市级智慧康养平台无疑是基础设施级机会。而目前，东软睿新相关业务刚刚起步，增长空间还未完全打开。但是随着东软睿新完成10城上线、23城拓展的势头来看，这条增长曲线已经开始抬头。

 


当“养老”移至城市级平台，产业游戏规则无疑也将发生变化——

对政府而言，有望从过往依赖“经验管理”走向“数据驱动决策”。随着平台实时呈现供需热力图，政府可以实现补贴精准到服务对象发放，面对应急情况也可实现一键调度响应。


对机构而言，有望从过往“单打独斗”进入到“生态赋能”阶段。大量机构过往凭借自身经验摸索管理、经营、培训，耗时漫长且效率不高。而随着接入平台，企业可以链接平台最优秀的资源，实现自身能力的提升，将更多精力专注于服务本身。


对服务商而言，有望从“小散乱”走向“标准化”。平台本身设定服务标准和评价体系，优质服务商有望获得更多资源与订单，它将促成服务商提升自己的服务质量与标准。


对老人和家庭而言，有望从“找不到优质服务资源”转而实现“服务一键触达”，通过一个入口即解决用户教育、医疗、康养多元需求，且服务可追溯、可评价。


在财报中，东软睿新表示，将加快城市级智慧养老平台全国布局，系统构建“一平台两中心”标准化的业态体系，线上聚焦平台交易与运营能力提升，线下建设人才培训与老年教育中心，通过打造标准化、可复制的运营模式，使每个平台成为一座城市养老服务体系运转的“数字底座”，并覆盖更多城市，成为中国银发经济高质量发展的“助推器”。此外，其计划结合“AI+大数据+云计算+物联网+移动互联”等技术，打造智慧康养解决方案，通过智能产品和信息系统平台，以智慧化、数字化、科技化驱动养老产业转型升级。

当前，客观来看，城市级智慧养老平台仍处于发展早期，竞争格局仍然未定。大量行业从业者正在投身其中。东软睿新的差异化优势在于其“教医养”融合业态。未来，随着更多具备不同资源禀赋的企业投身其中，我们也期待看到更多从业者走出创新路径，为中国银发难题提供智慧康养解决方案。

title: 诚邀医疗机构、HIT厂商参与《医疗机构信息技术创新实施指南》问卷调研
full_content:
来源：北京信创工委会

北京信息化协会信息技术应用创新工作委员会（简称“北京信创工委会”）联合中国软件评测中心、北京协和医院、解放军总医院、HIT专家网正在组织编制 《医疗机构信息技术创新实施指南》（以下简称《指南》）。

《指南》立足医疗卫生行业信创建设实际，围绕医疗机构规划设计、基础设施、基础软件、业务系统改造、实施路径、风险管控及典型实践等内容进行系统研究，旨在形成具有行业指导性和实际可操作性的实施参考。

为做好《指南》相关内容编制工作，进一步从产业供给、产品适配和项目实施等角度掌握医疗机构信创建设实际情况，分析当前医疗信创产品成熟度、适配能力、项目落地情况及产业协同过程中存在的共性问题，北京信创工委会拟于2026年8月26日至8月30日分别组织开展医疗机构与医疗信息化厂商专题调研。诚邀相关机构结合实际建设情况参与本次调研。

2026年8月26日至8月30日。
